text: The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing a single C–C bond, which gives a planar, rigid aromatic core. Attached to one of the alpha positions (the carbon adjacent to the ring-fusion atom) is an isocyanate group, –N=C=O, in which a nitrogen is bonded to a carbon that is double-bonded to oxygen. This substitution pattern places the functional group off-center and breaks any symmetry of the naphthalene framework, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar aromatic system. The isocyanate carbon is electrophilic and the molecule contains only a few heteroatoms: it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen and nitrogen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a fused polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built on a fluorene-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a five-membered ring that contains a single sp3 CH2 carbon. Its three rings are fused together, forming a rigid, nearly planar framework with no rotatable bonds in the core. A single methyl group sits on one of the outer benzene rings, adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, which breaks the symmetry of the otherwise symmetric skeleton. The molecule contains no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold, with no ring fusion and no heteroatoms within the ring. A single quaternary carbon sits on the ring and carries both a methyl group and a carboxylic acid group, so the substitution pattern is geminal (1,1-disubstituted). The carboxyl group, which is a C=O bearing an OH, is the only functional group present. Because the ring is fully saturated, the scaffold is conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair-type conformations, though the quaternary center restricts that flexibility somewhat. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane because of the asymmetric geminal substitution. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the OH) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens).

The molecule is built from two saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycles joined directly by a single carbon-nitrogen bond. One ring is an N-methylpiperazine, in which a methyl group sits on one ring nitrogen and the opposite nitrogen forms the linkage to the second ring. The second ring is a piperidine, a fully saturated six-membered ring containing one secondary amine nitrogen, and it is attached through the carbon at its position 4, so the two rings are symmetrically disposed about the bond. Neither ring is fused or aromatic, and the overall framework is flexible, since both rings can adopt chair conformations and rotate about the connecting bond. The molecule contains two tertiary amine nitrogens and one secondary amine nitrogen, all of which can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while only the secondary amine N–H provides a hydrogen-bond donor site.

This molecule is a small, acyclic aliphatic chain with no ring systems, so its scaffold is a flexible open-chain skeleton built from a two-carbon ethyl group, an ether oxygen, and a three-carbon unit. The main functional groups are a single ether linkage (C–O–C) and a secondary alcohol, with the hydroxyl carried on a branched carbon that also bears a methyl substituent. Because the chain contains multiple freely rotating single bonds and no rigid elements, the molecule is conformationally flexible. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry, since the branching point places the methyl group and the ether chain on different substitution patterns.

The molecule is a straight-chain alkyl halide built on a six-carbon saturated backbone, with no rings, no fused systems, and no branching. A single chlorine atom is attached to one terminal carbon, so the substitution pattern is simply monosubstitution at the end of the chain. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single mirror-equivalent orientation at each end, giving it an essentially symmetry-free, flexible structure that can adopt many conformations through rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds. Its only polar feature is the carbon-chlorine bond, and it lacks any hydrogen-bond donor; the chlorine can act only as a weak acceptor.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl halide: a seventeen-carbon saturated chain with no rings, no branching, and no double bonds. The chain terminates at one end in a chlorine atom, which is the only functional group present, and the other end is a methyl group. Because every carbon is sp3-hybridized and the chain has no ring constraints, the backbone is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations through rotation about its C–C single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry apart from the approximate mirror-like arrangement of its linear carbon framework, and it lacks any stereocenters. The chlorine atom can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused along a shared edge to form a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic system. A hydroxyl group sits on one carbon of the fused system, and a bromine atom is attached to the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents are ortho to each other on the same ring. The pattern is asymmetric, since the substituents occupy only one of the two rings and break any mirror symmetry the bare naphthalene core would have. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond through its oxygen and hydrogen, while the bromine contributes a polarizable halogen but no hydrogen-bonding ability. Because the aromatic framework is fully planar and carries no rotatable bonds, the overall structure is conformationally rigid.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying four substituents: two methoxy groups (–OCH3) and one bromine atom. Its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered carbon ring with no ring fusion, and the bromine sits between the two methoxy groups on adjacent-to-each-other positions, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern in which the bromine and one methoxy are ortho to each other. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the three substituents occupy unequal positions around the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two methoxy groups retain some rotational freedom about their C–O bonds. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, but the two ether oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused rings. It carries three halogen substituents: two chlorine atoms and one bromine atom. The chlorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, and the bromine sits on a carbon separated from one chlorine by a single ring carbon, giving a 1,2,3-trihalogenated pattern with the substituents on consecutive positions. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single mirror plane through the ring, so its symmetry is limited. The ring is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds beyond the C–halogen bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and only weak, halogen-based acceptor character.

This molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated-except-one-alkene carboxylic acid built on a straight aliphatic chain with no rings or fused ring systems. The terminal end carries a vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond at the very end of the chain), while the other end bears a carboxylic acid functional group, giving it two distinct reactive termini. Because the chain is linear and has no branching or substitution, the molecule has no stereocenters and possesses no meaningful internal symmetry. Its long, flexible methylene backbone allows many conformations, so it is conformationally mobile rather than rigid. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond from its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the rest of the structure contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain aliphatic diamine: a linear eight-carbon saturated backbone with an amino group bonded to each terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom-containing substituents beyond the two primary amine groups, which are the only functional groups present. The molecule is symmetric, since the two amino groups sit at opposite ends of an identical chain, and it is highly flexible because rotation about the many single C–C bonds gives it a wide range of conformations. Each primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor, through its N–H bonds, and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, through the nitrogen lone pair.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms and one nitro group, giving a simple aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The nitro group, drawn as a charge-separated N+ with an O- and an oxygen double bond, is attached to one ring carbon, and the two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, with one of them ortho to the nitro group and the other meta to it. This 1,2,4-type substitution pattern leaves the ring with no internal symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the nitro group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The nitro oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, the fluorines are weak acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small, fully unsaturated-to-partly-saturated six-membered heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, so it belongs to the pyridazinone family. The ring carries a ketone-type carbonyl on one side and a carboxylic acid group attached directly to a ring carbon that is double-bonded to a nitrogen, giving a C=N hydrazone-like linkage. The remaining two ring carbons are saturated methylene units, so the ring is only partly flattened and retains some conformational flexibility. The scaffold is non-symmetric, because the carbonyl and carboxylic acid sit on different parts of the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (its OH) and acceptor (its carbonyl oxygen), while the ring carbonyl oxygen and the imine-type nitrogen serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to adjacent carbons at positions 1, 2, and 3 of the ring, with the two outer methoxy groups flanking the central one, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstitution pattern. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane passing through the central methoxy group and the ring carbons it bears, so its two outer substituents are related by symmetry. Each ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the three methyl groups on the oxygens allow limited rotational flexibility.

This molecule is a linear trisiloxane, with a chain of three silicon atoms joined by two oxygen bridges (Si–O–Si–O–Si) and no rings. Each terminal silicon carries one methyl group and one hydrogen atom, while the central silicon bears two methyl groups, giving a symmetric arrangement about the middle silicon. The backbone is flexible, since the Si–O–Si linkages allow considerable rotation, so the molecule can adopt many conformations. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, because it has no N–H or O–H groups, and its two oxygen atoms are weak acceptors only, with no other functional groups present.

The molecule is built on a saturated cyclohexane ring, with no fused or bridged ring systems and no aromatic rings. A single quaternary carbon sits on the ring and carries two substituents: a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) and a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3). The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the trifluoromethyl group is a non-hydrogen-bonding, strongly electron-withdrawing substituent with three fluorine atoms that are weak acceptors at best. Because both substituents share the same ring carbon, the molecule has no stereocenter and lacks a symmetry axis through the ring beyond local mirror-like features of the cyclohexane. The cyclohexane ring is conformationally flexible, able to interconvert between chair forms, though the bulky geminal substituents bias the ring toward particular orientations.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a nitro group and a piperazine ring. The six-membered aromatic ring is substituted at two positions that sit para to each other, with a nitro group (NO2, drawn as a charge-separated N+ and O-) on one side and a nitrogen of the piperazine on the other. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogens placed opposite each other, so one nitrogen is bonded to the aryl ring as a tertiary amine while the other is a secondary amine with an N-H. The arrangement is largely planar in the aromatic portion, while the piperazine ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens, and the secondary piperazine N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, with the other amine nitrogen also acting as an acceptor.

This molecule is a bicyclic camphor-derived sultam: a fused bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) framework carries a gem-dimethyl bridge on one carbon, and a five-membered cyclic sulfonamide (a sultam, containing an SO2 group bonded to nitrogen) is fused across the skeleton through a quaternary carbon. The sulfonyl group is the only heteroatom-bearing functional unit, and the sulfonamide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor while the two sulfonyl oxygens act as acceptors. The rigid, cage-like polycyclic core, with several stereocenters defined by its bridged geometry, leaves little conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the sultam ring is fused asymmetrically onto the bicyclic framework.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring that contains two nitrogen atoms. Attached at the 2-position of the imidazole (the carbon between the two nitrogens) is a phenyl ring bearing a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, so the substitution pattern is ortho. The benzimidazole nitrogen bearing the hydrogen is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other imidazole nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and the two aromatic systems are joined by a single bond that permits some rotation, though the ortho chlorine introduces steric hindrance that restricts it. Overall the structure is largely planar and rigid, with extended aromatic character.

The molecule is a 2-substituted propanoic acid in which the alpha carbon bears a methyl group and an ether oxygen linking to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle carrying one chlorine atom at the meta position relative to the ether oxygen, giving a 1,3-disubstitution pattern with no ring fusion. The principal functional group is a terminal carboxylic acid, which together with the aryl ether oxygen makes up the molecule's polar region. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen is an additional acceptor. The alpha stereocenter and rotatable single bonds give the chain moderate flexibility, while the aromatic ring remains planar and rigid. The molecule has no symmetry, since the substituents on the ring and the chain are distinct.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a 2-hydroxyethyl chain, meaning a two-carbon saturated linker ending in a primary alcohol group. The other is a benzyloxy group, an ether oxygen bridging the ring to a second, unsubstituted benzene ring through a single methylene carbon. The two aromatic rings are joined only through this flexible ether linkage, so the scaffold is non-fused and has rotatable bonds that allow conformational flexibility. The overall shape has no rotational symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the para axis, since the two ends differ. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two adjacent substituents at positions 1 and 2, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is an ethyl ester group, in which a carbonyl is bonded to the ring and linked through an oxygen to an ethyl chain. The other substituent is a boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups. The two hydroxyls on boron and the carbonyl oxygen of the ester each supply hydrogen-bond acceptor or donor capability, with the boronic acid providing two donors and two acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the ethyl chain adds conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane through the ring.

This molecule is a fully fluorinated four-carbon chain, a saturated acyclic scaffold with no rings. Both ends terminate in a primary alcohol group, each attached to a CH2 unit adjacent to a difluorinated carbon, so the structure is symmetric about its central C–C bond. The four central carbons each carry two fluorine atoms, making the backbone rigid in its substitution pattern but still free to rotate about its single bonds. The two terminal hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the carbon-fluorine bonds contribute polarity but are poor hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a primary amide, with its carbonyl carbon bonded to an NH2 group and to a single sp3 carbon that carries two phenyl rings. The central carbon is a tetrahedral stereocenter bearing one hydrogen, so the two benzene rings are not equivalent to each other in a fixed arrangement. Each phenyl ring is unsubstituted and fused to nothing, so the scaffold is a simple diarylmethyl unit attached to a carboxamide. The molecule has rotatable single bonds around the central carbon, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The amide NH2 group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds and no fused rings. Four of the six ring positions carry fluorine atoms, and the remaining ring position bears a bromomethyl group (a CH2 unit linked to a bromine atom). The fluorine atoms sit on adjacent and near-adjacent carbons, giving the ring a densely halogenated substitution pattern, while the bromomethyl group occupies the one position that is not fluorinated. The overall framework is planar and rigid, with only the C–CH2–Br bond providing rotational freedom. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the single bromomethyl substituent breaks the symmetry of the fluorinated ring. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no O–H or N–H groups, but the fluorine atoms and bromine can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. Three of the four remaining ring positions carry fluorine atoms, with the pair of adjacent fluorines flanking the nitrogen on one side and a further fluorine on the carbon opposite, leaving the ring heavily and asymmetrically halogenated. Attached to the fourth ring carbon is a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal carboxylic acid group, which is both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The ring nitrogen provides an additional weak hydrogen-bond acceptor site. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the saturated ethylene linker gives the side chain rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, with no fused ring systems: a methyl group, two adjacent fluorine atoms, and a carboxamide group. The carboxamide (–C(=O)NH2) is the principal functional group and carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the NH2) and an acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen). The two fluorines sit next to each other on the ring, flanking the carboxamide's neighboring position, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and no mirror or rotational symmetry is present. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amide bond gives the carboxamide some limited rotational freedom relative to the ring. The methyl group contributes only a small nonpolar bulk, and the fluorines add electron-withdrawing character to the ring.

The molecule is a branched saturated hydrocarbon built on a single open-chain skeleton with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms. Its backbone is a seven-carbon main chain carrying two methyl branches near one end, so the arrangement is an isomer of heptane with a compact, highly branched shape. There are no functional groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The branching pattern gives it limited overall symmetry, and because all bonds are single and rotatable, the chain is fairly flexible with many accessible conformations.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries one primary amine group (an NH2 attached directly to the ring) and three fluorine atoms at separate ring positions, giving a trisubstituted pattern in which two fluorines sit on adjacent carbons. The ring and its substituents are essentially planar and rigid, with the molecule lacking any significant rotational flexibility or overall symmetry. The amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on a single six-membered aromatic core, with no fused rings. Three of the ring positions carry methyl groups and one carries a nitrile (cyano) group, giving a trimethyl-substituted benzonitrile scaffold. The methyl groups sit at the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to the nitrile carbon, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the nitrile and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the three methyl groups rotate freely. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since it lacks N–H or O–H groups, but the nitrogen of the nitrile group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, are attached at alternating positions around the ring, and a primary amino group sits on the carbon between two of them. The arrangement gives the ring a 2,4,6-trisubstituted pattern, with the amine flanked on both sides by bulky tert-butyl groups. The tert-butyl groups are large, rigid, and nonpolar, so the molecule is conformationally restricted and is not symmetric about all axes because the amine breaks the threefold pattern. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the rest of the molecule offers no hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an isocyanate group (–N=C=O) and two methoxy groups (–OCH3). The ring is a single, unfused six-membered aromatic system, with the isocyanate attached at one position and a methoxy group immediately adjacent to it, while a second methoxy group sits on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,3-relationship between the two oxygen substituents. The arrangement lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The aromatic core is rigid, whereas the methoxy and isocyanate groups have some rotational freedom about their single bonds. The isocyanate nitrogen and oxygen atoms and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitrile (cyano, C≡N) group and two chlorine atoms, giving a planar, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion and no stereocenters. Reading around the ring from the nitrile-bearing carbon, the chlorines sit at positions that place one ortho to the nitrile and the other meta to it on the opposite side, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical and the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar framework. The nitrile nitrogen carries a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it contains no N-H or O-H bonds. The chlorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the overall framework is conformationally rigid apart from the nitrile group, which is linear and fixed in line with its attachment carbon.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two methyl groups and an aryloxyacetic acid side chain. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered benzenoid core with no ring fusion, and the two methyl groups sit at positions that leave the ring with an asymmetric substitution pattern. Attached to the ring through an ether oxygen is a flexible two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, which contributes a free rotational degree of freedom and makes the overall scaffold moderately flexible while the benzene core stays rigid and planar. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the ether oxygen acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, with a single six-membered aromatic ring and no fused or additional ring systems. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one carbon, and a methyl group (-CH3) sits on each of the two carbons flanking it, giving a 2,6-disubstituted pattern around the amine. The arrangement is symmetric about an axis running through the amino-bearing carbon and the carbon opposite it, and the ring is rigid while the small methyl and amino groups add little flexibility. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through the nitrogen lone pair.

This molecule is a single benzene ring bearing one methyl group and two nitro groups, so it is a dinitrotoluene-type scaffold with no ring fusion. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the methyl group is its only sp3-hybridized carbon. The two nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons flanking the methyl, with a substitution pattern that makes the molecule asymmetric, so it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. Each nitro group contributes oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since it bears no N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a primary amino group (-NH2) on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, and the other is a nitro group (-NO2) on the neighboring carbon. The two substituents are ortho to each other, creating a compact, planar, and rigid scaffold with no stereocenters and no meaningful conformational flexibility beyond the rotation of the groups. The amino group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds, while the ring nitrogen and the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents differ in character.

The molecule is built on a six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, a single-ring heteroaromatic scaffold containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship. It carries three substituents: an amino group on the carbon between the two ring nitrogens, a hydroxyl group on a ring carbon, and a trifluoromethyl group on a third ring carbon. The trifluoromethyl group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky, rotationally symmetric unit, while the ring itself is planar and rigid, with no appreciable conformational flexibility. The amino and hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogens together with the oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, giving the molecule substantial hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. Substituents are arranged around the ring: an amino group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, a fluorine atom occupies the neighboring carbon on the other side of the amine, and a chlorine atom is placed at the meta-like position relative to the ring nitrogen. There is no ring fusion, and the structure is essentially planar and rigid, with only the amino hydrogens free to orient. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and the amine and ring nitrogen act as acceptors, while the halogens contribute weak acceptor character. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic 1,3,4-thiadiazole ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms and one sulfur atom in an alternating arrangement. At one ring carbon sits an ethylthio group, a sulfur atom bonded to a two-carbon ethyl chain, and at the other ring carbon sits a primary amino group. The ring itself is planar and fully conjugated, so the scaffold is rigid, while the ethyl chain adds the only real conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the two substituents differ in size and character. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the ring nitrogens together with the amine's lone pair provide several acceptor sites.

This molecule is 2-aminobiphenyl, built from two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond between adjacent positions, giving a biphenyl scaffold. Each ring is a simple six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the two rings are free to twist about the central bond, so the framework is partly flexible. One ring carries a primary amino group (–NH2) on the carbon adjacent to the inter-ring bond, which is the sole substituent and gives the molecule no symmetry through that ring. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The unsubstituted phenyl ring contributes only aromatic π-character and no polar contact points.

This molecule is an ethanolamine-derived borinate ester built around a single tetracoordinate-free trivalent boron atom bearing two phenyl rings and an oxygen link. The boron is bonded to an oxygen that connects through a two-carbon ethylene chain to a terminal primary amine, giving a flexible aminoethyl ether arm. Both phenyl groups are unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion has no substitution pattern beyond attachment to boron, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis aside from the local near-planar arrangement around boron. The primary amine provides both hydrogen-bond donor (N–H) and acceptor (lone pair) capability, while the ether-type oxygen serves as a weak acceptor. Overall the structure is moderately flexible along the ethylene linker, with the two aromatic rings giving rigid planar segments.

This molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic compound built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing both oxygen and nitrogen, forming a benzoxazolone scaffold. The fused ring system is planar and fully conjugated, which makes the framework rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core. The five-membered ring carries a carbonyl group at the carbon between the two heteroatoms, forming a cyclic carbamate-like lactone-amide unit. The nitrogen bears a hydrogen atom, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any substituents on the benzene ring, so it has no substitution pattern beyond the fusion itself and retains a simple, approximately symmetric outline.

The molecule is built from a six-membered cyclohexanone ring, a saturated carbocycle bearing a ketone (C=O) group. At the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl, a single methylene linker connects the ring to a benzene ring, giving a benzyl-type substituent at the alpha position. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and aromatic, so the scaffold is a non-fused, two-ring system joined by a flexible CH2 bridge that allows rotation about its bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane, since the alpha-substituent makes the two sides of the ketone inequivalent. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is as an acceptor, through the carbonyl oxygen, because it has no N–H or O–H donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: two methoxy groups (–OCH3) and one bromine atom. The methoxy groups sit at positions 1 and 3 relative to each other (meta), and the bromine is on the carbon between them, so the bromine is flanked by the two ether oxygens at the ortho positions. The ether oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its small, fairly rigid aromatic core, with the methoxy groups able to rotate about their C–O bonds, gives it only modest conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary sulfonamide group (–SO2NH2) at one position, with a bromine atom on the carbon adjacent to the sulfonamide and two fluorine atoms on the ring, positioned meta to each other across the ring. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is a simple substituted benzene with no ring fusion. The sulfonamide contributes two oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds and an NH2 group that can donate them. The halogen substituents make the ring electron-poor and asymmetric, and the overall framework is rigid, with only the sulfonamide nitrogen–sulfur bond offering rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzoic acid derivative, meaning a single benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group directly attached to the ring. The benzene core is a flat, fully aromatic six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid, with only the carboxylic acid group able to rotate about its single bond to the ring. Two halogen substituents sit on the ring: a bromine atom ortho to the carboxylic acid and a fluorine atom para to it, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the halogens are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a bromine atom, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid sits at one ring position, with the bromine on the adjacent carbon, making the two groups ortho to each other. The nitro group sits meta to the carboxylic acid, on the far side of the ring from the bromine. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, so the core scaffold is rigid, though the carboxylic acid and nitro groups can rotate somewhat about their bonds to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry because its three substituents are all different. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the oxygens), while the nitro group offers acceptor sites through its oxygen atoms.

This molecule is a diaryl ether, with two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen atom that acts as a flexible hinge. One ring carries a nitro group para to the ether oxygen, making it strongly electron-poor, and a chlorine atom ortho to the ether linkage. The second ring bears two chlorine atoms, one ortho and one meta to the ether oxygen, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The two aromatic rings are not fused and can rotate about the C–O–C bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a short, acyclic amide built on a two-carbon backbone. A primary amide group (a carbonyl bonded to an NH2 group) sits at one end, and the carbon alpha to the carbonyl carries two fluorine atoms and one chlorine atom, making it a fully halogenated, tetrahedral center. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely flexible, with free rotation around the single bond between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl carbon. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three different halogen substituents on the alpha carbon are not equivalent in the two fluorines versus the one chlorine. The amide group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites from the NH2 and one hydrogen-bond acceptor site at the carbonyl oxygen, while the halogens are weak acceptors at best.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a sulfonyl chloride group (–SO2Cl) at one position, a chlorine atom on the adjacent carbon, and a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3) positioned para to the sulfonyl group. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring itself. The sulfonyl chloride and trifluoromethyl groups are strongly electron-withdrawing, and the arrangement lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy different positions. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, which consists of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and single-bonded to a chlorine atom. The aromatic ring is substituted at three positions: the sulfonyl chloride sits at one carbon, a chlorine atom occupies the adjacent ortho position, and a fluorine atom is located para to the sulfonyl group. The scaffold is a single unfused six-membered aromatic ring with no stereocenters, and the rigid planar ring limits conformational flexibility, though the sulfonyl chloride can rotate about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The halogen substituents contribute additional weak acceptor character through the fluorine and chlorine atoms.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern. One position carries an isocyanate group (-N=C=O), with the nitrogen attached directly to the ring. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the isocyanate, and a nitro group (-NO2) occupies the position para to the isocyanate. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the linear isocyanate adds little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry because the three substituents are different. The nitro group offers two oxygen atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the isocyanate oxygen and nitrogen can also accept hydrogen bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every N-H or O-H position is absent.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, and it is fully aromatic with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on that ring: a nitro group (an electron-withdrawing N-oxide-type group), an isothiocyanate group (-N=C=S, a linear, cumulated unit), and a chlorine atom positioned ortho to the isothiocyanate. Because the nitro group and isothiocyanate sit para to each other on the ring, the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the planar ring itself. The rigid aromatic core and the linear isothiocyanate make the structure largely planar and conformationally restricted, with only the nitro group's rotation being meaningfully free. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitro oxygens and the sulfur and nitrogen atoms of the isothiocyanate can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions: a nitro group, a chlorine atom, and a trifluoromethyl group. The nitro group sits at one position, the chlorine on the para-related carbon, and the trifluoromethyl group on the carbon between the chlorine and the ring's other side, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is flat and rigid, with only the nitro and trifluoromethyl groups able to rotate about their bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond its local planarity, since the three substituents are all different. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent because there are no N–H or O–H groups, while the nitro oxygens and the fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzenesulfonamide, with a benzene ring bearing a primary sulfonamide group (–SO2NH2) on one carbon and a chlorine atom on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The benzene ring is a single planar, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The sulfonamide sulfur is tetrahedral, bonded to two oxygen atoms and the nitrogen, and the chlorine is a simple aryl halide substituent. The sulfonamide NH2 group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is small and largely rigid, with only modest rotational freedom around the aryl–sulfur bond.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached to one carbon of the naphthalene ring adjacent to the ring-fusion position, and a diphenylphosphino group (–P(C6H5)2) sits on the neighboring carbon, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern. The phosphorus center carries two unsubstituted phenyl rings, which are attached to it through single bonds and can rotate, adding some conformational flexibility to the otherwise rigid aromatic core. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the two substituents differ in character and sit at non-equivalent positions. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the C=O and O), while the phosphorus lone pair offers an additional acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, which gives a flat, rigid aromatic core. A carboxylic acid group (-COOH) is attached to one ring position adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon, and an ethoxy group (-OCH2CH3) sits on the other ring, para-related through the fused system. The ethoxy tail adds some conformational flexibility, while the aromatic core remains planar and fixed. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, whereas the ether oxygen acts only as an acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituents sit at different positions on the bicyclic system.

The molecule is an acyclic hydrocarbon built on a straight-chain skeleton with no rings, heteroatoms, or functional groups. Its backbone is a six-carbon chain in which the second carbon bears a carbon-carbon double bond, making it a terminal alkene with the double bond at the end of the chain. The substituent pattern places an ethyl group on the sp2 carbon, so the overall framework is branched rather than linear. Because it contains only carbon and hydrogen and has no polar groups, it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor. The molecule is highly flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds, and it lacks any meaningful symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with substituents at four of its six positions. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits on one carbon, a fluorine atom on another, and a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) on an adjacent carbon, giving a contiguous ortho-disposed nitrile and fluorine pair. The aromatic core is planar and fully conjugated, while the methoxy group adds limited rotational flexibility around its ether bonds. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The nitrogen of the nitrile and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,3-pattern: a nitrile group, a fluorine atom, and a trifluoromethyl group, with the nitrile and trifluoromethyl groups in an ortho relationship and the fluorine sitting between the nitrile and the ring's remaining unsubstituted positions. The aromatic core is planar and fully rigid, with no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and the substitution pattern leaves the molecule without any rotational symmetry. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The trifluoromethyl group gives a compact, electron-withdrawing region that is bulkier than the fluorine, and only the trifluoromethyl bond can rotate freely.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents on adjacent and nearby carbons. A methyl group and a nitro group occupy ortho positions relative to each other, while a fluorine atom sits on the carbon next to the methyl-bearing carbon, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing functional group with two oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl and nitro substituents add limited rotational freedom. The arrangement lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different.

This molecule is a 2-arylpropanoic acid built on a biphenyl scaffold. A propanoic acid chain bears a methyl group at its alpha carbon, which is attached to one ring of a biphenyl unit, where two benzene rings are joined by a single bond. The first ring carries a fluorine atom adjacent to the biaryl linkage, while the other phenyl ring is unsubstituted. The carboxylic acid group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the fluorine acts as a weak acceptor. The alpha carbon is a stereocenter, and the biaryl bond allows moderate rotational flexibility, with the molecule lacking any internal symmetry.

This molecule is a quinoline-based boronic acid. Its core is a bicyclic aromatic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming a fully conjugated, planar, and rigid system with no rotatable bonds in the core. A boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached directly to the carbon at the 3-position of the pyridine-type ring, and a fluorine atom sits on the adjacent carbon at the 2-position, creating an ortho-fluoro substitution pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are not equivalent. The boronic acid contributes two hydrogen-bond donors through its hydroxyl groups and two oxygen acceptors, while the ring nitrogen provides an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor site.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons (an ortho-disubstituted pattern): one is a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O attached to the ring) and the other is an oxyacetic acid chain, where an ether oxygen links the ring to a CH2 that is part of a terminal carboxylic acid. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, and the overall framework is largely planar in the ring but flexible in the two-atom ether-acetic acid side chain. Hydrogen-bond capability is asymmetric: the carboxylic acid offers both a donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the C=O), the aldehyde carbonyl and ether oxygen act as acceptors only, and there is no internal symmetry because the two substituents differ.

This molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a three-carbon framework: a central quaternary carbon bearing a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, a carboxylic acid group, and a trifluoromethyl group. Because the central carbon is attached to four different substituents, it is a stereogenic center, so the molecule can exist as two mirror-image forms. There are no rings or ring fusions, and the structure is fairly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group and the hydroxyl group each supply hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the three fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group act only as weak acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry.

This molecule is a 1,4-benzodioxane scaffold, meaning a benzene ring fused to a six-membered 1,4-dioxane ring through two adjacent aromatic carbons bearing ether oxygens. The saturated dioxane ring carries a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) on the carbon next to one ring oxygen, so the stereocenter at that position makes the substitution pattern asymmetric. The benzo portion is unsubstituted, and the bicyclic framework is largely rigid while the dioxane ring can adopt a half-chair conformation. The two ring ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the primary alcohol provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl-type scaffold: a central benzene ring bearing two phenyl substituents, making it a terphenyl-type framework with three benzene rings linked in sequence. The first ring carries an iodine atom at one position adjacent to a phenyl group, so the substitution pattern is an ortho-disubstituted core on that ring. The two outer rings are unsubstituted phenyl groups, giving the molecule a largely aromatic, planar-leaning character with single C–C bonds allowing some rotation between rings. The structure contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors beyond the halogen, which is a weak acceptor at most. Overall it is a hydrophobic, all-carbon aromatic framework with only moderate flexibility around its inter-ring bonds.

The molecule is built around a single sp3 carbon that carries three phenyl rings and is also bonded to the N1 nitrogen of an imidazole ring. The imidazole is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogens separated by one carbon, and it bears an iodine atom on the carbon adjacent to the substituted nitrogen. The three phenyl groups are unsubstituted benzene rings, giving a propeller-like, bulky arrangement around the central carbon with no fused ring systems. The structure has only a rough threefold-type arrangement of the phenyl groups and lacks any stereocenter, so it is achiral. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene rings sharing a common edge to form a fused bicyclic aromatic system. A single methyl group is attached to one of the rings at a position adjacent to the fusion region, giving it a 2-methyl substitution pattern. The fused aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it contains no heteroatoms. Its symmetry is limited by the asymmetric methyl placement, so the two rings are not equivalent.

This molecule is a fused tricyclic heteroaromatic system built on a planar linear scaffold. A five-membered oxazole ring, bearing a methyl group at the carbon between the oxygen and nitrogen, is fused to a six-membered benzene-type ring, which is in turn fused to a second benzene ring, giving an angularly extended naphthalene-like core with an additional heteroatom-containing ring. The ring system is fully aromatic and rigid, with essentially no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group. The oxazole nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ring oxygen contributes weak acceptor character, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the approximate planarity of its fused ring framework.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to the ring carbon that sits immediately next to the nitrogen, which places the two groups in an ortho-like arrangement. The acid group contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional acceptor. The scaffold is small, planar, and rigid, with only rotation about the bond linking the acid group to the ring as a source of conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a methyl group, and the other is a four-carbon chain that begins with a ketone carbonyl attached directly to the ring, followed by two methylene units and terminating in a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the saturated linker gives the chain some conformational flexibility. Because the para pattern places the two groups on opposite sides of the ring, the molecule has an approximate elongated, linear shape with a mirror-plane symmetry through the ring axis. The carbonyl oxygen and the carboxylic acid oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the acidic hydroxyl of the carboxyl group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement, giving it a flat, rigid aromatic core with no ring fusion. One side bears a methylsulfonyl group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and attached to a methyl group. The opposite side carries a ketone linked to a four-carbon chain that terminates in a free carboxylic acid. Together, the sulfonyl oxygens and the carbonyl and carboxyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the carboxylic acid OH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The aliphatic chain between the ketone and the acid gives the molecule a degree of conformational flexibility, and the overall structure has no internal symmetry because the two ends differ.

The molecule is an acyclic-chain-substituted morpholine: a six-membered saturated ring containing one nitrogen and one oxygen atom, arranged as a 1,4-oxazinane scaffold. The ring nitrogen carries a three-carbon linker that terminates in a primary amine, so the substitution pattern is a single chain on the ring nitrogen with no other ring substituents. The ring is fully saturated and adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the propyl chain contributes further rotational freedom. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited, approximate local symmetry. Hydrogen-bond capability is provided by the terminal primary amine, which can act as both donor and acceptor, and by the ring oxygen and tertiary nitrogen, which act as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds, and carries four substituents. Three methoxy groups (oxygen atoms bonded to a methyl) are attached to adjacent ring positions and the remaining position bears an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen). The three methoxy groups cluster together on one side of the ring, while the aldehyde sits on the opposite side, giving an asymmetric but partly symmetric substitution pattern with a mirror-like axis through the aldehyde and the central methoxy group. The ring is rigid and planar, though the methoxy methyls can rotate around their single bonds. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups and the carbonyl oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups, placed at the 3, 4 and 5 positions relative to the carbonyl-bearing carbon, giving a symmetric 3,4,5-trimethoxy substitution pattern. Attached to the ring at position 1 is a carbohydrazide group, in which a carbonyl is bonded to an NH that carries a free NH2 terminus. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the three methoxy ether oxygens and the rotatable C–O bonds add some conformational flexibility at the periphery. The methoxy oxygens and the amide carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the two NH groups of the hydrazide act as hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule has a mirror-symmetric arrangement of its two outer methoxy groups about the ring's central axis.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to adjacent and nearby ring positions, while one methyl group (–CH3) sits on the ring at a position separated from the methoxy groups, giving a 1,2,3,5-type substitution pattern across the aromatic core. The arrangement is not symmetric, because the methyl group breaks any mirror relationship the three methoxy groups might otherwise share. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, though the methoxy groups can rotate about their C–O bonds. The ether oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type scaffold built from two fused six-membered rings sharing one edge, with an angular methyl group on the ring-fusion carbon. One ring contains a ketone and a conjugated carbon-carbon double bond, forming an α,β-unsaturated enone system, while the other ring bears a second ketone adjacent to the fusion point. The two carbonyl groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused ring framework is fairly rigid, with the sp2 carbons of the enone holding part of the structure flat, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ketones sit in different positions.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone: two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl group, giving a benzophenone-type scaffold. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries two adjacent chlorine atoms at the 3- and 4-positions relative to the carbonyl attachment, creating a 3,4-dichlorophenyl unit. Both rings are aromatic and planar, and the carbonyl carbon is sp2-hybridized, so the framework is fairly rigid with moderate rotational freedom around the two aryl-carbonyl bonds. The molecule lacks a plane or axis of full symmetry because of the asymmetric chlorine pattern on only one ring. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a phenylacetic acid, consisting of a single benzene ring bearing a carboxymethyl group (-CH2-COOH) attached to one carbon of the ring. Two fluorine atoms are attached to adjacent ring carbons at the 3- and 4-positions relative to the side chain, giving a 3,4-difluoro substitution pattern on an otherwise unfused aromatic scaffold. The ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2-COOH tail provides a degree of rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the substituted benzene ring.

This molecule is a phenylalanine derivative: an alpha-amino acid whose side chain is a benzyl group bearing two adjacent methoxy substituents on the aromatic ring, at the 3 and 4 positions relative to the CH2 attachment. The benzene ring is a single unfused six-membered aromatic system, with no additional fused rings. The alpha carbon is a stereocenter with a defined configuration and carries a primary amino group and a carboxylic acid group. The two ether oxygens and the amine and acid groups make the molecule a donor and acceptor of hydrogen bonds, while the aromatic core and linker add moderate flexibility around the rotatable side chain.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with an isocyanate group (–N=C=O) attached directly to one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at positions meta to the isocyanate and meta to each other, giving a 1,3,5-substitution pattern that yields a symmetric arrangement about an axis running through the isocyanate carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the linear N=C=O unit extends from it with little conformational freedom. The isocyanate carbon is strongly electrophilic and the oxygen and nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors. The chlorine substituents add electron-withdrawing character and bulk to the otherwise simple aromatic framework.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four substituents. An amino group sits on one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by chlorine atoms at the adjacent (ortho) positions, which gives a 2,6-dichloro-substituted aniline core. A primary sulfonamide group, consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to a nitrogen bearing two hydrogens, is attached at the position opposite the amino group. The aromatic scaffold is rigid and planar, with no additional rings or fused systems, and the substituents are arranged with a high degree of symmetry about the axis running through the amino and sulfonamide carbons. The amino and sulfonamide groups each provide hydrogen-bond donor sites through their N–H bonds, while the sulfonyl oxygens and the nitrogen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group (a primary amide, C(=O)NH2) on one carbon. Two fluorine atoms are attached to the ring at the meta positions relative to the amide, both on the same side of the ring, giving a 3,5-difluoro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the scaffold is essentially planar and rigid. The substitution pattern gives the molecule a mirror plane running through the amide carbon and the ring carbon para to it, so the two fluorine atoms are symmetry-equivalent. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donors (the NH2) and one acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an isoxazole ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom that are adjacent to each other. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring carbons, one on the carbon next to the nitrogen and one on the carbon adjacent to the oxygen, so the substitution is on the two carbons flanking the heteroatoms. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds and no stereocenters, and it has no fused rings. There are no polar functional groups beyond the ring heteroatoms: the nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, the oxygen contributes little to acceptance, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methyl groups sit on the ring at positions meta to each other, and a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a nitrile, C≡N) occupies the remaining position flanked by the two methyls, giving a 3,5-dimethyl substitution pattern. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the nitrile-bearing carbon and the ring's para carbon, so its substitution pattern is symmetric, though the CH2CN arm rotates freely. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a primary carboxamide group and two nitro groups. The carboxamide sits at one position on the aromatic ring, while the two nitro groups occupy the two positions meta to it and to each other, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern around a single fused-free six-membered ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the nitro and amide groups conjugated to the ring. The amide NH2 and C=O provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the nitro oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 (meta) pattern, giving it threefold-type symmetry about the ring. One substituent is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to chlorine, attached directly to the aromatic ring. The other two positions carry nitro groups, each a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formal positive and one negative charge. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the substituents are essentially coplanar with it. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its oxygen atoms of the carbonyl and nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a flavonol-type scaffold built from a fused benzopyranone (chromone) core, with a phenyl ring attached at the 2-position of the pyranone ring. The bicyclic chromone system is planar and fully aromatic-like, which makes the overall framework rigid, with the 2-phenyl ring able to rotate only slightly about its single bond to the core. Two hydroxyl groups are present: one on the 3-position of the pyranone ring and one on the benzo ring at the 7-position, while the ring carbonyl at the 4-position acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the two hydroxyls sit on different rings and the pendant phenyl is unsubstituted. Together, the hydroxyl groups and carbonyl oxygen give it multiple hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a bromine atom, and a fluorine atom. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring at one position, with the fluorine on the adjacent carbon (ortho to the acid) and the bromine on the carbon meta to the acid, making a 2-fluoro-3-bromo-benzoic acid substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single, planar, fully conjugated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the molecule as a whole is asymmetric because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (via its hydroxyl) and an acceptor (via its carbonyl oxygen), while the fluorine and bromine provide only weak acceptor character. Rotation about the bond linking the carboxyl group to the ring gives limited conformational flexibility, so the scaffold is fairly rigid overall.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with a nitrogen atom at one position in the ring. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a bromine atom is attached to the neighboring carbon, so the two substituents occupy adjacent positions on the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the free OH group and no ring fusion or additional rings. Because the substituents are not symmetric to one another, the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond its overall planar shape. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond and accept one, while the ring nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, giving the molecule several sites for intermolecular interaction.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a bromine atom, and a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linker bonded to a nitrile). The methoxy and bromine groups sit on adjacent carbons, while the cyanomethyl group is positioned para to the methoxy group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the nitrile carbon-nitrogen triple bond is linear, which makes the molecule fairly rigid, with only the single bonds of the methoxy and cyanomethyl groups allowing limited rotation. The ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent-to-each-other positions in a meta relationship: an acetyl group (a two-carbon ketone, CH3-C(=O)-) and a bromine atom. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with no additional ring fusion, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene. The ketone carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The bromine provides a heavy halogen substituent on the ring, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring and the acetyl group, which keeps it rather compact.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring: a dimethylamino group, where a nitrogen bears two methyl groups, and a bromine atom. They are placed meta to each other, with one carbon of the ring between them on one side, which gives the molecule an asymmetric substitution pattern. The nitrogen lone pair conjugates with the aromatic pi system, making the ring electron-rich, while the bromine adds a heavy halogen and polarizes the carbon to which it is attached. The structure is rigid and planar apart from the rotatable N–C and C–Br bonds and the methyl groups. The tertiary amine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but cannot donate a hydrogen bond, and the bromine is a weak acceptor only.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing four substituents. Going around the ring, there is an amino group (-NH2) on one carbon, flanked on one side by a methyl group and on the other by a neighboring methyl-substituted carbon, while a chlorine atom sits on the carbon across the ring from the amine's neighbor. Thus the ring carries two methyl groups, one chloro group, and one primary amine, all in a contiguous 1,2,3,4-substitution pattern with one ring position left as a C-H. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are all different. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl and amino groups have only limited rotational freedom. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair acceptor site, and the chlorine can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) at one position, with a chlorine atom and a fluorine atom on adjacent carbons located meta and ortho to the amide respectively, giving a 2-fluoro-3-chloro substitution pattern relative to the carboxamide. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the scaffold is essentially planar with the amide conjugated to the ring. The only rotatable bonds are the C–C bond linking the amide to the ring and the C–N bond of the amide, so the molecule is fairly rigid. The amide nitrogen carries two hydrogens that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the fluorine can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the two halogens occupy non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is an anilide built on a single benzene ring, with an acetamide group (CH3C(=O)NH-) attached directly to the ring carbon. The ring carries two further substituents on adjacent positions: a methyl group next to the amide-bearing carbon and a chlorine atom on the carbon beyond the methyl, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern in which the three ring carbons bearing substituents are contiguous. The benzene ring is planar and aromatic, while the amide linkage is conjugated with it and tends to hold the N-H and C=O in a near-planar arrangement, so the overall scaffold is fairly rigid with only the acetyl methyl and the ring methyl rotating freely. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three ring substituents are different. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the chlorine is a weak halogen acceptor and the ring itself offers aromatic surface for stacking interactions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four substituents in a 1,2,4-pattern: a methoxy group, a nitrile (cyano) group, and a chlorine atom, with the remaining positions carrying hydrogen. The methoxy group (an aryl ether, C–O–CH3) and the chlorine are adjacent on the ring, while the nitrile sits para to the methoxy group, giving an asymmetric, unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with only the methoxy methyl group providing rotational flexibility. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N–H or O–H groups. Its acceptors are the ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen, which can each accept a hydrogen bond.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, with no ring fusion present. Three substituents are attached around the ring: a methyl group, an amino group, and a chlorine atom, giving a trisubstituted aromatic pattern in which the methyl and chlorine sit adjacent to each other and the amino group is positioned para to the methyl group. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl group contributes only minimal flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site on the nitrogen lone pair, whereas the chlorine atom acts only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor and the aromatic ring offers no meaningful hydrogen-bonding capability of its own.

The molecule is a phenylacetic acid derivative: a benzene ring bearing a carboxymethyl group (–CH2–COOH) at one position. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit meta to each other relative to the side chain: a chlorine atom and a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3), giving a 1,3,5-trisubstituted benzene pattern with no internal symmetry beyond the mirror plane through the side chain and the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2 linker gives the acid group some rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, whereas the halogen and fluorine atoms serve only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a short, acyclic, saturated carbon chain of three carbons bearing an acyl chloride at one end and a chlorine atom at the other terminus. The carbonyl carbon is bonded to both a chlorine and a double-bonded oxygen, making it the most reactive site and a strong electrophile. The chain is flexible with free rotation about its single bonds, and the molecule has no rings and no internal symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor is the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is a substituted benzaldehyde built on a single benzene ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. The aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) is attached directly to the ring, and a hydroxyl group and a fluorine atom sit on adjacent ring carbons, creating a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no molecular symmetry. The aromatic core and the directly attached carbonyl make the scaffold largely rigid, while the hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond. The aldehyde oxygen and the fluorine atom act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, giving the molecule several sites for intermolecular interactions.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional rings. A hydroxyl group is attached to one of the ring carbons adjacent to the carbon bearing the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is 1,2 on the ring relative to the nitrogen's neighboring position. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen free to rotate, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is an acyclic, saturated aliphatic dicarboxylic acid built on a short carbon chain. Its backbone is a branched five-carbon framework with a methyl group on the central carbon, and each of the two terminal carbons carries a carboxylic acid group, giving a symmetric arrangement about the central carbon. Because there are no rings, no double bonds, and no aromatic groups, the molecule is conformationally flexible, with free rotation about its single C–C bonds. Both carboxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their hydroxyl hydrogens and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, so the molecule offers two donor and four acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents at the 1, 3, and 5 positions, giving a meta-disubstituted-plus-one pattern with a symmetric arrangement of the three groups around the ring. One substituent is a nitro group, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Another is a hydroxyl group, which can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The third is a trifluoromethyl group, a bulky, lipophilic, electron-poor moiety with three fluorine atoms that are weak acceptors. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the substituents rotate only modestly about their single bonds to the ring.

The molecule is a five-membered heterocycle built around a pyrazolone scaffold, containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms within the ring. It carries a carbonyl group on the ring carbon adjacent to an NH, making it a cyclic hydrazide-type lactam, and the remaining ring carbon is sp2-hybridized through a C=N double bond. A straight three-carbon propyl chain is attached to the ring carbon that bears the imine-type double bond, providing the only substituent and a flexible alkyl appendage. The ring is small and essentially planar, so the core is rigid while the propyl group retains rotational freedom. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the imine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a phthalimide scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring containing a nitrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups. The nitrogen carries a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal carboxylic acid, so the structure contains a flat, rigid fused bicyclic core attached to a flexible saturated linker. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the chain sits on only one side of the imide. The carboxylic acid group can donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one through its carbonyl oxygen, while the imide carbonyl oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.
