The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone with a straight, unbranched carbon chain of eleven carbons, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems. A single carbonyl group (C=O) sits at the internal position, with a two-carbon ethyl group on one side and a longer eight-carbon chain on the other, so the substitution pattern is linear rather than branched. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two alkyl arms differ in length. Its chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds that allow numerous conformations. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C=O flanked by a methyl) on one side and an imidazole ring attached through its nitrogen on the opposite side. The imidazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogens separated by one carbon, and it is linked to the phenyl ring via an N-aryl bond, so the two rings are not fused but joined directly. The ketone carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the imidazole's unsubstituted nitrogen provides an additional acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure has an overall planar, rigid aromatic framework with only limited rotational freedom about the single bond joining the two rings and the bond to the acetyl group.

This molecule is a thiosemicarbazide, built around a thiourea-like core in which a thiocarbonyl carbon bears a hydrazine group (–NH–NH₂) on one side and an arylamine on the other. The aryl portion is a single benzene ring carrying a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen attachment, giving an ortho-substitution pattern. The molecule has no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and its only rigid element is the aromatic ring, while the linear thiourea-hydrazine chain remains relatively flexible. Multiple N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the thiocarbonyl sulfur and the terminal nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring carrying a methyl group and a thiosemicarbazide-type side chain. The methyl substituent sits para to the nitrogen attachment point, giving a 1,4-disubstituted aromatic ring with a simple, symmetric substitution pattern. The side chain is a thiourea unit in which one nitrogen is bonded to the ring and the carbon is double-bonded to sulfur, and the other terminus carries a free hydrazine (NH-NH2) group. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the thiourea-hydrazine tail is comparatively flexible and can rotate about its single bonds. The NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur and terminal nitrogen provide hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

The molecule is a phenylboronic acid, with a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, at one position. Para to that group sits a tertiary amine nitrogen carrying two benzyl substituents, each a phenyl ring attached through a CH2 linker. The structure contains three aromatic six-membered rings, none fused to one another, so the core is a para-disubstituted benzene flanked by two freely rotating benzyl arms. The boronic acid contributes two hydroxyl groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the tertiary amine nitrogen is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The benzyl groups add conformational flexibility, and the overall molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis because the two benzyl arms and the boronic acid group differ in their orientation.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a single sulfur atom that bears two double-bonded oxygen atoms, giving a central sulfone (diaryl sulfone) linker. Each aromatic ring is a simple, unfused six-membered carbon ring, and each carries a primary amino group (–NH2) positioned para to the sulfone attachment point, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the sulfur. The overall skeleton is rigid and largely planar within each ring, with the tetrahedral sulfone geometry introducing a fixed angular kink between the two aryl groups. The two amino groups can each donate hydrogen bonds through their N–H bonds, while the amine nitrogens and the sulfone oxygens can accept them.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond with no fused ring system. Each ring carries one isopropyl group (a propan-2-yl substituent) attached at the position para to the biaryl linkage, so the substitution pattern is symmetrical about the central axis. The two aryl rings can rotate relative to one another about the single bond, giving some conformational flexibility, while each ring itself is rigid and planar. The molecule contains no heteroatoms and no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor groups, so it is purely hydrocarbon in character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving a single aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. A nitrile group (carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) sits on one ring carbon, and a primary amine (NH2) occupies the position para to it on the opposite side of the ring. A trifluoromethyl group (CF3) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the nitrile, so the three substituents form a 1,2,4-pattern around the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the three groups differ and sit at unequal positions. The aromatic core and the linear nitrile make it fairly rigid, with only limited rotational freedom in the amine and trifluoromethyl groups. The amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and the nitrile nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Three substituents are attached around the ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl group), a carboxylic acid group, and an amino group. The carboxylic acid and the amino group sit on positions para to each other, while the methoxy group is meta to the acid and ortho to the amino group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are distinct, and the aromatic ring is rigid while the methoxy and acid groups retain some rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, the amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, and the methoxy oxygen and carbonyl oxygen can act as acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two ring nitrogens, a pyrimidine core. It carries an amino group on one ring carbon and a hydroxyl group on another, giving it a 1,3-diazine scaffold with substitution at two positions. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds and no stereocenters, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the amino and hydroxyl groups sit in different positions around the ring. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds while both ring nitrogens and the oxygen can accept them. Overall, the structure is compact, flat, and polar in its hydrogen-bonding pattern.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring linked through a single methylene (CH2) bridge to a piperidine ring at its 4-position, giving a simple benzyl-substituted saturated heterocycle. The six-membered piperidine ring is fully saturated and adopts a chair-like conformation, while the aromatic phenyl ring is planar and unsubstituted, so the scaffold contains no ring fusion. The only heteroatom is the secondary amine nitrogen within the piperidine ring, which carries an N-H group that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The overall structure has a degree of rotational flexibility around the CH2 linker, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local mirror relationship of the piperidine ring.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and a methyl group occupies the adjacent position, making the two substituents ortho to each other. A bromine atom is attached to the ring at a meta position relative to the methyl group and para to the hydroxyl group. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine and methyl groups contribute only lipophilic bulk and no hydrogen-bonding capability. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the three different substituents are placed asymmetrically, and its rigid aromatic core allows only limited conformational flexibility from the rotation of the hydroxyl group.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitro group, a bromine atom, and a hydroxyl group. The hydroxyl and nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons, while the bromine is positioned meta to the nitro group and para to the hydroxyl group, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar. The phenolic hydroxyl acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The bromine adds a heavy halogen substituent but no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that shares one carbon-carbon bond with it. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a hydrogen, giving the core an N-H group that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. A bromine atom is attached to the benzene portion at the carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, at a position flanking the fused junction. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the single bromine substituent breaks it. The pyrrole nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic system, so the nitrogen is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the N-H serves as the primary donor site.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a methylsulfonyl group and a bromine atom. The methylsulfonyl group, CH3-SO2-, is attached to the ring through a sulfur atom that is bonded to two doubly bonded oxygen atoms and one methyl carbon, forming a sulfone functional group. The bromine sits on the opposite side of the ring, giving the molecule a clear axis of near two-fold symmetry through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the sulfone group contributes some conformational freedom around the carbon-sulfur bonds. The two sulfone oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3), a chlorine atom, and a trifluoromethyl group. The acetyl group sits at one ring position, with the chlorine and trifluoromethyl group adjacent to each other on the ring in a 1,3,4-pattern relative to it, which gives an asymmetric substitution arrangement. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, so the scaffold is rigid apart from rotation of the acetyl group and the trifluoromethyl group. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since its only hydrogens sit on carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, with no fused or additional rings. An amino group (-NH2) sits on one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom and a fluorine atom occupy two adjacent positions on the ring, with the fluorine located between the chlorine and the amino-bearing carbon. This leaves the ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 arrangement, which lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the molecule has little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the amino group. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the halogen atoms can only act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that is para-disubstituted, meaning its two substituents sit on opposite carbons. One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which is a linear, strongly electron-withdrawing unit. The other is a CH2 linker bearing a carboxylic acid, so the aromatic core is connected to a short flexible chain ending in a -COOH group. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methylene and carboxyl portion gives the molecule some rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the nitrile nitrogen acts as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall arrangement has no internal symmetry beyond the local two-fold pattern of the para-substituted ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. One carbon of the ring carries an ethyl group (a two-carbon saturated chain) and the carbon directly opposite it, at the para position, carries a carboxylic acid group. This 1,4-disubstitution gives the aromatic core a symmetrical, linear arrangement. The ethyl chain adds some conformational flexibility, while the aromatic ring and the planar carboxyl group keep the core fairly rigid. The carboxylic acid contributes both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability through its hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four fluorine atoms, one hydroxyl group, and one carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid is attached to the ring at one carbon, and the hydroxyl sits directly opposite it at the para position, so the substitution pattern is symmetric across the ring's central axis. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the four fluorines occupy the remaining positions in two pairs flanking the carboxyl and hydroxyl groups. The carboxylic acid and hydroxyl together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and several acceptor oxygens. Overall, the scaffold is rigid, with only the bonds of the carboxyl and hydroxyl groups free to rotate.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents arranged around the aromatic core: a methoxy group, a primary amino group, and a nitro group. The methoxy group (an aryl ether, O-CH3) sits para to the amino group, while the nitro group occupies the position ortho to the amine and meta to the methoxy group, giving a trisubstituted pattern with the amine flanked by the nitro group. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the substituents add little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the methoxy methyl group. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the nitro oxygens, the methoxy oxygen, and the amine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane through the methoxy group in its preferred conformation, since the three substituents differ in character and position.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring carries a methoxy group in the para position relative to the carbonyl, while the other carries a nitro group, also para to the carbonyl. Both rings are simple, unfused aromatic systems, so the scaffold is planar and fairly rigid, though the two rings can twist somewhat about the carbonyl bonds. The molecule is asymmetric because the electron-donating methoxy and electron-withdrawing nitro groups sit on different rings. The ketone oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and a nitrile group (a carbon triply bonded to nitrogen). The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern gives the molecule a pseudo-two-fold symmetry along the axis through both substituents. The nitrile and the aromatic core are rigid and linear in their geometry, while the methoxy group has limited rotational freedom about its C–O bonds. The ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement: a methoxy group (an O-methyl ether) on one side and a benzylic CH2 linked to a carbamate on the other. The carbamate portion is an O-alkyl ester of a hydrazinecarboxylic acid, containing a carbonyl flanked by an ether oxygen and an N-NH2 hydrazine unit. The aromatic core is flat and rigid, while the CH2-O-C(=O)-NH-NH2 chain adds rotational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring axis but no true symmetry beyond that. Hydrogen-bond donors come from the terminal NH and NH2 groups, and acceptors from the carbonyl oxygen, the two ether oxygens, and the hydrazine nitrogens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), and the other is an ether oxygen linked to a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, so the aryl ether is connected to a CH2 unit that is itself bonded to the terminal C(=O)OH group. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, and the molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the ring axis, while the oxyacetic acid side chain gives it some rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the two ether oxygens contribute additional hydrogen-bond acceptor capacity.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents. A methyl group and a carboxylic acid group sit para to each other on the ring, and a nitro group sits ortho to the methyl and meta to the carboxylic acid, so the pattern is 1,2,4-trisubstituted. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing acceptor. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only the carboxyl rotation and the methyl group adding limited conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different and placed asymmetrically.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears a nitro group, a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, which acts as a strong electron-withdrawing group. The other side bears a benzamide linkage, where the ring carbon is attached to a carbonyl that connects through an amide nitrogen to a CH2 group, which in turn links to a terminal carboxylic acid. The molecule is largely planar in its aromatic core but has a flexible two-atom chain leading to the acid. It contains a secondary amide N-H and a carboxylic acid O-H that can each donate hydrogen bonds, while the amide and acid carbonyls, the nitro oxygens, and the carboxylic hydroxyl oxygen can accept them. Its overall symmetry is low because the two ends differ in functionality.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents placed para to each other: a nitro group, in which a nitrogen is bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged, and a hydroxyl group bearing an OH. The arrangement gives the ring a symmetric, linear 1,4-substitution pattern. The aromatic core and the rigid planar nitro group make the scaffold largely inflexible, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen free to rotate. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a para-substituted benzene ring, with a nonyl chain (nine carbons in a straight line) on one side and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, on the opposite side. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered unit with no ring fusion. The boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups, giving the group two hydrogen-bond donor sites (the O–H groups) and two acceptor sites on the oxygens. The alkyl chain is long and highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, while the benzene ring and the boron center are rigid and planar. The molecule has an elongated, rod-like overall shape, and it lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the para-substituted ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries a primary sulfonamide group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to an NH2 group. The opposite side carries a phenoxy linkage, where an oxygen atom connects the first ring to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring, giving a diaryl ether scaffold. The two aromatic rings are flexible about the ether oxygen, which allows some rotational freedom. The sulfonamide contributes two hydrogen-bond donor N–H protons and two acceptor sulfonyl oxygens, while the ether oxygen acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a partial, approximate symmetry.

The molecule is built around a five-membered cyclic imide, a maleimide ring, in which a C=C double bond sits between two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen. That nitrogen is bonded to a para-substituted benzene ring, and the opposite para position carries an azo linker (-N=N-) that connects to an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The result is a largely planar, conjugated, extended aromatic system with an E-configured azo double bond, which limits rotational freedom and makes the molecule fairly rigid. There is no internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of each ring, because the two terminal rings differ. The imide carbonyl oxygens and the azo nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a biaryl-type structure built from a benzene ring bearing two chlorine substituents at the meta positions relative to each other and a tetrazole ring attached at the third position of the benzene. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, while the five-membered tetrazole ring is also aromatic, containing four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, with no fused ring system. The two aryl rings connect through a single C–C bond, allowing rotation about that bond and giving the molecule moderate flexibility. The tetrazole carries an N–H group that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while its ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The two chlorine atoms are electron-withdrawing substituents that make the molecule asymmetric in their placement, though the overall arrangement has an approximate mirror plane through the biaryl bond.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an isoxazole ring containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms within a single planar ring. A methyl group sits on one carbon of the ring, and an amino group is attached to a different ring carbon, so the two substituents occupy non-adjacent positions on the scaffold. The ring is fully conjugated and rigid, with essentially no conformational flexibility beyond the rotation of the small substituents. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the ring nitrogen and oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the planar framework because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. An ethoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to an ethyl chain) is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a bromine atom sits on a carbon further around the ring, creating a 2,5-disubstitution pattern. The ring is planar and fully unsaturated, and the ethoxy chain adds some conformational flexibility, though the core remains rigid. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ether oxygen provides a second, weaker acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, bearing four substituents. An acetyl group (a ketone attached through a methyl) sits at one ring carbon, a bromine atom is placed meta to it, and a nitro group occupies the position between the acetyl and the hydroxyl groups. The hydroxyl group is ortho to the acetyl group, so the two form a potential intramolecular hydrogen bond. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the acetyl and nitro groups add limited rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. The phenolic hydroxyl group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a bromine atom, and an aldehyde group, placed on adjacent and para positions so the scaffold is a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic ring. The benzene core is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the substituents are fairly rigid, though the methoxy and aldehyde groups can rotate about their single bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local plane of symmetry through the ring. Functional groups include an aryl ether, an aryl halide, and an aromatic aldehyde. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ether oxygen and the carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic scaffold: a pyridine ring fused to a pyrrole ring, forming a 7-azaindole-type framework. The six-membered ring contains one aromatic nitrogen, and the five-membered ring carries an N-H group, so the system has both a hydrogen-bond donor (the pyrrole N-H) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (the pyridine-type nitrogen). A bromine atom sits on the six-membered ring at the position meta to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the pyridine nitrogen's neighbor, giving a single halogen substituent on the pyridine half. The fused system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the bromine breaks the symmetry of the bicyclic core.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole-type ring that contains an N-H group. The ring system is planar and rigid, with the fusion sharing a C-C bond between the two rings. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) is attached to the carbon at position 3 of the five-membered ring, while a bromine atom sits on the benzene portion at position 5. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single minor axis of asymmetry from the substitution pattern. The indole N-H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the aldehyde oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: two methoxy groups, one chlorine atom, and one isocyanate group (–N=C=O). Reading around the ring, the methoxy groups sit meta to each other, the chlorine is adjacent to one methoxy group, and the isocyanate is positioned next to the other methoxy group, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is a single rigid, planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion, while the methoxy oxygens and the linear isocyanate add modest conformational freedom at their attachment points. The methoxy oxygens and the isocyanate oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: a primary carboxamide group (-C(=O)NH2) on one ring carbon, a hydroxyl group (-OH) on the adjacent carbon, and a chlorine atom on a carbon meta to the carboxamide and para to the hydroxyl. The carboxamide and hydroxyl groups sit ortho to each other, which allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond between the phenolic oxygen and the amide. The molecule is largely planar and rigid, with only limited rotation about the amide and hydroxyl bonds, and it has no symmetry element beyond the local planarity of the ring. The amide NH2 and the hydroxyl group act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the ring nitrogen-free framework provide acceptor sites through the oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions: an amino group, a chlorine atom, and a nitro group. The amino group sits ortho to the nitro group, while the chlorine is positioned meta to the amino group and para to the nitro group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ from one another. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and rotationally constrained relative to the ring, contributing to overall rigidity. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the nitro oxygens and the amine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that contains an NH group. It carries an aldehyde (formyl) group attached to the carbon at position 3 of the five-membered ring, where the carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds. A chlorine atom sits on the benzene portion of the bicycle, at the position para to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen-adjacent carbon side. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the aldehyde group largely coplanar with the ring system. The indole NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the aldehyde oxygen acts as an acceptor.

This molecule is a naphthoquinone-type scaffold: a naphthalene-derived bicyclic system in which one fused ring bears two carbonyl groups positioned para to each other across a non-aromatic six-membered ring, and the other ring is a benzene ring. The quinone-like ring contains a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with both carbonyls, making it planar and electron-poor. A hydroxyl group sits on the benzenoid ring adjacent to the ring fusion, forming a substituent that is ortho to a carbonyl-bearing carbon. The whole fused framework is rigid and essentially flat, with no rotatable bonds. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the phenolic hydroxyl provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor site.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid and the nitro group sit on adjacent carbons, so the nitro group is ortho to the carboxyl, while the hydroxyl is positioned meta to the carboxyl and para to the nitro group. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring itself, and only the carboxyl and nitro groups have limited rotation about their attachment bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. Hydrogen-bond capability is distinct on each side: the carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl can each donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, along with the nitro oxygens, can accept them.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic furan ring bearing two substituents on adjacent positions. A methyl group sits on one alpha carbon of the ring, and an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl bonded to a chlorine atom, sits on the other alpha carbon. The ring oxygen is part of the aromatic system and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The carbonyl oxygen also serves as an acceptor, and the acyl chloride is a reactive electrophilic center. The scaffold is small, planar, and rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the substituents.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Three hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent carbons of the ring, forming a contiguous 1,2,3-triol arrangement, and a tert-butyl group occupies the position opposite the central hydroxyl. The tert-butyl group is a bulky, branched alkyl substituent that adds steric bulk and is essentially nonpolar, while the ring itself is rigid apart from rotation of the hydroxyl hydrogens. The compound has an approximate mirror plane passing through the tert-butyl carbon and the central hydroxyl-bearing carbon. Each phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the adjacent pair of hydroxyls allows intramolecular hydrogen bonding across the ring.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a six-membered pyrimidine-type ring joined along one edge to a five-membered imidazole-type ring, giving a purine-like scaffold. The six-membered ring carries a fluorine atom on the carbon between its two nitrogens and a chlorine atom on an adjacent fused-ring carbon, so the substitution is asymmetric. The five-membered ring contains an N-H group, which serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the remaining ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fully aromatic, planar framework is rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and its halogen substituents sit in the plane of the rings.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered pyridine ring, an aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen atom, and it carries two substituents. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, placing it at the 2-position. A carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) sits on the ring carbon at the 5-position, para-like to the methyl across the ring. There is no ring fusion, and the molecule is flat and rigid apart from rotation of the amide group. The pyridine nitrogen and the amide carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two amide N–H hydrogens act as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on an indazole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrazole ring that contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms. The fusion is ortho, sharing one carbon-carbon bond between the two rings, and the fused framework is fully aromatic and planar. A single bromine atom is attached to the benzene ring at a carbon adjacent to the fusion point, so the substitution pattern is an aryl halide on the carbocyclic half. The N-H group on the pyrazole nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated pyridine-type nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The structure is rigid with no rotatable bonds and lacks any internal symmetry because the bromine breaks the potential mirror plane.

The molecule is a bicyclic heterocycle in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered sulfur- and nitrogen-containing ring, forming a 1,4-benzothiazine-type scaffold. The saturated ring contains a thioether sulfur, a methylene group, a lactam carbonyl, and an amide nitrogen, so the fused system is partly planar (the aromatic ring and the amide) and partly puckered. A single bromine atom sits on the benzene ring, para to the sulfur-bearing carbon's position relative to the nitrogen-bearing side, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The lactam carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. Overall the structure is moderately rigid, with limited conformational freedom confined mainly to the non-aromatic ring.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system built from two six-membered rings fused along a shared edge, forming a naphthalene-like scaffold in which one ring contains a nitrogen atom at a position that makes it a quinoline framework. A hydroxyl group is attached to the carbocyclic ring, making it a phenolic substituent at a position on the benzo portion of the fused system. The fused rings are fully aromatic and planar, giving the structure a rigid, flat geometry with no rotatable bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the hydroxyl group breaks the symmetry of the framework. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a flavanone-type scaffold: a bicyclic benzopyranone in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing heterocycle that carries a ketone at the position adjacent to the CH2 group, so it is best described as a chroman-4-one core bearing a phenyl substituent at the 2-position. The fused aromatic ring carries a single methoxy ether group, placed meta to the ring oxygen on the benzo portion, giving the benzene ring an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The molecule has one stereocenter at the carbon bearing the phenyl group, so it lacks overall mirror symmetry in its substitution. Its partly saturated pyranone ring gives moderate conformational flexibility while the fused and pendant aromatic rings remain planar and rigid. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ketone oxygen and the ether oxygens act as acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that contains an N-H group. A carboxylic acid group (-COOH) is attached at the 2-position of the pyrrole ring. A nitro group (-NO2) sits on the benzene portion, at the position adjacent to the ring fusion carbon bonded to the nitrogen, which places it close to the N-H. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the substituents adding little conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, the indole N-H is a donor, and the nitro and carbonyl oxygens serve as acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry.

The molecule is built on a carbazole scaffold, a rigid tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central five-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The nitrogen atom carries an ethyl group, which replaces the N–H that would otherwise be present, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor. The unsubstituted benzene rings give the structure no additional substituents, and the fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and conformationally rigid, with only the small ethyl side chain showing flexibility. The nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic system, so the ring nitrogen acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor at most.

This molecule is a very small acyclic structure built on a short two-carbon-plus-one skeleton. It contains no ring systems, so there is no ring fusion, and it has no substitution pattern beyond its methyl groups. A single carbonyl group, a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, sits between two methyl groups, which makes the molecule symmetric about the plane through the carbonyl carbon and oxygen. Its overall shape is rigid and planar around the carbonyl, while the two methyl groups can rotate freely. The oxygen atom can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a dicarboxylic acid built on a three-carbon chain: two carboxylic acid groups sit at opposite ends of the backbone, and a benzyl group is attached to the central carbon. The benzyl substituent is an unfused phenyl ring linked through a methylene bridge, so there is no ring fusion, and the phenyl ring is fully aromatic with its six carbons all sharing delocalized electrons. The molecule has a stereocenter at the central carbon, so it is chiral and lacks any internal mirror symmetry. The chain bearing the substituent is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds. Each carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen) capability, giving the molecule two donor sites and four acceptor sites overall.

This molecule is a benzenesulfonohydrazide: a single unfused benzene ring carries a sulfonyl group attached directly to one carbon of the ring, giving a monosubstituted aromatic system with no further ring substituents. The sulfur atom is in the hexavalent sulfonyl oxidation state, bearing two terminal oxygen atoms double-bonded to it, and it links the aryl ring to a hydrazine unit (an N–N chain) through an N–S bond. The aryl ring is planar and rigid, while the sulfonyl-hydrazide tail offers some rotational flexibility around the C–S and S–N bonds. The molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the aromatic ring and sulfur atom, and it is achiral. Its hydrogen-bond donor capacity comes from the N–H groups of the terminal hydrazide nitrogen, while the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is benzilic acid, built on a two-carbon scaffold where a single quaternary carbon bears a hydroxyl group, a carboxylic acid group, and two phenyl rings. Each phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring attached directly to that central carbon, so the two rings are not fused to each other. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the tertiary alcohol adds another donor and acceptor site. The central sp3 carbon makes the molecule fairly flexible around its single bonds, though the bulky twin phenyl groups restrict rotation. The arrangement is not symmetric overall because the carboxyl and hydroxyl groups sit on different sides of the core, even though the two phenyl rings are chemically identical.

The molecule is a tertiary phosphine built around a single phosphorus atom bearing three substituents: one phenyl ring and two identical 2-cyanoethyl chains. The phenyl group is an unsubstituted benzene ring attached directly to phosphorus, giving the molecule an aromatic, planar region. Each cyanoethyl arm contains a flexible two-carbon linker ending in a nitrile group, a carbon-nitrogen triple bond that is linear and strongly electron-withdrawing. The two arms are constitutionally identical, so the molecule has a mirror-type symmetry about the P–phenyl axis, and the phosphorus center is pyramidal with a lone pair. The molecule has no ring fusion and no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two nitrile nitrogens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and the phosphorus lone pair offers additional basic character.

This molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a single methylene (CH2) bridge, giving a diarylmethane scaffold with no fused ring systems. Each phenyl ring carries one fluorine atom located para to the bridging carbon, so the substitution pattern is symmetric, and the molecule as a whole possesses approximately twofold symmetry through the central CH2 group. The aromatic rings are planar and rigid, while the methylene linker allows rotation about its two C–C bonds, giving the molecule moderate conformational flexibility. The structure contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, and the fluorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a flexible acyclic backbone: two phosphorus atoms joined by a single methylene bridge, forming a P–CH2–P unit. Each phosphorus carries two saturated cyclohexyl rings, so the scaffold is a bis(dicyclohexylphosphino)methane-type framework with four independent cyclohexane rings and no ring fusion between them. The rings are fully saturated, adopt chair conformations, and attach to phosphorus through single bonds, which gives the molecule considerable conformational flexibility around the central P–CH2–P linkage. The structure is not symmetrical in a strict sense, though the two phosphorus centers are chemically similar and each bears two identical cyclohexyl groups. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N–H or O–H groups are present, and the only potential acceptors are the lone pairs on the phosphorus atoms.

This molecule is a short aliphatic carboxylic acid with no rings, so its scaffold is a single two-carbon chain. The terminal carbon is a carboxyl group (-COOH), bearing a hydroxyl and a carbonyl oxygen, while the alpha carbon carries one chlorine and one bromine atom, giving it a stereogenic center with no defined configuration in the SMILES. The structure is small and flexible, with free rotation about the single bonds, and it has no internal symmetry because the two different halogens on the alpha carbon break any mirror or rotational equivalence. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its two oxygen atoms, while the halogens act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is an aliphatic oxime, built on a straight four-carbon chain with no rings present. A propyl group is attached to a carbon-nitrogen double bond, forming a C=N-OH unit at the terminal end of the chain. The oxime hydroxyl group carries a hydrogen that can be donated in hydrogen bonding, while the nitrogen lone pair and oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the local geometry around the double bond. The C=N bond can exist in E or Z configurations, which is a stereochemical feature of the structure.

The molecule is carbohydrazide, a small acyclic scaffold built around a single central carbonyl carbon. That carbonyl is flanked on both sides by nitrogen atoms, each of which carries a further nitrogen, so the core is a urea-like C=O bearing two hydrazine units, one at each end. There are no rings, no aromatic systems, and no stereocenters, and the molecule is essentially symmetric about the central carbonyl. Its rotatable N–C and N–N bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. Each terminal and internal NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pairs can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing one substituent, a two-carbon chain attached at one ring carbon, so the scaffold is a monosubstituted aromatic ring with no ring fusion. The side chain contains a carbon-carbon double bond with trans (E) geometry, which keeps the chain extended and fairly rigid, while the terminal carbon carries a primary alcohol group. The phenyl ring is planar and unsubstituted elsewhere, giving the molecule an approximate local mirror symmetry across the chain axis. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic ring offers only weak pi-based interactions.

The molecule is an acyclic, linear four-carbon chain built around a central carbon-carbon double bond with (E) geometry, the two carbons flanking it each bearing a methyl or a carbonyl. Both terminal ends of the chain are carbonyl groups, each bonded to a hydrazide unit (C(=O)NN), so the molecule contains two hydrazide functional groups in a symmetric-looking arrangement across the alkene. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical at the alkene because one carbon carries a methyl group and the other carries a hydrogen, so the two hydrazide arms are not chemically identical. The backbone is fairly rigid around the double bond but otherwise flexible through its single bonds. Each hydrazide provides multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites through its N–H groups and carbonyl oxygen acceptor sites, giving the molecule a high capacity for hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic ring containing three carbon atoms and three nitrogen atoms placed alternately around the ring, which makes it a 1,3,5-triazine scaffold. Each of the three carbon positions carries one chlorine atom, so the substitution pattern is fully symmetrical, with the three chlorines spaced evenly around the ring. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the core a rigid, flat geometry with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, but the three ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a cycloheptane ring bearing a single acetic acid side chain, meaning a two-carbon unit ending in a carboxylic acid group attached to one ring carbon through a methylene linker. The seven-membered saturated carbocycle has no ring fusion, unsaturation, or heteroatoms, and the substitution pattern is monosubstituted, so the ring carries no symmetry element beyond the local mirror plane through the substituted carbon. The cycloheptane ring is conformationally flexible and can interconvert among several puckered forms, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate about its single bonds. The carboxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The remainder of the molecule is purely hydrocarbon and offers no additional hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is a five-membered carbocycle with no heteroatoms, built from a cyclopentene scaffold containing a single carbon-carbon double bond. The ring is a simple monocyclic system with no fusion, bridging, or additional rings attached. There are no functional groups beyond the alkene, and the ring carries no substituents, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted. The ring is nearly planar and conformationally flexible through puckering, with the double bond locally restricting motion. Because the molecule contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites.

This molecule is a seven-membered cyclic ester, specifically a lactone built from a single saturated ring of six carbons and one oxygen in the ring, with a carbonyl carbon adjacent to that ring oxygen. The ring is a simple, unfused monocycle with no additional rings attached. Its only functional group is the ester linkage, in which the carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the ring oxygen contributes a second, weaker acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H groups. The ring has no substituents beyond the ester, so the substitution pattern is unbranched and the molecule has no stereocenters. The seven-membered ring is conformationally flexible and can adopt several puckered forms rather than a single rigid shape.

This molecule is a boronic acid attached to a dibenzofuran scaffold. The core is a tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central five-membered furan ring containing one oxygen atom, giving a flat, rigid aromatic framework. The boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is bonded to one carbon of the outer ring, adjacent to the carbon that connects to the furan oxygen, so the substitution pattern is ortho to the ring oxygen. Because of the fused, planar ring system, the molecule has little conformational flexibility, and the scaffold is largely unsymmetrical due to the single substituent. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the hydroxyls and the furan ring oxygen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a dibenzo-fused seven-membered ring: two benzene rings are joined through a central ring that contains a carbon-carbon double bond, giving a tricyclic scaffold with a rigid, largely planar aromatic framework. One sp3-hybridized carbon in the central ring bears a hydroxyl group, so the only functional group present is a secondary alcohol at that bridging position, with no other substituents on the aromatic rings. The molecule lacks a mirror-symmetric arrangement because the hydroxyl-bearing carbon breaks the symmetry of the central ring, and it contains a stereogenic center there. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the rest of the skeleton offers only weak, nonpolar interaction surfaces.

This molecule is a tartaric acid derivative in which both secondary hydroxyl groups have been esterified with benzoic acid, giving a central two-carbon backbone bearing two benzoyloxy groups and two terminal carboxylic acid groups. The two stereogenic carbons sit in a flexible, chain-like arrangement with no ring systems in the core, though each of the two phenyl rings is a fully aromatic, planar six-membered ring. The molecule has an approximate twofold symmetry through its central carbon-carbon bond, since the two halves are constitutionally identical. Its carbonyl and ester oxygens, together with the two acidic hydroxyl groups, provide multiple hydrogen-bond acceptor sites and four hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is dichlorophenylborane, built on a single benzene ring with a boron atom attached directly to one of its carbons. Boron carries two chlorine substituents, so the boron center is trivalent and bears no additional organic groups beyond the phenyl ring. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted otherwise, giving a simple monosubstituted benzene scaffold with no ring fusion. The molecule has a planar, rigid aromatic core with limited conformational flexibility around the carbon-boron bond. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor sites are the chlorine atoms, which are weak.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring, which carries an NH group and is fully substituted at the other positions. Two ethyl ester groups are attached directly to the ring carbons flanking the nitrogen and at the adjacent carbon, while a methyl group sits on the remaining ring carbon, giving the pyrrole a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern. There are no fused or additional rings, so the scaffold is compact and monocyclic. The ester carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the pyrrole N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor. The ester linkages and ethyl tails add some conformational flexibility, while the aromatic core remains rigid and planar.

The molecule is built around a phthalimide scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imide ring bearing two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen atom. The nitrogen is substituted with a methylene linker that connects to a dimethyl phosphonate group, where a tetrahedral phosphorus carries a double-bonded oxygen and two methoxy ester arms. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the phosphonate side chain adds conformational flexibility through its rotatable single bonds. Symmetry is limited because the substituent sits on one nitrogen, although the two methoxy groups on phosphorus are chemically equivalent. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all N–H and O–H positions are absent. Its acceptors include the two imide carbonyl oxygens and the phosphoryl oxygen plus the two ester-type oxygens.

The molecule is a simple acyclic sulfoxide built from two identical n-butyl chains joined to a single sulfur atom that carries one oxygen as an S=O group. There are no rings, no aromatic systems, and no fused scaffold, so the structure is entirely saturated and carbon-chain based. The sulfoxide group is the only functional group present, and it is located at the center of the molecule, giving the structure a symmetric arrangement about the sulfur atom. Both butyl arms are flexible, freely rotating alkyl chains, so the molecule has considerable conformational freedom. The oxygen of the sulfoxide acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a malonic acid derivative in which the central carbon carries two n-propyl groups, making it a 2,2-dipropylmalonic acid skeleton. Its core is a single quaternary sp3 carbon bonded to two carboxylic acid groups, giving no ring systems or ring fusion at all. The two carboxyl groups are attached to the same carbon, so the substitution pattern is geminal and the molecule has a local two-fold symmetry about that central carbon. The two flexible propyl chains add conformational freedom, so the structure is fairly flexible rather than rigid. Each carboxyl group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and acceptor (the C=O), so the molecule can form multiple hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched saturated carbon chain of twelve carbons, with no rings and no fused ring systems, so its scaffold is entirely acyclic. Its only functional group is a carboxylic acid located at one terminus, where a carbonyl carbon bears both a double-bonded oxygen and a hydroxyl group. Because the chain is linear and carries no substituents along its length, the molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond a mirror-like arrangement of the alkyl tail. The long hydrocarbon segment is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through rotation about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group provides one hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites through its oxygen atoms.

This molecule is a straight-chain saturated alkane: a single unbranched backbone of carbon atoms, each joined to its neighbors by single bonds, with no rings, no double or triple bonds, and no heteroatoms. Because there is no ring system or ring fusion, the scaffold is simply a long linear chain. It carries no functional groups and no substitution pattern, since every carbon is a methylene unit except the two terminal methyl groups, so the molecule is symmetric about its midpoint. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its C–C single bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. The ring carries an ethyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is attached to an ethyl chain) on one carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, along with two hydroxyl groups and a methyl group at other positions around the ring. The hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, while the ester carbonyl oxygen, the ester ether oxygen, and the ring nitrogen can accept them. The ring is planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester tail adds some conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a thiophene five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom. The ring carries three substituents: a primary amine on the carbon next to sulfur, an ethyl ester (ethoxycarbonyl) group on the adjacent carbon, and a para-methoxyphenyl ring attached to the carbon next to the ester. The amino and ester groups are ortho to each other, forming a push-pull arrangement across the thiophene. The aryl ring is linked by a single bond, so it can rotate, giving the molecule moderate flexibility around that bond while the thiophene core stays planar. The amine provides hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the ester carbonyl and ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any true symmetry axis because the substituents differ.

The molecule is an ethyl ester of a benzoic acid bearing a pyrrole ring on the para position. A benzene ring sits at the core, with an ethoxycarbonyl group (–C(=O)OCH2CH3) on one side and a five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring attached through its nitrogen atom on the opposite side, giving a linear, para-disubstituted arrangement. The ester carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ether oxygen adds a second weak acceptor site, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aromatic rings are connected by a single N–C bond, so they can rotate relative to one another, and the ethyl tail adds further conformational flexibility. Overall the scaffold is largely planar and aromatic, with the flexible ester and ethyl portions extending from it.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, bearing an NH group at one ring nitrogen and no fused rings. Substituents sit on three of the ring carbons: an ethyl ester group (a carbonyl attached to an ethoxy chain) on one carbon, a methyl group on the adjacent carbon, and a primary amino group on the carbon next to the NH. The ester and amino groups are positioned on neighboring carbons, which gives a densely substituted, planar heteroaromatic core with no internal symmetry. The ethyl ester chain provides the only notable conformational flexibility, while the ring itself is rigid. The amino group and the ring NH can each donate hydrogen bonds, and the ring's unprotonated nitrogen, the ester carbonyl oxygen, and the ester ether oxygen can accept them.

This molecule is a small acyclic ester built on a two-carbon acetyl backbone. An ethyl group is attached through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon that also bears a methyl group, so the scaffold is a simple linear chain with no rings and no ring fusion. The defining functional group is the ester, in which a carbonyl double bond sits adjacent to a single-bonded ether-type oxygen linked to the ethyl chain. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local arrangement around the ester group, and its single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since no hydrogens are attached to electronegative atoms, but both oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

Ethyl 4-methyl-3-oxopentanoate is an acyclic molecule built on a short linear carbon chain with no rings or fused ring systems. Its skeleton contains an ethyl ester at one end, where an ethoxy group is bonded to a carbonyl carbon, followed by a methylene group and a ketone carbonyl. The ketone is flanked by an isopropyl group, which places a branched methyl-substituted terminus on the chain. Because the molecule has no ring and several single bonds, it is conformationally flexible, and it lacks any symmetry element beyond local rotational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its two carbonyl oxygens and the ester oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built on a short, unbranched-then-branched carbon chain with no ring systems or aromatic rings. An ethyl group is bonded through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon, which forms the ester functional group. From the carbonyl carbon, a methylene links to a carbon that carries a methyl branch and terminates in a second methyl group, giving an isobutyl-type end. The skeleton is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds and no fused or rigid framework. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ester ether oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an ethyl ester built on a pyridine ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic ring, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. An ethoxycarbonyl group, consisting of a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries an ethyl chain, is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, giving a 2-substituted pyridine pattern. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ester carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen add further acceptor sites, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ethyl ester tail is flexible, whereas the planar aromatic ring is rigid, and the overall structure lacks any internal symmetry axis.

The molecule is an acyclic three-carbon chain with a hydroxyl group on each carbon, giving a linear, straight-backbone scaffold with no rings and no ring fusion. Each of the three carbons carries one hydroxyl (alcohol) functional group, so the substitution pattern is uniform across the chain, and the central carbon's hydroxyl sits symmetrically between the two terminal ones. The two terminal carbons are equivalent, giving the molecule a mirror-plane symmetry through the central carbon. The chain is highly flexible, since all single bonds can rotate freely. Each of the three hydroxyl groups can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, so the molecule offers six hydrogen-bond sites in total.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic nitrile, with no rings, fused systems, or aromatic groups. Its skeleton is a linear, unbranched chain of seven carbon atoms, with the terminal carbon bearing a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen). Because there are no branches or ring constraints, the molecule has no stereocenters and its only symmetry is the approximate linear arrangement of the carbon backbone and the cyano end. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single C–C bonds, while the nitrile carbon-nitrogen unit is rigid and linear. The nitrogen atom of the nitrile is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring is fused to a benzene ring along a shared edge. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) is attached to the carbon at position 3 of the pyrrole ring, which is the most electron-rich site of the indole core. The indole nitrogen carries a hydrogen, so the ring system is an N-unsubstituted indole. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with the aldehyde extending from one face of the plane and little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the rings. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the indole N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen of the aldehyde serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

Isopropylamine is a small, acyclic molecule built on a three-carbon propane backbone. Its only functional group is a primary amine, with the nitrogen bonded to one carbon of the chain. The central carbon bears two methyl groups, so the molecule has a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the C–N axis, and the chain is flexible with free rotation about its single bonds. The amine nitrogen carries two hydrogen atoms, allowing it to act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and its lone pair lets it serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an alpha-amino acid built on a short, acyclic carbon backbone with no ring systems and no ring fusion. The central stereogenic carbon carries a primary amino group, a carboxylic acid group, and an isopropyl side chain, which is a branched alkyl group with two methyl groups on a single carbon. The amine and carboxyl groups sit on adjacent carbons, giving the scaffold a zwitterion-capable arrangement. The molecule has a single defined stereocenter and no internal symmetry. Its backbone is relatively flexible because of free rotation about its single bonds. It can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through the amine and hydroxyl hydrogens and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens and the amine nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three hydroxyl groups sit at the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to the methyl ester carbonyl, which occupies position 1, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern around the ring. The ester is a methyl carboxylate, bearing a carbonyl oxygen and an ether-type oxygen bonded to a methyl group. The two hydroxyls flanking the ester can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the carbonyl oxygen, which constrains local conformation. The molecule has three hydrogen-bond donors from the phenolic OH groups and four acceptor oxygens across the ester and hydroxyl groups.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused partners. The ring carries a methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that bears a methyl group) at one position, and three oxygen-containing substituents at the remaining positions: two methoxy groups (oxygen bonded to a methyl) flanking a free hydroxyl group in the middle. This arrangement gives the ring a symmetric 3,5-dimethoxy-4-hydroxy pattern relative to the ester. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a donor and an acceptor. Overall the core is rigid and planar, with only the methyl groups and the ester contributing modest conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic furan ring, which contains one oxygen atom and four carbons. A methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries a methyl group) is attached to one carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, while a methyl group sits on the neighboring carbon on the other side of the carbon bearing the ester, giving a 2,3-disubstituted pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited rotational freedom about the single bonds linking the ester to the ring, so it is essentially planar and rigid. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries a methyl group) is attached to one ring carbon, which makes the ring an aromatic ester scaffold. Adjacent to that ester-bearing carbon sits a nitro group, while a chlorine atom occupies the position para to the ester on the far side of the ring. The result is a trisubstituted benzene with a contiguous ortho-arrangement of the nitro and chloro groups, and the ring itself is planar and rigid. The ester oxygens and the nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since every available hydrogen sits on carbon.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries two substituents: a methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is in turn bonded to a methyl group) attached at the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, and a bromine atom on the ring at the position meta to the nitrogen (para to the ester-bearing carbon). The structure is essentially planar and rigid, with only modest rotational freedom around the ester C–C and C–O bonds. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited to acceptors: the ring nitrogen and the two oxygens of the ester can accept hydrogen bonds, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a short, fully fluorinated ester built on a linear three-carbon-plus-one chain. Starting from one end, a methyl group is bonded to an oxygen that connects to a carbonyl carbon, forming a methyl ester. The carbonyl carbon is attached to a difluoromethylene unit, followed by a second difluoromethylene unit and a terminal trifluoromethyl group. There are no rings, so the scaffold is acyclic and the molecule has no ring fusion. The chain is fully substituted with fluorine atoms, leaving no C–H bonds on the perfluorinated portion. The molecule is flexible about its C–C single bonds, and it has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local CF2/CF3 arrangement. The ester oxygen and carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. A methyl ester group, consisting of a carbonyl carbon bonded to a ring carbon and an oxygen that carries a methyl group, is attached at the carbon position four steps around the ring from the nitrogen, giving a para-type substitution pattern. The molecule has a mirror plane running through the nitrogen and the substituted carbon, and it is essentially planar and rigid apart from rotation of the methyl ester group. The ring nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond through its lone pair, while the ester's carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen can also act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One side carries a methyl group, while the other carries a sulfonyl group, specifically a sulfone in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and attached to the ring. That sulfonyl carbon is further bonded to a methylthiomethyl chain, meaning a CH2 linked to a sulfur that carries a methyl group. The ring is a single unfused aromatic system with no additional rings, and the overall shape has a rough mirror-like arrangement along the ring axis, though the flexible sulfur-containing chain breaks perfect symmetry. The sulfone oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all hydrogens sit on carbon.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing two methyl groups on adjacent positions, so it is an ortho-disubstituted toluene-type scaffold (a dimethylbenzene). Both substituents are simple alkyl groups attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the molecule contains no heteroatoms or other functional groups. The arrangement gives the molecule a mirror plane running through the two substituted carbons, so its structure is largely symmetric about that axis. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the two methyl groups can rotate freely about their single bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no lone-pair-bearing atoms that could act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an anilide built from a maleamic-type acid: a cis/trans-agnostic C=C double bond links a terminal carboxylic acid to a secondary amide carbonyl, giving a short, fairly rigid, linear chain. The amide nitrogen is attached to a benzene ring that carries two chlorine atoms at the 2 and 5 positions relative to the nitrogen, a pattern that breaks the ring's symmetry. The carboxylic acid OH and the amide N–H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the carboxylic acid oxygens act as acceptors. The two chlorines add lipophilic, electron-withdrawing bulk without introducing any additional polar donor or acceptor sites.

The molecule is an N-aryl maleimide: a five-membered unsaturated imide ring (a pyrrole-2,5-dione) bearing a carbon-carbon double bond flanked by two carbonyl groups. The imide nitrogen is attached to a benzene ring, which carries an ethyl group on the carbon para to the nitrogen, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern. The two rings are joined through a single N-aryl bond, so the molecule is rigid and largely planar within each ring, with the rotation about that bond being the main source of flexibility. The imide carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor, since the nitrogen carries no hydrogen.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, with two benzene rings joined by a single bond. One ring carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) at the para position relative to the biaryl linkage. The other ring bears a sulfonamide group, where a sulfur atom with two oxygens is bonded to a nitrogen, at the para position. That nitrogen connects to an alpha-carbon bearing a methyl and a carboxylic acid, giving an amino acid-like tail. The two aromatic rings are planar and conjugated, while the sulfonamide and side chain add some rotational flexibility. Overall the molecule is asymmetric, with hydrogen-bond donors from the sulfonamide N-H and carboxylic acid O-H, and multiple acceptors from the oxygens of the methoxy, sulfonyl, and carbonyl groups.

The molecule is built on a simple, acyclic scaffold with no rings or ring fusion. Its central atom is a single nitrogen bearing two ethyl groups, and the remaining position on that nitrogen is occupied by a hydroxyl group, making it an N,N-disubstituted hydroxylamine. The nitrogen-oxygen bond is the only heteroatom-to-heteroatom linkage, and the molecule has no aromatic character. Because it is small and open-chained with freely rotating C–C and C–N bonds, it is highly flexible and lacks any fixed geometry. The hydroxyl hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the oxygen and the nitrogen lone pair can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a dimethylamino group (N,N-dimethylamine attached directly to the aromatic carbon) at one position and a piperazine ring at the para position. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 4, with the aryl group attached to a carbon adjacent to one nitrogen, so the ring is 2-substituted rather than N-substituted. The aromatic ring is para-disubstituted, giving the molecule a roughly linear, elongated shape with limited symmetry because the piperazine is not symmetrically attached. The piperazine ring can adopt chair conformations, adding some flexibility, while the aryl portion is rigid. The secondary amine N-H in the piperazine serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a symmetric diaryl urea, built from a central carbonyl group flanked on both sides by an NH linked to a phenyl ring. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry across the urea carbonyl. The central C(=O)N–H–N unit is planar and conjugated, which restricts rotation about the C–N bonds and gives the scaffold moderate rigidity, while the bonds to the phenyl rings allow some flexibility. Each N–H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving the molecule two donor sites and one acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a phthalimide-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring containing a nitrogen atom flanked by two carbonyl groups. The fused benzo-pyrrolidinedione system is planar and rigid, with the ortho-disubstituted benzene ring giving an unsubstituted aromatic pattern. The imide nitrogen carries an acetyl group, which is an N-acyl substituent that adds a second carbonyl and a short, flexible rotatable bond. The molecule has no stereocenters and its arrangement is largely symmetric across the aromatic ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen is fully substituted, but its three carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a diaryl imine built around a central carbon-nitrogen double bond, with one carbon bearing a phenyl ring directly and the nitrogen bearing a second phenyl ring, so the scaffold is two benzene rings linked through a C=N unit. Both rings are simple unsubstituted benzene rings with no fused or heteroatom-containing ring systems. The C=N double bond has a defined geometry, which places the two phenyl groups on opposite sides of the bond, giving a fairly extended and rigid arrangement that is largely planar across the rings and the imine linkage. The molecule has no stereocenters and is close to a two-fold symmetric shape, though the aryl groups are not identical in their attachment. The imine nitrogen carries a lone pair that makes it a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic carbamate, with no ring systems present. Its backbone is a short saturated chain built around a stereogenic carbon bearing a methyl group, a hydroxymethyl arm, and a carbamate nitrogen.
