The carbamate linkage (N-C(=O)-O) bridges this chain to a tert-butyl group, which is a bulky, branched, and nonpolar substituent. The terminal primary hydroxyl group and the N-H of the carbamate both act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, the ester-type oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors. The chain is flexible with several rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its single chiral center.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched saturated carboxylic acid built from a single linear chain of ten carbon atoms, with no rings, no double bonds other than the carbonyl, and no aromatic or heteroatom-containing substituents. The terminal carbon of the chain carries a carboxyl group, so the scaffold is an aliphatic acid with one polar head and a long nonpolar tail. Because the chain is entirely sp3 apart from the carbonyl carbon, the molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry beyond a rough mirror-like arrangement of its methylene units. The chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through free rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds. The carboxyl group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the rest of the molecule offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a diarylamine scaffold, with a secondary amine nitrogen bridging two benzene rings. One ring carries a carboxylic acid group at the position adjacent to the nitrogen, so the two aromatic rings are ortho-related through the amine linkage. Each benzene ring is unsubstituted otherwise, and the overall framework has no fused ring systems. The C–N and N–aryl bonds allow considerable rotational flexibility around the central linkage, so the two rings can adopt varied relative orientations. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the amine N–H serves as an additional donor and the nitrogen as a weak acceptor.

This molecule is tridecane, a straight, fully saturated hydrocarbon chain of thirteen carbon atoms joined by single bonds, with no rings, branches, or heteroatoms. Its scaffold is entirely acyclic and unbranched, so there are no ring systems, ring fusion, or functional groups to describe. The chain carries no substitution pattern, and its ends are identical methyl groups, giving it a simple mirror-symmetric linear form. Because the carbon-carbon single bonds allow free rotation, the chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing five methyl groups and one sulfonyl chloride group, so the aromatic core is fully substituted with the sulfonyl chloride occupying the position between two methyl groups. The aromatic ring is fused to nothing else, making this a monocyclic scaffold with no additional rings. The sulfonyl chloride group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to chlorine, is the only polar, reactive functional group, while the five methyl groups are nonpolar alkyl substituents. The substitution pattern is highly symmetric about the axis running through the sulfonyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon, and the bulky, rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility apart from rotation of the sulfonyl group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two sulfonyl oxygens.

The molecule is phenyl isothiocyanate, built on a single benzene ring bearing one substituent. That substituent is an isothiocyanate group, where a nitrogen is double-bonded to a central carbon that is double-bonded to a sulfur atom, giving a linear N=C=S unit attached directly to the aromatic ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted otherwise, so the molecule has no additional ring fusion and only one point of substitution. Its overall shape is largely planar, with the linear isothiocyanate group extending from the ring. The nitrogen and sulfur atoms carry lone pairs, so the group can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a phenylpropiolic-type scaffold: a benzene ring bonded directly to a carbon-carbon triple bond, which connects to a carboxylic acid group at the far end. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, a simple monosubstituted aromatic ring with no fused rings present. The alkyne linker is rigid and linear, forcing the aromatic ring and the carboxyl carbon into a collinear arrangement and limiting conformational flexibility to little more than rotation of the carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and hydrogen-bond acceptors through its carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen. The overall molecule has an approximately linear, elongated shape with a single mirror-plane-like symmetry through the aromatic ring axis.

The molecule is a saturated six-membered heterocycle built from five carbon atoms and one nitrogen atom, giving a piperidine scaffold with no ring fusion and no additional substituents. Every ring atom is sp3-hybridized, so the ring is conformationally flexible and tends to adopt a chair-like geometry in which the carbon framework is free of double bonds or aromatic character. The single secondary amine nitrogen, which carries one hydrogen, is the only functional group present. Because of this, the molecule is unsubstituted and symmetric about the axis running through the nitrogen and the opposite carbon. The nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond, and the N–H bond can donate one.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring along a shared edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic framework. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position of the pyridine-type ring, and no other substituents are present. The structure has no stereocenters and is essentially rigid and planar, with the only rotatable bond being the one connecting the nitrile carbon to the ring. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen provides a second, weaker acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared edge. The nitrogen sits in the six-membered heteroaromatic ring, adjacent to the fusion carbon, and the fully aromatic framework is planar and rigid. A formyl group (an aldehyde, CHO) is attached to the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is a single substituent at the position flanking the nitrogen. The ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the aldehyde oxygen provides a second acceptor site and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the planar framework because the aldehyde breaks the symmetry of the bicyclic core.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent at one position, making it a monosubstituted aromatic compound with no additional ring fusion. That substituent is a thioamide group, in which a carbon is double-bonded to sulfur and single-bonded to an amino nitrogen, directly attached to the ring carbon. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the thioamide unit is nearly planar with the ring, giving the overall framework limited conformational flexibility. The NH2 group can donate hydrogen bonds, and the sulfur atom acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local mirror plane of the ring.

The molecule is a small aromatic thioamide built from a single five-membered thiophene ring, with no fused rings. A thioamide group, carbon double-bonded to sulfur and bearing a primary amino group, is attached directly to carbon 2 of the thiophene, leaving the ring's other positions unsubstituted. The aromatic ring and the thioamide carbon are conjugated, so the core is largely planar and fairly rigid, with only limited rotation about the bond linking the two parts. The thioamide nitrogen carries two hydrogens, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur atom of the thiocarbonyl group serves as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the approximate mirror plane of the planar core.

This molecule is a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3, which is the pyrimidine-type scaffold, with two carbonyl groups at the 2 and 4 positions, making it a pyrimidinedione. The ring is fully unsaturated with a conjugated arrangement of double bonds, so it is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. There are no fused or pendant ring systems, and the two ring nitrogens each carry a hydrogen, so the substitution pattern is unbranched and the molecule has no stereocenters. Its two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring, giving it a relatively simple and symmetric overall shape.

The molecule is built on a short, linear skeleton with no rings, so it is fully acyclic and rather flexible. It contains a vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond with two terminal carbons) attached through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon bearing a methyl group, which together form an ester functional group. The arrangement is unsymmetrical, since the vinyl end and the methyl end are chemically distinct. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks any N-H or O-H bonds.

This molecule is an ester built around a central tetrahedral carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and two unsubstituted phenyl rings, giving a diaryl glycolic acid scaffold. The carboxyl carbon is esterified to a two-carbon ethyl linker that terminates in a tertiary diethylamino group. Both aromatic rings are simple benzene rings with no ring fusion and no ring substituents, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the central carbon. The chain linking the ester oxygen to the amine is flexible, while the diphenyl-substituted center adds bulk and restricts rotation nearby. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ester carbonyl and ether oxygen serve as acceptors, and the tertiary amine nitrogen is a basic acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three methoxy groups in a 3,4,5-trimethoxy pattern, which gives it a symmetric arrangement about the axis through the ring's C-1 and C-4 positions. At the remaining ring position sits a carboxamide, which links to a linear, flexible six-carbon chain ending in a terminal carboxylic acid. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the alkyl chain adds considerable conformational freedom. The amide N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H can both act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the amide and ether oxygens, along with the carboxyl oxygens, serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is carbamazepine-type tricyclic scaffold: a dibenzazepine core in which two benzene rings are fused to a central seven-membered ring containing a nitrogen atom and a carbon-carbon double bond bridging the two aryl units. The nitrogen is substituted by a carbamoyl group, a urea-like amide bearing a carbonyl and a primary NH2. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted, so the aromatic substitution pattern is simple and unbranched. The central ring is non-planar and somewhat rigid, with the fused aromatic rings held in a folded, butterfly-like arrangement. The primary amide provides two N-H hydrogen-bond donors and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ring nitrogen is a poor acceptor because its lone pair is delocalized into the amide.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring with two substituents placed para to each other, giving it a flat, symmetric, rod-like scaffold. One substituent is a two-carbon chain ending in a primary amine (–CH2CH2NH2), which adds conformational flexibility to an otherwise rigid aromatic core. The other substituent is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring, making it a phenol. Together these groups give the molecule two hydrogen-bond donor sites from the amine and hydroxyl, and two acceptor sites from the nitrogen lone pair and the oxygen. The ring carries no fused rings and no additional stereocenters.

This molecule is built on a fused polycyclic scaffold containing an indole-like unit whose nitrogen is bridged into a second saturated ring, creating a rigid, largely planar aromatic core fused to a partially saturated nitrogen-containing ring system. A methoxy group is attached to the benzene ring of the indole portion, placing a single electron-donating ether substituent on one edge of the aromatic framework. Within the fused rings sits a tertiary amine bearing an N-methyl group, along with an amidine-type C=N double bond conjugated into the polycycle. The overall ring system is conformationally constrained, with limited rotational freedom, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. The methoxy oxygen and the ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no strong hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a pyridine ring bearing a sulfonylurea-type linkage. A meta-tolyl group (a benzene ring with a methyl substituent at the meta position) is attached through an NH bridge to the 4-position of the pyridine, while a sulfonyl group sits at the adjacent 3-position. The sulfonyl nitrogen connects to a urea unit that terminates in an isopropyl group. The two aromatic rings are joined by a flexible secondary amine, giving the molecule moderate conformational freedom around that bond, while the aromatic rings themselves remain rigid and planar. The sulfonylurea segment contributes several hydrogen-bond donors (two N–H groups) and acceptors (the sulfonyl oxygens, the urea carbonyl, and the pyridine nitrogen), and the molecule has no internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built on a quinolin-2-one core: a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring bearing a lactam carbonyl, with the ring nitrogen carrying an N-methyl group. The carbon adjacent to the carbonyl bears a hydroxyl group on the fused-ring system, giving a 4-hydroxy substitution pattern. At the 3-position sits a pyrazolone unit, a five-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogens and a carbonyl, connected through an exocyclic aminomethylene linkage that carries a pyrimidin-2-yl group on its nitrogen. The fused bicyclic core is rigid and planar, while the exocyclic linkages add some conformational flexibility. The molecule offers several hydrogen-bond donors (the hydroxyl and the NH groups) and multiple acceptors (the carbonyl oxygens and the ring nitrogens of the pyrimidine and pyrazolone).

The molecule is built on a five-membered 1,3,4-thiadiazole-type ring that carries an exocyclic imine (=NH) on one carbon, making it a 2-imino-substituted heterocycle with a sulfur and two nitrogens in the ring. A carbonyl linker attaches the ring to a thiophene, so a ketone bridges two aromatic five-membered rings. On the adjacent ring nitrogen sits a phenyl group bearing a trifluoromethyl substituent at the meta position. The imine nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the N–H of the imine can donate one. The aromatic rings are planar and conjugated, giving the core a fairly rigid character, with the ketone and N-aryl bonds allowing some rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the thiophene, carbonyl, and meta-substituted phenyl groups are arranged asymmetrically.

The molecule is built around a central amidine-type carbon that is double-bonded to one nitrogen and single-bonded to a second nitrogen, with both nitrogens bearing para-tolyl rings (benzene rings carrying a methyl group opposite the attachment point). The central carbon also bonds to a third aromatic ring, a phenol bearing two tert-butyl groups flanking the hydroxyl group, which sits at the position meta to the attachment point. The two tolyl groups are related by an approximate two-fold relationship through the amidine core, but the tert-butyl substitution on the phenol ring breaks any overall symmetry. The scaffold is fairly rigid across its aromatic portions, while the bulky tert-butyl groups restrict rotation around the phenol ring. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond donor, the phenolic OH, and several acceptors, including the phenolic oxygen and the imine-type nitrogen.

The molecule is a symmetric, extended aromatic scaffold built from two para-substituted phenylene rings joined through an azo bridge (N=N) and an azoxy-type linkage. Each terminal ring carries a primary amino group at the para position, while the central phenylene bears the two nitrogen-containing bridges, so the substitution pattern is linear and centrosymmetric in its overall arrangement. The aromatic rings are planar and conjugated through the N=N and N-oxide-containing bridges, which makes the core rigid and elongated, with limited rotational freedom. The two terminal amino groups are hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen atoms of the bridging azo and azoxy units and the oxygen of the N-oxide unit serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central stilbene-like C=C linker joining two aromatic rings, with a hydrazone (C=N–NH) arm extending from the second ring. One terminal ring is a benzene bearing two nitro groups in a 2,4-relationship to the vinyl attachment, which creates a strongly electron-poor, planar aromatic unit. The other central ring is an ortho-disubstituted benzene linking the vinyl group and the hydrazone carbon, while the hydrazone terminates in a second unsubstituted phenyl ring attached through nitrogen. The overall scaffold is largely planar and conjugated, with the alkene and hydrazone units providing limited rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, and it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through the N–H of the hydrazine and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the nitro oxygens and the imine nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a 4-quinolone core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridinone ring that carries an N-phenyl group on the ring nitrogen and a carbonyl at the position adjacent to it. A hydroxyl group sits on the fused benzo ring's neighboring carbon, and a small acetyl-derived unit is attached at the adjacent position of the pyridinone ring, where its carbon forms a C=N imine bond to a second aromatic ring. That second ring is a phenol bearing an ortho hydroxyl group and a methyl group para to the imine nitrogen, giving it a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has no overall symmetry, and its fused and linked aromatic rings, together with the imine, make it fairly rigid, with rotation limited mainly around the single bonds to the N-phenyl group and the imine-bearing carbon. Several hydroxyl oxygens and the carbonyl and imine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two phenolic hydroxyl groups provide hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is built on a tricyclic diterpenoid-like scaffold in which a saturated decalin-type bicyclic framework is fused to a quinone-containing six-membered ring. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the aromatic ring and the saturated carbon framework contribute no additional hydrogen-bonding capability. This molecule is an acetamide-type compound built from a two-carbon ethyl linker connecting a benzene ring to an acetylated amide nitrogen. The aromatic core is a single, unfused benzene ring, and the ethyl chain attaches at one carbon while a nitro group ([N+](=O)[O-]) sits on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The amide group (–NH–C(=O)–CH3) provides one hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and one acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the nitro group contributes two additional oxygen acceptor sites. The flexible ethyl linker and rotatable amide bond give the molecule considerable conformational freedom, whereas the benzene ring remains planar and rigid.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a nitro group, a chlorine atom, a second chlorine atom, and a dichloromethyl group. The nitro group and the dichloromethyl group sit on adjacent ring carbons, while the two chlorines occupy the remaining positions in a 1,3-relationship across the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and its planar, rigid framework is only modestly flexible through rotation about the bonds to the substituents. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites since every substituent lacks an N–H or O–H bond.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic terpenoid-like skeleton, specifically a bornane-type framework in which a six-membered ring and a five-membered ring share two adjacent carbons, creating a rigid, bridged cage. Three methyl groups are attached to the quaternary carbons of this cage, one of which sits on a bridgehead-adjacent position with a gem-dimethyl arrangement. A secondary alcohol hydroxyl group is located on a carbon of the ring system, and a two-carbon hydroxyethyl side chain extends from an adjacent ring carbon. The molecule therefore has two hydroxyl groups, each able to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Its overall shape is largely fixed by the bridged ring system, while the terminal hydroxyethyl chain provides the only significant conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of its substituents.

The molecule is built around a central azo group (two nitrogen atoms joined by a double bond) that links two meta-substituted phenyl rings, giving a roughly linear, extended scaffold. Each of these central rings carries an ester oxygen at the meta position, and each of those esters is capped by an unsubstituted benzoyl group, so the two outer phenyl rings are attached through their ester linkages. The molecule is symmetric about the central azo axis, with both halves identical in substitution pattern. It contains five aromatic rings in total, and the ester and azo linkages provide considerable conformational flexibility around the single bonds. The oxygen atoms of the ester carbonyls and the ester ether linkages can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring carrying a nitro group, with two identical 2-quinolinyl-substituted ethanol side chains on the ring. Each side chain bears a secondary alcohol at the carbon adjacent to the benzene ring and a methylene linking to a quinoline ring system, which is a benzene fused to a pyridine ring. The two side chains sit in a para-like relationship across the central ring, with the nitro group ortho to one of them, giving a moderately asymmetric arrangement. The aromatic systems make the framework largely rigid, while the two CH2 linkers and the carbinol carbons add some conformational flexibility. The two hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, the nitro group and the quinoline nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no other donor sites.

This molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring, forming a tetrahydroquinoline-type core. The aromatic ring carries a nitro group on one carbon and a 3-oxobutyl side chain (a methyl ketone linked through two methylene units) on the adjacent position, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern on the benzene ring. The saturated ring bears a methyl substituent on the carbon next to the nitrogen, which introduces a stereocenter. The side chain and the saturated ring add conformational flexibility, while the fused aromatic portion remains rigid and planar. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the ketone carbonyl and nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused along a shared edge to form a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) is attached to one ring, and a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing two oxygens, one charged) sits on the other ring, giving a 2-substituted naphthalene with a 6-substitution pattern across the fused system. The rigid, planar aromatic framework has essentially no conformational flexibility, apart from rotation of the methoxy group. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the methoxy and nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that bears a hydroxyl group and is attached to three aromatic rings: two unsubstituted phenyl rings and one benzene ring carrying an amino group at the position adjacent to the attachment point. The central carbon is sp3-hybridized, so the three aryl groups radiate out in a propeller-like arrangement, giving the scaffold a three-dimensional, non-planar shape. The two phenyl rings are symmetrically equivalent, while the aminated ring breaks that symmetry. The amino group, a primary aromatic amine, and the tertiary alcohol supply hydrogen-bond donor capability, and both the nitrogen and the oxygen can also act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The three benzene rings are rigid, but rotation around the bonds to the central carbon gives the overall molecule moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing a methoxy group (an oxygen attached to a methyl) on one carbon and an amide nitrogen on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho-substitution pattern. The amide links to a carbonyl that is bonded to a central carbon carrying two separate trifluoromethyl-type arms: one CF3 group and one CF2-CF3 pentafluoroethyl-like unit, making the side chain heavily fluorinated. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the aliphatic fluorinated tail is comparatively flexible, with rotation possible around its single bonds. The amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two sides of the amide differ.

This molecule is a 1,4-dihydropyridine built on a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that bears two methyl groups, two butyl ester groups, and a furan ring. The central ring is partially saturated, with one sp3 carbon carrying the furan substituent, and the adjacent nitrogen bears a hydrogen. Each of the two ester groups is a butoxycarbonyl unit attached to a ring carbon, giving the molecule a pronounced, roughly symmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The furan is a five-membered aromatic oxygen heterocycle attached at its 2-position, which adds an aromatic, planar component to one side. The dihydropyridine ring is non-planar and somewhat flexible, while the flexible butyl chains contribute considerable conformational freedom. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygens of the esters and the furan oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a fully saturated tetracyclic steroid-like skeleton built from four fused rings, with three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring typical of a cyclopenta-phenanthrene framework. Its first ring is an aromatic benzene ring carrying two adjacent methyl substituents, which places the aromatic unit at one end of the fused system. A quaternary carbon bearing an angular methyl group sits at a ring junction, giving the scaffold a rigid, bulky, three-dimensional shape. The remaining rings are all-carbon aliphatic rings, so the molecule contains no heteroatoms, no hydrogen-bond donors, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall it is a rigid, hydrophobic hydrocarbon framework with limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a 1,2,4-triazole ring fused to a six-membered 1,3,5-thiadiazine-type ring containing sulfur and two nitrogen atoms in a saturated, partly flexible arrangement. A 4-nitrophenyl group is attached directly to the triazole carbon, placing a para-substituted nitro group on one side of the scaffold. The second ring nitrogen of the thiadiazine carries an ortho-nitrophenyl group, so the molecule contains two nitro substituents on separate aromatic rings. Overall the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the two aryl groups differ in their substitution pattern. The fused core is rigid and planar, while the CH2 linkers allow some conformational flexibility; the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no classic hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core in which a six-membered thiazine-type ring shares an edge with a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring, giving a planar, rigid scaffold. A phenyl ring is attached through a saturated sp3 carbon that sits between a ring nitrogen and a sulfur atom, which introduces a small, bent point of flexibility. A pyridin-3-yl group is bonded directly to the triazole ring, extending the aromatic framework. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the local ring geometry, and its substitution is asymmetric. Hydrogen-bond capability is modest: the pyridine and triazole nitrogens serve as acceptors, and there are no strong N–H or O–H donors.

This molecule is a linear, acyclic chain built from a central six-carbon backbone with two hydroxamic acid end groups, one at each terminus. It contains two amide linkages (secondary amides) and two terminal N-hydroxy amide (hydroxamic acid) units, giving it no ring systems and no ring fusion. The chain is unbranched and highly flexible, with no stereocenters and a roughly mirror-symmetric arrangement about its center. Each end group offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (N–H and O–H) and acceptor (carbonyl and N-oxide-type oxygen) capability, and the internal amide N–H and C=O groups provide additional donor and acceptor sites along the chain.

Parsing the SMILES: CC1=C(C(=O)OCc2ccccc2)C(c2ccccc2)NC(=O)N1C. The core is a six-membered dihydropyrimidinone ring containing two nitrogens, one of which is N-methylated, with a cyclic urea carbonyl. The ring carries a methyl group and a benzyl ester on the alkene carbons, and a phenyl group sits on the sp3 carbon between the alkene and the NH. Two monocyclic benzene rings are present as pendant aryl groups, with no ring fusion. The molecule has one NH hydrogen-bond donor and several acceptors from the carbonyl oxygens. The ring is partly rigid due to the alkene and urea, while the benzyl ester adds rotational flexibility. There is no molecular symmetry, since the substituents are distinct.

The molecule is a thiobarbiturate-type ring: a six-membered pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione core in which one carbonyl oxygen at the 2-position is replaced by sulfur, giving a thiourea-like unit flanked by two amide carbonyls. The C5 carbon of this ring bears an exocyclic double bond linked to a 5-bromofuran ring, creating a conjugated, largely planar arylidene system. The bromine sits at the 5-position of the furan, adjacent to the oxygen heteroatom, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis of note. Two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the three carbonyl oxygens, the thiocarbonyl sulfur, and the furan oxygen serve as acceptors. The extended conjugation keeps the scaffold fairly rigid.

The molecule is built around a benzofuran core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a furan ring, and that core carries a second furan ring attached directly to the C3 position of the benzofuran. On the benzofuran, the C2 position bears a four-carbon side chain ending in a ketone, so there is a methyl ketone with an ethylene linker to the ring. The benzene portion carries a single methyl substituent, and the 5-methylfuran unit contributes a second methyl on its far side. The ketone's carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor of note apart from the two ring oxygens, and no hydrogen-bond donors are present. The biaryl linkage between the two furan-containing rings gives moderate rotational freedom, while the fused bicyclic framework is rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is an alpha-phenylcinnamic acid built on a three-carbon acrylic backbone, with a carboxylic acid group on one end and a carbon-carbon double bond connecting to a benzylidene unit. Two separate phenyl rings are attached: one sits at the alpha carbon bearing the carboxyl group and the other terminates the vinyl chain, so the scaffold is a stilbene-like diaryl alkene bearing a carboxyl group. The two aromatic rings are unfused, monocyclic benzene rings with no substituents on them, giving an unsubstituted pattern. The alkene is largely planar, and the molecule has only partial symmetry, since the carboxylic acid breaks the symmetry between the two aryl ends. Rotation about the single bonds to the phenyl rings allows some flexibility, though conjugation favors a fairly extended arrangement. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak pi-type interactions.

The molecule is built around a six-membered 1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione ring, a cyclic malonate-type diester bearing a gem-dimethyl group on the carbon between the two ring oxygens, which makes that part of the scaffold rigid and sterically crowded. An exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond at the 5-position links this ring to a furan ring, which in turn carries a para-nitrophenyl group at its 5-position, giving an extended, largely planar conjugated system. The nitro group sits on the terminal benzene ring and acts as a strong electron-withdrawing substituent. The two carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall framework is fairly rigid, with limited rotational freedom apart from the gem-dimethyl groups.

The molecule is built around an isatin-type bicyclic core: a five-membered lactam ring (an indolin-2-one skeleton) fused to a benzene ring, with the C3 carbonyl converted into an exocyclic imine (C=N) linking to the nitrogen of a 1,2,4-triazole. That triazole carries a thiol group on one carbon and a trifluoromethyl group on the other, both on the aromatic heterocycle. The ring fusion is planar and fully aromatic on the benzene side, giving the molecule a largely rigid, flat framework with limited rotational freedom apart from the N–N bond. Its hydrogen-bond capacity is mixed: the lactam N–H and the thiol S–H can act as donors, while the lactam carbonyl, the imine nitrogen, and the triazole ring nitrogens serve as acceptors. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the benzo ring, lactam, and substituted triazole are arranged asymmetrically.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic core in which a pyridine ring is fused to a coumarin-type lactone ring and a benzene ring, giving a largely planar, rigid aromatic framework. A 2-ethylamino substituent (an N-ethyl amine attached to the carbon next to the pyridine nitrogen) sits on the pyridine ring, while an ethyl ester group (an ethoxycarbonyl) is attached at the adjacent carbon. The lactone carbonyl and ester carbonyl oxygens, together with the pyridine nitrogen, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the secondary amine N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents occupy non-equivalent positions, and only the terminal ethyl groups show some conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a single tertiary amide: a nitrogen bearing two isopropyl groups, with its carbonyl carbon attached to a central carbon that carries two trifluoromethyl groups. The scaffold is acyclic, so there are no ring systems or ring fusions. The functional groups are the amide and the six fluorine atoms in the two CF3 units, which make the terminal portion highly fluorinated and electron-poor. The two isopropyl groups on nitrogen are equivalent, giving the molecule a local mirror-like symmetry around the amide nitrogen. Rotation about the C–N and C–C single bonds leaves the molecule fairly flexible, though the bulky isopropyl and trifluoromethyl groups restrict some conformations. The carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused tetracyclic scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, with the rings fused in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene arrangement. Its C-17 side chain is an eight-carbon branched alkyl chain ending in an isopropyl terminus, and two angular methyl groups project from the ring junctions. Three hydroxyl groups are placed on the ring framework, two of them on a single carbon that sits at a ring junction, which makes that region of the scaffold more crowded. The saturated, fully aliphatic ring system is rigid overall, with only the side chain and the hydroxyls contributing conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl groups serve as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the rest of the skeleton is hydrophobic and offers no additional polar contacts.

The molecule is built on an indole core, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole-type ring containing nitrogen. The nitrogen carries an N-methyl group, so it has no N-H and cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor, though its lone pair is not available for acceptance either since it is part of the aromatic system. The pyrrole ring bears a methyl group at the carbon adjacent to nitrogen and a phenyl ring attached at the neighboring carbon, giving a 2,3-substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core and the directly bonded phenyl ring make the framework largely planar and rigid, with only modest rotational freedom around the single bond to the phenyl group. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry axis, and it presents essentially no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship, forming a cyclic imide-like scaffold. One ring nitrogen carries a methyl group, while the other nitrogen is part of a secondary amide (lactam) linkage. Two carbonyl groups sit at the ring positions adjacent to the nitrogens: one amide carbonyl within the ring and one urea-type carbonyl flanked by both nitrogens. The remaining ring carbons are sp3-hybridized CH2 groups, so the ring is non-aromatic and rather compact. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a 1,2-diketone, specifically 1,4-diphenylbutane-2,3-dione, with two benzyl groups flanking a central vicinal dicarbonyl unit. Each terminal end carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring attached through a single methylene linker, so the scaffold is a flexible, acyclic chain bearing two aromatic rings and no fused ring system. The two carbonyl groups are directly bonded to each other, giving an adjacent diketone motif, and the phenyl rings are unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple and symmetric. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the central C–C bond of the dicarbonyl unit. Rotation about the methylene and carbonyl bonds gives considerable conformational flexibility. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, with two nitrogen atoms adjacent to each other in the ring. The ring carries three substituents: a primary carboxamide group (-C(=O)NH2) on one carbon, a free primary amino group (-NH2) on the neighboring carbon, and a 2-hydroxyethyl chain (-CH2CH2OH) on one of the ring nitrogens. There is no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is non-symmetric. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the hydroxyethyl chain adds some conformational flexibility. The amide and amino groups, together with the terminal hydroxyl, supply several hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogen, amide oxygen, and hydroxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a steroidal scaffold built from four fused rings in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene arrangement: three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring, with trans-fused junctions giving a rigid, largely planar-stacked framework. A ketone sits on one of the six-membered rings, and two acetate esters are attached to the ring system at separate positions, one on the A-ring and one on the B-ring region. A methyl ester side chain extends from the five-membered ring, linked by a flexible alkyl chain, while two angular methyl groups project from the ring junctions. The molecule is asymmetric because of its substitution pattern and multiple stereocenters. Its hydrogen-bond capability is limited: it has no donor groups, while the carbonyl and ester oxygens act as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a phenylglycine-type core, with a benzene ring attached to a stereocenter bearing a free carboxylic acid group. That alpha carbon also connects to a carbamate nitrogen, which is acylated by a carbonyl linked through an oxygen to a CH2 group bearing a trichloromethyl terminus. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion has no ring substitution pattern to speak of. The molecule has no ring fusion and is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds linking the aromatic ring, the chiral center, and the trichloroethyl ester-like tail. The carboxylic acid offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the carbamate N-H adds a donor, and the carbonyl and ether oxygens act as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a propanoic acid skeleton in which the alpha carbon carries both a methyl group and two phenyl rings, making it a quaternary carbon bearing two aromatic substituents. The two benzene rings are unfused and attached to the same central carbon, so they are not part of a fused ring system. The terminal carboxylic acid group provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens. The two phenyl groups are bulky and sterically crowded around the central carbon, which restricts rotation somewhat, though the carboxylic acid end retains some flexibility. The molecule lacks a plane or axis of symmetry overall, though the two phenyl rings are chemically equivalent to each other.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold. The ring carries three substituents: a hydroxyl group, a thiol group, and two tert-butyl groups. Both tert-butyl groups are bulky quaternary carbon substituents attached at positions flanking the hydroxyl group, one on each side, so the hydroxyl sits between them. The thiol group sits on the carbon opposite the hydroxyl, giving a 1,3,5-type arrangement across the ring. The ring is fully aromatic and rigid, while the tert-butyl groups add steric bulk with little conformational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the hydroxyl and thiol carbons, so it is nearly symmetric. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the thiol can serve as a weak donor and acceptor.

This molecule is a tricyclic, fully aromatic-looking framework built from a pyridine-type ring fused to a benzene-type ring and a saturated cyclohexane ring. The central unit is a quinoline-like system, in which a six-membered ring containing one sp2 nitrogen is fused to a second aromatic six-membered ring, and a cyclohexane ring is fused onto the nitrogen-containing ring at the adjacent carbons. The nitrogen is the only heteroatom, and it sits within the aromatic system as an acceptor with no attached hydrogen, so it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the saturated carbocyclic ring adds some conformational flexibility at its edge. The overall structure is asymmetric, since the two sides of the fused framework are not equivalent.

This molecule is a branched, fully saturated-except-for-one-site aliphatic hydrocarbon built on a linear chain of nine carbons. Its backbone is an open chain with no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms. The one unsaturation is a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, with a methyl group on the internal alkene carbon, which creates a short branch at one end of the chain. Because the molecule lacks any symmetry-breaking polar groups beyond the alkene, its structure is essentially nonpolar, and it is highly flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated alkane-based alcohol built on a branched carbon skeleton. A central quaternary carbon bears two methyl groups, an ethyl group, and a substituted carbinol carbon that carries two methyl groups and one hydroxyl group. The only polar functional group is the single tertiary hydroxyl (-OH), which can both donate one hydrogen bond and accept one. Apart from that group, the structure consists entirely of sp3 carbons with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic units. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the ethyl and methyl substituents differ, and its many single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three alkyl substituents: an ethyl group and two methyl groups, arranged on adjacent carbons so that the ethyl sits next to a methyl and the second methyl sits on the far side of that same pair. This is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings and no heteroatoms. It contains no functional groups beyond the carbon-hydrogen framework, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The three substituents break the ring's symmetry, giving it only a mirror plane through the ring's substitution pattern, while the aromatic core itself is rigid and the ethyl group adds modest conformational flexibility.

The molecule is an aliphatic secondary amine built on a straight, unbranched eight-carbon chain. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and open. The nitrogen sits at one end of the chain and carries a single methyl group, which makes it a secondary amine with one N-H bond. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond the trivial, since the methyl group and the octyl chain sit at opposite ends. Its long saturated chain gives it considerable conformational flexibility, while the nitrogen lone pair and single N-H group allow it to act as both a hydrogen-bond acceptor and a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is an acetyl group, a ketone in which a methyl group is bonded to a carbonyl carbon attached to the ring. The other is a nitrile, a carbon-nitrogen triple bond directly attached to the ring. The benzene core is fully aromatic and planar, while the acetyl group has a single rotatable bond that gives it modest conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen provides a second acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, since the two substituents differ in identity.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds, bearing a single substituent at one position, so it is a monosubstituted benzene rather than a fused or multi-ring system. Attached to that ring is a three-carbon chain containing a carbon-carbon double bond directly next to the ring, forming a styrenyl-type unit. The far end of the chain carries a chlorine atom on a terminal methylene group, making it a primary alkyl chloride (an allylic halide, since the chlorine sits adjacent to the alkene). The molecule has no stereocenters and the aromatic ring has a local mirror plane through the substituent, giving it a flat, rather rigid aromatic core with a more flexible allylic tail. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatom, the chlorine, is a weak acceptor.

This molecule is an acyclic ether built from two linear five-carbon alkyl chains joined through a single oxygen atom, giving a symmetric C5-O-C5 skeleton with no rings and no additional substituents. Its carbon framework is fully saturated, containing only single bonds, so the molecule is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations through rotation about its C-C and C-O bonds. The sole functional group is the central ether oxygen, which is bonded to two alkyl carbons and has no hydrogen on it. Because that oxygen lacks any hydrogen, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, but the oxygen's lone pairs allow it to act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The structure is essentially symmetric about the central oxygen, with both pentyl arms identical in length and connectivity.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond with no fused ring system. One ring carries a chlorine atom at the meta position relative to the bond connecting the two rings, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The only functional group present is the aryl chloride, and the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors beyond the halogen. The two rings can rotate about the central single bond, giving the framework moderate conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry because of the asymmetric chlorine placement.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a single methylene (CH2) bridge, giving a diarylmethane scaffold. One ring carries an ethyl group (a two-carbon alkyl chain) at the position para to the bridge, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The two aromatic rings are not fused; each is an isolated, planar six-membered ring with delocalized pi electrons. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it cannot accept hydrogen bonds either. The CH2 bridge and the ethyl chain provide some rotational flexibility, while the aromatic rings themselves are rigid.

The molecule is built on a single saturated carbon chain bearing two phenyl rings, giving a 1,2-diphenylpropane scaffold. The central carbon is a methine that carries a methyl group, linking one benzyl-type arm (a CH2 attached to a phenyl ring) with a directly attached phenyl ring, so the two aromatic rings are not fused and are separated by flexible sp3 carbons. The structure has no heteroatoms and therefore no functional groups beyond the two unsubstituted benzene rings and alkyl substituents. Because the central carbon is a stereocenter, the molecule is chiral, and the rotatable single bonds make its overall shape fairly flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is a fully saturated, acyclic hydrocarbon with a single unbranched chain of carbons and one methyl branch placed near the terminus. The longest backbone runs through a long run of CH2 units, ending in a CH3 group at one end, while the other end carries a CH carrying a methyl substituent, giving the scaffold an isoalkane-like shape. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups of any kind. The molecule is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many C–C single bonds, and it has no symmetry beyond local conformational freedom. It lacks any hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, since all atoms are carbon and hydrogen only.

The molecule is built from a single benzene ring bearing one long, unbranched alkyl chain of eleven carbons attached to the ring at one position, so it has a monosubstituted aromatic scaffold. The benzene ring is a fully aromatic, planar six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion and no heteroatoms. There are no functional groups beyond the hydrocarbon framework, so the molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. The structure has a rigid, flat aromatic head joined to a highly flexible, freely rotating aliphatic tail, and it lacks any internal symmetry axis that would make both ends equivalent. Overall, it is a largely nonpolar, elongated hydrocarbon in which the aromatic ring and the linear chain contribute distinctly different conformational behavior.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Five of the six ring positions carry chlorine atoms, and the remaining position bears a nitro group (–NO2), so the substitution pattern is fully crowded around the ring with one carbon left unsubstituted in the sense that every position is occupied. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and is attached to a ring carbon flanked by two chlorine-bearing carbons, which places it in a sterically congested environment. The ring is rigid and planar, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the nitro group. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a symmetric diketone built from a linear five-carbon chain (pentane-1,5-dione skeleton) whose two terminal carbonyl carbons are each bonded to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, giving an aryl-ketone scaffold with no ring fusion. Each aromatic ring is a simple benzene ring with no substituents, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted at every ring position. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the central methylene carbon and is quite flexible because of the four sp3 methylene units in the chain. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all its hydrogens sit on carbon.

This molecule is built on a diarylmethane scaffold, with two benzene rings joined through a single saturated methylene carbon. Each ring is a simple unfused six-membered aromatic ring, so there is no ring fusion. One ring carries a primary amino group on the position adjacent to the methylene bridge, while the other carries an ethyl group on the ortho position relative to that bridge, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern on the second ring. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the two rings bear different substituents. The central CH2 linker allows rotation, so the structure is moderately flexible rather than rigid. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the rest of the molecule contributes only hydrophobic aromatic and alkyl surface.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near-adjacent positions: a carboxylic acid group, an acetamido group (an acetyl group bonded through nitrogen to the ring), and a primary amino group. The carboxylic acid and the acetamido nitrogen sit on neighboring carbons, while the amino group is positioned on the far side of the ring, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amide and acid substituents can rotate about their single bonds. The molecule offers several hydrogen-bond donors, including the amide N-H, the amino N-H groups, and the carboxylic O-H, and several acceptors, including the amide and carboxyl carbonyl oxygens and the nitrogen atoms.

This molecule is a cage-like tricyclic scaffold built from three saturated six-membered rings sharing nitrogen and methylene bridges, resembling a bicyclic diazabicyclooctane-type framework extended into a fused polyaza cage. It contains two N-nitroso groups (N–N=O), each attached to a ring nitrogen, which serve as the principal functional groups and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms. The ring nitrogens are tertiary amine centers bridging the cage, while the methylene carbons link them into a rigid, highly constrained three-dimensional framework with little conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is symmetric, with the two nitroso-bearing nitrogens occupying equivalent positions across the cage. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogen atoms reside on carbon.

The molecule is an azo dye built on a naphthalene core bearing a sulfonic acid and a hydroxyl group, linked through a trans N=N bridge to a substituted phenol ring. The phenol ring carries a methyl group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent-to-azo positions, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern across the two aromatic units. The naphthalene unit is a fused bicyclic aromatic system, while the azo linkage keeps the two ring systems conjugated and largely planar, so the scaffold is rigid apart from rotation at the sulfonic acid group. Hydroxyl groups and the sulfonic acid provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, and the sulfonyl oxygens, the phenolic oxygens, and the azo nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built from two pyrazolone rings joined by a methylene bridge at their 4-positions. Each pyrazolone is a five-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and a carbonyl group, with a methyl group on the ring carbon and an N-phenyl group on one nitrogen, while the other nitrogen carries a methyl group. The two ring units are chemically identical, so the overall structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry about the central CH2 linker. Each pyrazolone carbonyl acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are substituted. The two phenyl rings add bulk and aromatic character, and the connecting methylene bridge gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on an adamantane-type cage, a rigid, three-dimensionally bridged polycyclic hydrocarbon framework made of fused cyclohexane rings. Its only substituent is a single iodine atom attached to one of the bridgehead carbons, so there is no functional group beyond the carbon-iodine bond. The cage contains no heteroatoms, meaning it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. The framework is highly symmetric, with a near-threefold axis through the substituted bridgehead, and it is conformationally locked with essentially no flexibility.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone, benzophenone, in which both phenyl rings carry deuterium at every ring position, so all ten aromatic hydrogens are replaced by deuterium atoms. The central carbonyl carbon links two unsubstituted phenyl rings directly, with no additional substituents on either ring, giving a symmetrical scaffold. Each benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the two rings are rotationally twisted relative to the carbonyl plane, which limits conformational freedom to rotation about the two aryl-carbonyl bonds. The ketone oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single benzene ring in which all six carbon positions carry a chlorine atom, so the scaffold is a fully substituted aromatic six-membered ring with no remaining aromatic hydrogens. Its structure is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the six chlorine substituents are arranged symmetrically around the ring. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites beyond the weakly electronegative halogen atoms, which contribute only modest polar character. Its chemistry is dominated by the aromatic core and the carbon-chlorine bonds attached to it.

This molecule is a linear peptide-like chain built from a repeating unit of amide-linked residues, with no rings and no aromatic groups, so its scaffold is an acyclic polyamide backbone. It contains several amide bonds, and two of its residues carry hydroxyl groups on a carbon adjacent to a side-chain fragment, while the chain terminates in a free carboxylic acid at one end and an acylated amine at the other. The molecule is largely composed of branched alkyl side chains, including several isopropyl and isobutyl groups, giving it an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Its many rotatable single bonds make it highly flexible, while the stereocenters fix the spatial arrangement of its substituents. The amide N-H groups and the hydroxyl and carboxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygens along the backbone and the terminal acid serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries a methyl group, and the other carries a sulfonamide unit: a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to an NH group that is itself attached to an ethyl chain. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered system with no additional rings, so the overall scaffold is compact and fairly rigid, though the ethyl chain and the S–N bond allow some conformational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring's long axis, broken only by the different ends of the substituents. The sulfonamide N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an organophosphorus compound built around a central phosphorus atom bearing a double-bonded sulfur (a thiophosphate core), with two methoxy groups attached to it. The third oxygen links the phosphorus to a benzene ring, which is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no fusion. That ring carries a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing two oxygens, one charged) positioned para to the phosphate ester oxygen, giving a linear 1,4-substitution pattern. The phosphorus center is tetrahedral and the molecule has considerable conformational flexibility around the P–O bonds, while the aromatic ring is rigid and planar. The sulfur and the nitro oxygens and the phosphate oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a phenanthrene-type tricyclic scaffold: three fused six-membered aromatic rings arranged in an angular rather than linear fashion. A carbonitrile group (a nitrile, C≡N) is attached to the central ring at a single position, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted with no other functional groups. The fused aromatic framework is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond its planar framework because the nitrile sits off-center. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: there are no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a single central sulfur atom, so it has no carbon skeleton and no rings or ring fusion. Sulfur is bonded to two oxygen atoms through double bonds and to two chlorine atoms through single bonds, giving a tetrahedral-type arrangement of four substituents around that center. The two chlorine atoms and the two oxygen atoms are the only functional features, and the sulfur-oxygen and sulfur-chlorine bonds define a compact, rigid geometry with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has a high degree of local symmetry: the two oxygens are equivalent, and the two chlorines are equivalent. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no hydrogen atoms, but the oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single carbon atom bearing three fluorine atoms and one additional fluorine atom, giving a tetrahedral scaffold with no rings, no ring fusion, and no other functional groups. Its substitution pattern is fully symmetric, with four identical fluorine substituents arranged around the central carbon at roughly equal angles, so the structure has high local symmetry. Because there are no rotatable bonds, the molecule is entirely rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, since no hydrogen atoms are attached to heteroatoms. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor character comes from the lone pairs on the four electronegative fluorine atoms.

The molecule is a phosphate triester: a central phosphorus atom doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly bonded to three ortho-tolyloxy groups. Each aryl ring is a benzene ring bearing a methyl group adjacent to the oxygen linkage, so the substitution pattern is ortho on all three arms. The three aromatic rings are not fused to one another and are connected only through the flexible P–O–C linkages, giving a propeller-like, conformationally flexible framework without a rigid ring system. The phosphoryl oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ester oxygens are weaker acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its three arms are related by an approximate threefold arrangement around the phosphorus center.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The thiazole carries a primary amino group on the carbon between the sulfur and the ring nitrogen, which is the position typically reactive in this heterocycle. On the benzene portion, a trifluoromethoxy group is attached at a position para to the ring fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen side, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with only the exocyclic amino and trifluoromethoxy groups offering rotational freedom. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the ring nitrogen and the oxygen of the ether serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a pentacyclic fused framework containing a quinoline unit merged with a pyrrolo-fused pyridone and a lactone ring, giving a rigid, largely planar polycyclic core. An ethyl group sits on one aromatic carbon and a second ethyl group sits on a tertiary carbon bearing a hydroxyl, which together create a stereocenter in the lactone-containing ring. The aromatic system is decorated at one position by a carbamate linkage that connects to a piperidine ring, which itself carries a piperidinyl substituent, adding conformational flexibility to that peripheral region. Hydrogen-bond capability is present through the tertiary hydroxyl group, which acts as a donor, along with several carbonyl oxygens and ring nitrogens that serve as acceptors. Overall the molecule has no internal symmetry, and its rigid fused core contrasts with the flexible appendage.

This molecule is a methyl ester of a phenyl-substituted piperidine-based amino acid scaffold. A central carbon bears a methoxycarbonyl group (a methyl ester), a phenyl ring, and a piperidine ring attached through its carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, so the stereocenter-rich core links three distinct units. The benzene ring is unsubstituted and planar, while the piperidine is a saturated six-membered ring with a secondary amine that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The ester carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule lacks any fused ring system, giving it moderate conformational flexibility around the single bonds that connect the three fragments.

This molecule is built on a steroid-like four-ring fused skeleton, with three cyclohexane-type rings and a fourth cyclopentane-like ring that is bridged into a fused polycyclic framework. A cyclic acetal (a dioxolane-type ring) is formed across the lower portion of the scaffold, bearing an n-propyl substituent on the acetal carbon. The upper A ring is a cross-conjugated dienone, containing two carbon-carbon double bonds and a ketone, and a secondary alcohol sits on the B-ring region. A two-carbon ketol side chain (a ketone bearing a hydroxymethyl group) is attached at the ring-junction carbon. The molecule is rigid and bulky with several stereocenters, providing a single hydroxyl donor and multiple oxygen acceptor sites from the ketones, the alcohol, and the acetal oxygens.

This molecule is built on a two-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring, giving a phenyl-substituted scaffold with no fused ring systems. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion is a simple monosubstituted phenyl group. The chain carries two adjacent stereogenic carbons: one bearing a primary amino group and a methyl group, and the other bearing a hydroxyl group that connects directly to the ring. Because the aromatic ring sits on one end and a small methyl group on the other, the molecule is only moderately flexible, with rotation possible around the single bonds of the side chain. Both the amine and the hydroxyl can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aromatic ring offers a region capable of pi interactions.

The molecule is built around a sulfonamide linker joining two aromatic rings. One ring is a benzene bearing a sulfonyl group at one position and a primary amino group para to it, giving a para-disubstituted, planar aromatic core. The other ring is a pyrazine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4 arrangement, which carries a methoxy group on a carbon adjacent to one ring nitrogen and the sulfonamide nitrogen on the neighboring carbon. The sulfonamide nitrogen bears one hydrogen, so it can donate a hydrogen bond, while the sulfonyl oxygens and the pyrazine nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the primary amine offers two additional donor hydrogens. The two aromatic rings are connected through the flexible S–N bond, so the molecule is moderately flexible rather than fully rigid, and it has no internal symmetry because the substituents on the two rings differ.

This molecule is built on a fused bicyclic decalin-type core, consisting of two six-membered carbocyclic rings sharing a common edge, with one ring bearing a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with a second alkene. A 2,2-dimethylbutanoate ester is attached to one ring, adding a bulky quaternary carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. A second, separate six-membered lactone ring hangs off an ethyl linker from the fused core, and it carries a secondary hydroxyl group beside its ring carbonyl. Several methyl substituents and multiple stereocenters decorate the framework, which makes the scaffold rigid in its fused portion but flexible in the side chains. The ester and lactone carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl hydrogen serves as the only hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built on a tricyclic dibenzo-oxazepine core, in which two benzene rings are fused to a seven-membered ring containing an oxygen atom and a C=N imine bond. One benzene ring carries a chlorine substituent positioned para to the ring oxygen, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern. At the imine carbon sits a piperazine ring bearing an N-methyl group on its distal nitrogen, adding a flexible, saturated, basic amine region to the otherwise rigid, planar aromatic framework. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are tertiary or imine-type, while the ring nitrogens and the ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a tetracyclic anthracyclinone-type scaffold, with three fused six-membered rings that share edges plus an attached aminosugar. The two outer rings are aromatic, with a methoxy group on one of them, and the central ring carries two quinone-type carbonyl groups that bridge the aromatic rings. The saturated ring fused to the aromatic system bears a tertiary alcohol and an acetyl side chain, and a glycosidic linkage attaches a six-membered sugar ring containing a primary amine and two hydroxyl groups. The fused framework is largely rigid, while the sugar and side chain add some flexibility. Several hydroxyl, carbonyl, ether, and amine groups together give the molecule many hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

This molecule is a bicyclic saturated hydrocarbon built on a norbornane-type scaffold, with a seven-carbon framework in which two carbon bridges link a central pair of bridgehead atoms. Its two bridgehead carbons are both quaternary-like tertiary centers, and the structure carries three methyl groups, two on one bridge carbon and one on a bridgehead, which gives it a compact, bulky shape. The ring system is fully saturated, containing no double bonds, aromatic rings, or heteroatoms. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, since only carbon and hydrogen are present. The rigid, cage-like bicyclic core restricts conformational freedom, while the defined stereocenters fix the three-dimensional arrangement of the methyl substituents.

The molecule is built around a 4-(methylthio)phenyl ring attached to a ketone carbonyl that bridges to a five-membered heteroaromatic ring. That five-membered ring contains two nitrogen atoms, with an NH group adjacent to a carbonyl (a cyclic urea-like, imidazolone-type arrangement), and a methyl group sits on the carbon next to the other NH. The para-substituted benzene ring carries a methylthio group (a thioether), giving a relatively flat, conjugated aryl-ketone-heterocycle framework with limited rotational freedom apart from the ring linkages. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the two ring NH groups, while the ketone oxygen, the ring carbonyl oxygen, and the sulfur atom serve as acceptor sites. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two rings are substituted differently.

This molecule is a para-aminobenzoate ester built on a benzene ring, with an ester linkage connecting the aromatic core to a flexible two-carbon chain. The ring carries a primary amino group (–NH2) and a carbonyl ester at positions 1 and 4, giving a symmetric para substitution pattern. The ester side chain ends in a tertiary diethylamino group, which contains no hydrogen-bond donors but offers a basic nitrogen acceptor. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ethoxy-linked chain is highly flexible due to its rotatable single bonds. Overall, the molecule has both hydrogen-bond donor capability (from the amino N–H bonds) and acceptor capability (from the ester oxygens and the nitrogens).

This molecule is a tricyclic fused system built around a central seven-membered diazepinone-type ring bridging a methyl-substituted pyridine and a second pyridine ring. The left pyridine carries a methyl group and is fused to the central ring through a nitrogen-adjacent carbon, while the right pyridine is fused through its own ring carbons and bears a carbonyl that forms a lactam (amide) with an adjacent NH. The remaining ring nitrogen is substituted with a cyclopropyl group, which adds a small, rigid, three-membered ring. The amide N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the two pyridine nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fused, partly non-planar framework gives the molecule limited conformational flexibility, and it lacks any significant molecular symmetry.

The molecule is a fully aromatic bicyclic heterocycle built from two six-membered rings fused along a shared edge, so the scaffold is a pyrazine-like bicycle containing four ring nitrogen atoms. One ring is a pyrazine and the other is a pyrimidine, and the two share a carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat, rigid, planar framework with no rotatable bonds and no stereocenters. Because there are no hydrogen-bond-donating groups, every nitrogen acts only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the four ring nitrogens are arranged asymmetrically across the two rings. The unsubstituted carbon positions carry only hydrogen atoms, so there are no appended functional groups or substituents.

The molecule is a short, flexible aliphatic chain built from a two-carbon backbone with no rings and no fused ring systems. One terminus carries a carboxylic acid group, consisting of a carbonyl oxygen and a hydroxyl, while the other terminus is a sulfonic acid group, where a sulfur atom bears two double-bonded oxygens and one hydroxyl. The two acidic groups are joined through a single methylene carbon, giving a linear, unbranched arrangement with no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry. Because the scaffold is small and contains only single-bond rotations, its conformational freedom is high. Both acidic groups act as hydrogen-bond donors through their hydroxyl hydrogens and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their multiple oxygen atoms.

This molecule is a phosphorothioate triester: a central phosphorus atom bearing a double-bonded sulfur and two methoxy groups, linked through an oxygen to a substituted benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying a nitro group para to the phosphate ester oxygen and a methyl group ortho to the nitro group, which gives an asymmetric substitution pattern. The phosphorus center is tetrahedral and the two methyl ester arms are conformationally flexible, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are on carbon. Its hydrogen-bond acceptors include the nitro oxygens, the ester oxygens, and the thiophosphoryl sulfur.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing six substituents in a contiguous pattern. A dipropylamino group sits on one ring carbon, flanked by two nitro groups (one ortho on each side) and a primary sulfonamide placed meta to the amine, so the ring is heavily substituted and essentially planar. The two propyl chains attached to the tertiary nitrogen are flexible and lack symmetry with respect to the rest of the framework, although the two nitro groups give a partly symmetric electron-withdrawing arrangement. The nitro groups can accept hydrogen bonds through their oxygen atoms, while the sulfonamide offers both donor (NH2) and acceptor (sulfonyl oxygens) capability. The tertiary amine nitrogen is conjugated with the aromatic ring and contributes little hydrogen-bond donor capacity.

The molecule is a diaryl ether, with two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen bridge. One ring carries a nitro group para to the ether oxygen, giving a simple para-disubstituted pattern. The other ring bears a trifluoromethyl group para to the ether oxygen and a nitro group ortho to it, so it is trisubstituted. Both nitro groups are strongly electron-withdrawing, and the trifluoromethyl group adds further electron withdrawal on the second ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygens of the two nitro groups and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The two rings are linked through a flexible C–O–C bridge, so they can rotate relative to one another, while each aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no fused or additional rings. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a hydroxyl group, which makes it an alcohol, and a methyl group, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern with the two stereocenters defined.
