The ring is fully sp3-hybridized and conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair-type conformations that place the substituents in axial or equatorial positions. The hydroxyl oxygen serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the framework is purely hydrocarbon and offers no further polar contact points. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because of its two distinct substituents and chiral centers.

The molecule is a fused polycyclic compound built around a coumarin-type lactone core, with a fused furanone-like ring bearing a ketone. A methoxy group sits on one aromatic ring, and the aromatic portion is fused to a partially saturated oxygen-containing bridged ring system, giving a rigid, largely planar fused framework with a stereogenic center at the junction of the saturated rings. The lactone carbonyl and the cyclopentanone-type ketone serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the ether oxygens, including the methoxy oxygen and the ring ether oxygens, provide additional acceptor sites. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, and its overall shape is asymmetric because of the single methoxy substituent and the non-equivalent fused rings.

The molecule is built around a five-membered aromatic imidazole ring bearing a nitro group, specifically a 5-nitroimidazole with the nitrogen at position 1 linked through a two-carbon ethyl chain to a morpholine ring. The nitro group, attached directly to a ring carbon, is a strong electron-withdrawing feature and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms. The morpholine is a saturated six-membered ring containing both an ether oxygen and a tertiary amine nitrogen, which serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor and contributes basic character to the structure. The ethylene linker gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility between the two ring systems, while the aromatic core remains planar and rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry axis, since the nitro group and the side chain occupy different positions on the imidazole.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. A methyl group and a nitro group sit on neighboring carbons, with a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the nitro-bearing carbon, creating a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and is oriented toward the hydroxyl, which can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with one of its oxygens. The hydroxyl group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro oxygens act as acceptors. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ.

This molecule is an azo dye built around a central N=N double bond linking two substituted benzene rings, giving an extended, largely planar aromatic framework. One ring carries a methyl group and a bis(2-hydroxyethyl)amino substituent, which contributes two terminal primary alcohol groups. The other ring bears a nitro group and a chlorine atom, placed on the same side of the azo linkage. The azo nitrogens and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two hydroxyl groups serve as both donors and acceptors. The overall structure is asymmetric, and the azo bridge keeps the molecule fairly rigid, with the hydroxyethyl arms offering the main conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. A methyl group and an amino group sit on adjacent carbons, and a hydroxyl group is placed on the ring so that it lies para to the methyl group. Because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond its flat aromatic framework. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl and hydroxyl groups add only limited conformational freedom. The amino and hydroxyl groups each provide hydrogen-bond donor capability through their N–H and O–H bonds and can also act as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents on adjacent (ortho) positions. One substituent is a carbamate group, in which an oxygen links the ring to a carbonyl carbon that is also bonded to an N-methylamino nitrogen. The other is an isopropyl group, a branched alkyl chain attached through a single carbon. The ring is aromatic and planar, while the carbamate and isopropyl groups are non-fused and rotatable, which gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility. The carbamate contributes one hydrogen-bond donor from its N-H and several acceptors from its carbonyl and ether-type oxygens. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two ortho substituents differ.

The molecule is built on a five-membered 1,2,4-thiadiazole aromatic ring containing one sulfur and two nitrogen atoms. An ethoxy group, a two-carbon chain attached through an oxygen, is bonded to one of the ring carbons, giving a simple ether substituent. The other ring carbon carries a trichloromethyl group, a carbon bearing three chlorine atoms, which makes this substituent bulky and electron-withdrawing. The ring nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused-free, planar scaffold is fairly rigid, with only the ethyl and trichloromethyl groups offering rotational freedom, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is a simple alkylbenzene: a single benzene ring carrying one long, unbranched alkyl chain of twenty carbon atoms attached at one position. The aromatic ring is a planar, fully conjugated six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, heteroatoms, or additional substituents, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The molecule has no functional groups beyond the hydrocarbon framework, and its only polar feature is the aromatic pi system. Because the chain can rotate freely about its many single bonds, the structure is highly flexible, with the rigid ring at one end. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, and it has no meaningful symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the phenyl ring.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two adjacent carbons on the ring carry hydroxyl groups, making it a catechol-type diol, while a third substituent, an isopropyl group, sits on a neighboring carbon, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstitution pattern. The arrangement lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the isopropyl group adds modest conformational freedom. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, so the molecule can engage in hydrogen bonding through its two phenolic OH groups.

The molecule is built on a short, acyclic three-carbon chain with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple open-chain hydrocarbon backbone. At its core is a terminal alkene, a carbon-carbon double bond at one end, where the second carbon carries two substituents: a chloromethyl group and a chloromethyl-bearing ethyl branch. Each of the two carbon-chlorine bonds is a polar, electron-withdrawing alkyl halide functional group, making the molecule a bis(halomethyl) alkene. The structure is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds, and it lacks any symmetry-breaking rigidity. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the chlorine atoms, which are weak.

The molecule is built on a dibenzo-fused seven-membered ring: two benzene rings are joined through a central saturated ethylene bridge (CH2-CH2) and a carbon that carries an oxime group (C=N-OH). The oxime is attached to the central ring carbon, which sits between the two aromatic rings, giving a tricyclic framework that is fairly rigid in its aromatic portions but has some conformational flexibility in the non-aromatic seven-membered ring. Each benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic systems carry only ring fusion, with no additional substituents. The oxime hydroxyl group can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the imine nitrogen acts as an acceptor. Overall, the molecule lacks any true symmetry element because the oxime breaks the potential mirror relationship of the two halves.

The molecule is a small acyclic carbamate built around a single carbonyl carbon bonded to an isopropyl ester oxygen and a primary amino group. It has no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system, and the skeleton is a short, flexible chain with the isopropyl group branching from the central oxygen. The carbamate unit (an ester oxygen attached to a carbonyl that also carries an NH2 group) is the only functional group present. The NH2 group can donate hydrogen bonds, while the carbonyl oxygen and ester oxygen can accept them. The isopropyl portion has no stereocenters and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the two equivalent methyl groups.

The molecule is a short, acyclic amide built on a straight-chain scaffold with no ring systems and no fused rings. It contains a three-carbon acyl unit: a terminal ethyl group attached to a carbonyl carbon, which is bonded to a nitrogen that carries a single methyl substituent, making it a secondary amide. The carbonyl oxygen and the amide N-H together provide one hydrogen-bond acceptor and one hydrogen-bond donor site. The chain is small and conformationally flexible, with rotation possible about the single bonds, although the amide C–N bond has partial double-bond character that restricts rotation there. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry element beyond its overall extended shape.

This molecule is a tricyclic scaffold in which two benzene rings are joined through a central seven-membered ring containing both a nitrogen and an amide-type carbonyl. The lactam carbonyl sits between the N-substituted nitrogen and one aromatic ring, while the other ring is linked through a secondary aryl amine (NH), giving the core a partially folded, non-planar shape. One benzene ring carries a chlorine atom on the opposite side from the amide linkage, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The N-substituent is a flexible 2-(dimethylamino)ethyl chain, which adds rotational freedom and a basic tertiary amine. Overall the molecule has one hydrogen-bond donor (the NH) and several acceptors (the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen atoms).

The molecule is built on a three-ring fused aromatic scaffold, a phenanthrene-type arrangement in which two benzene rings are joined to a central ring at angular positions rather than in a straight line. All ring atoms are sp2-hybridized and the system is fully aromatic and planar, which makes the framework rigid with no rotatable bonds. The only substituent is a primary amine group (–NH2) attached to one carbon of the outer ring, so the molecule has a single functional group and no meaningful symmetry. The amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the aromatic rings offer additional pi-electron density for weak interactions.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic amine with no rings, aromatic groups, or fused systems. Its scaffold is a short carbon chain: a central tertiary nitrogen bears two ethyl groups and a two-carbon-plus-chloro chain, with the chlorine located at the terminal carbon of a three-carbon propyl-type arm. The only functional groups are the tertiary amine nitrogen and a primary alkyl chloride, and there is no substitution pattern on any ring. Because the chain is flexible and freely rotatable, the molecule has no fixed three-dimensional shape and little conformational rigidity. The nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair but has no N–H, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds, and the chlorine is a weak acceptor only.

This molecule is a fully fluorinated, straight-chain alkane built from five carbon atoms, with every hydrogen position replaced by fluorine, giving a perfluoropentane backbone. The skeleton is entirely acyclic, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom functional groups beyond the carbon-fluorine bonds. Each internal carbon carries two fluorines and each terminal carbon carries three, producing a uniform substitution pattern along the chain. The molecule has a symmetric, linear arrangement, with its two ends mirroring each other. Because it has no hydrogen-bond donors and its fluorine atoms are very weak acceptors, it offers essentially no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic dinitrile: a linear six-carbon methylene backbone capped at both ends by a nitrile group, so the skeleton is a simple, unbranched chain with no rings and no substituents. Each terminal carbon is part of a carbon-nitrogen triple bond, making the two nitrile groups the only functional groups present. The molecule possesses a two-fold symmetry axis running through the middle of the chain, since the two ends are identical. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds, while the linear nitrile units themselves are rigid and rod-like. The nitrogen atoms carry lone pairs and can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, one adjacent to the nitrogen and one positioned on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 2,5-dimethyl substitution pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The only functional groups are the two methyl substituents, which are nonpolar alkyl groups, so the molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor. The ring nitrogen, with its lone pair held in the plane of the ring, serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall, the structure is small, rigid, and asymmetric, since the two methyl groups occupy non-equivalent positions relative to the nitrogen.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming a quinoline scaffold. The amino group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position of the pyridine-type ring, giving a primary aromatic amine substituent. The fused rings are fully planar and conjugated, so the framework is rigid with no rotatable bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a single mirror plane through the ring system, and it is structurally asymmetric in its substitution. The exocyclic amino group can donate two hydrogen bonds, while the ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a two-carbon acyl fluoride, built on a single linear chain with no rings. One terminal carbon is a methyl group bonded to a carbonyl carbon, which is double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to a fluorine atom. The carbonyl-fluoride unit is the sole functional group, and the skeleton is small, compact, and essentially rigid around the planar acyl center, with only free rotation about the methyl-to-carbonyl bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local threefold rotation of the methyl group. As a hydrogen-bond participant, it has no donor sites, while the carbonyl oxygen can act as a weak acceptor.

This molecule is a benzylhydrazine-type structure: a single benzene ring bearing one substituent, a CH2 linker that connects the aromatic ring to a hydrazine group (two nitrogen atoms joined by a single N–N bond). The six-membered aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no fused ring systems, and its substitution pattern is monosubstituted, so it carries no positional isomerism or symmetry-breaking pattern beyond the ring itself. The flexible CH2 and N–N linkages allow rotation about several single bonds, so the molecule is conformationally flexible relative to the rigid aromatic core. The terminal –NH–NH2 group contains three N–H bonds that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the two nitrogen lone pairs can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The benzene ring itself contributes a π-electron system that can participate in weak non-covalent aromatic interactions.

The molecule is a symmetric disulfide built from two identical benzene rings, each bearing a nitro group, joined through a sulfur-sulfur bond. Each aromatic ring is a simple, unfused six-membered carbocycle with no heteroatoms in the ring. Both nitro groups sit at the meta position relative to the disulfide linkage, giving the molecule a two-fold symmetry across the central S–S bond. The nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms but contribute no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aryl rings are rigid and planar, while the disulfide bridge allows some rotational flexibility about the sulfur-sulfur axis.

This molecule is an acyclic (non-ring) structure built around a central carbon bearing a propenyl-type allyl chain, an isopropyl group, and a ureido-carbonyl unit. The carbonyl is part of an amide linked to a urea, giving a -C(=O)NH-C(=O)NH2 arrangement. Its scaffold is entirely aliphatic with no aromatic rings or ring fusion. The terminal vinyl (C=C) provides a site of unsaturation, while the branching at the stereocenter-bearing carbon makes the molecule conformationally flexible. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the NH and NH2 groups, and the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single sp3-hybridized carbon atom bearing three nitro groups, giving a compact, acyclic scaffold with no ring systems and no ring fusion. The central carbon also carries one hydrogen, and each of the three nitro groups (N attached to two oxygens, one formally charged) is attached through nitrogen directly to that carbon. The three nitro substituents are arranged identically around the central carbon, producing a threefold symmetric pattern. The framework is fairly rigid around the central carbon, though rotation about each carbon–nitrogen bond remains possible. Each nitro group contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since its only C–H is not polarized enough to serve as one.

The molecule is built around a compact spirocyclic scaffold in which two five-membered lactone-type rings share a single quaternary carbon, and a cyclopropane-like three-membered carbocycle is fused to one of them, giving a strained, rigid, three-dimensional framework. Both lactone rings contain a ring oxygen bonded to a carbonyl, and each carbonyl is conjugated with a C=C double bond, forming two α,β-unsaturated ester (butenolide) units. The arrangement has no obvious mirror or rotational symmetry because the two halves differ in their fusion pattern. The carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl fluoride built on a nine-carbon saturated backbone, with a fluorine atom bonded to the terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups, so its scaffold is purely aliphatic and linear. The only polar feature is the carbon-fluorine bond, which makes the fluorine end weakly electronegative, but the rest of the chain is nonpolar hydrocarbon. The molecule is highly flexible, since rotation about its many single bonds allows many conformations, and it has no internal symmetry beyond the local arrangement of its methylene units. It can accept a weak hydrogen bond at the fluorine atom but has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a perfluorinated ether: two fully fluorinated alkyl chains joined through a single oxygen atom, with no hydrogens on any carbon. Each chain is a linear, unbranched four-carbon perfluorobutyl segment, so the scaffold is essentially a symmetric C4F9–O–C4F9 framework. The molecule has no rings and no ring fusion, and the only heteroatom is the central ether oxygen, which carries two bonds and no hydrogen. Because the two halves are identical and mirror each other about that oxygen, the molecule has a clear two-fold symmetry. The fluorine-rich chains are conformationally flexible about their C–C bonds, yet the bulky, electron-dense fluorine atoms shield the backbone. The molecule offers no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor site is the ether oxygen, which is sterically hindered and weakly basic.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group on the adjacent carbon, and a phenyl ring attached at the position meta to the carboxyl group. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid sit next to each other on the central ring, forming an ortho arrangement that allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond between them. The second benzene ring is linked by a single bond, giving a biaryl scaffold with two aromatic rings joined directly. The biaryl bond allows some rotation, so the molecule is only moderately flexible, while the fused-free aromatic rings remain planar. The carboxylic acid and phenol supply both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, whereas the unsubstituted phenyl ring contributes only hydrophobic, aromatic character.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated-at-the-ends scaffold built around a central carbon-carbon triple bond, with two identical tertiary carbinol units attached at either end. Each terminus is a carbon bearing two methyl groups and one hydroxyl group, so the two alcohol functions are the only functional groups present. The alkyne linker is linear, giving the molecule a rod-like, rigid central segment, while the methyl-substituted ends rotate freely about their single bonds. The structure possesses a twofold symmetry axis through the middle of the triple bond. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, so the molecule offers two such sites.

This molecule is a single benzene ring, so it has no ring fusion, and it carries three substituents arranged around it. An ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain) sits on one ring carbon, and an amino group (a primary NH2) sits on the adjacent carbon, making these two neighboring positions. A nitro group (NO2, with the nitrogen bearing a formal positive charge and one oxygen negatively charged) occupies a position para to the ethoxy group, across the ring from it. The ring is planar and rigid, while the ethyl chain of the ethoxy group provides a small amount of conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ in both identity and placement. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds, and the oxygens of the nitro and ethoxy groups can accept them.

The molecule is an ester built from a long, straight, unbranched saturated carbon chain of eighteen carbons attached to a single carbonyl group, which is bonded through an oxygen to an isopropyl group (a secondary three-carbon unit bearing two terminal methyls). There are no rings, no aromatic systems, and no double bonds other than the carbonyl C=O, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic. The ester linkage is the only functional group, providing one carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and one ether-type oxygen that is a weaker acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule is highly flexible, since the long alkyl chain has many freely rotatable single bonds, and it lacks any meaningful molecular symmetry because the two ends differ markedly in size and shape.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with a linear twelve-carbon alkyl chain (dodecyl) on one side and a primary amine group on the opposite side. The benzene core is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the two substituents sit at positions 1 and 4, giving the molecule a clear mirror-plane symmetry along its long axis. The long saturated chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotatable single bonds, while the aromatic ring remains planar and rigid. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The alkyl tail contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability, so the molecule's polar character is concentrated at the amine end.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached to one ring carbon, while a hydroxyl group and a nitro group (–NO2) sit on the two adjacent positions, making a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern in which the hydroxyl is flanked by the carboxyl and nitro groups. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens plus the nitro oxygens serve as acceptors. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the carboxyl and nitro groups can rotate somewhat about their bonds to the ring. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry across the ring.

This molecule is a fully aromatic, planar tricyclic system built from three fused six-membered rings in an angular arrangement, with all carbon atoms sp2-hybridized. One of the three rings contains a single nitrogen atom at a ring-fusion-adjacent position, making it a benzo-fused quinoline-type heteroaromatic framework. The absence of any substituents means there are no functional groups beyond the aromatic ring system itself, and the scaffold has no rotatable bonds, so it is entirely rigid. The aromatic nitrogen provides a single hydrogen-bond acceptor site via its lone pair, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors present. The overall shape is close to C2v-like in its heavy-atom framework, though the angular fusion pattern breaks any higher symmetry.

This molecule is a simple acyclic saturated hydrocarbon skeleton consisting of two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, a two-carbon ethane-type scaffold. Each carbon carries three chlorine substituents, so every carbon is fully substituted with halogen atoms and no hydrogens remain on the framework. The structure contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms other than the six chlorines. The molecule has high local symmetry, with the two CCl3 groups related by a rotation about the central carbon-carbon bond, and it is flexible because it can rotate freely around that single bond. Chlorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and carry no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is a tricyclic fused system built from a coumarin-type lactone ring (a 2H-chromen-2-one) that is linearly fused to a furan ring, giving a flat, fully aromatic-looking framework. The lactone carbonyl sits on the pyranone ring, which is conjugated with the benzenoid ring and the fused furan, so the three rings lie essentially in one plane. Because the scaffold is rigid and largely planar, there are no rotatable bonds and no stereocenters, and it carries no substituents beyond the ring fusion and the lactone group. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the carbonyl oxygen and the two ring oxygens, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The arrangement is essentially symmetric about a single axis running through the lactone and furan oxygens.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with a nitrogen atom in the ring and no fused ring systems. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to the ring carbon at the position opposite the nitrogen, which corresponds to the para (4-) position relative to the nitrogen. The acid group contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only a single rotatable bond connecting the carboxyl group to the ring, and the substitution pattern gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis through the nitrogen and the substituted carbon.

The molecule is an organophosphorus thioester built around a central phosphorus atom bearing a double-bonded sulfur and two methoxy groups, with the third oxygen linking it to a benzene ring. That benzene ring is para-substituted, carrying on the opposite side a sulfonamide group in which the sulfur is doubly oxygenated and bonded to a nitrogen that carries two methyl groups. The aromatic core is the only ring system, so the scaffold is a single planar six-membered ring flanked by flexible, rotatable linkers. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors because every nitrogen and hydrogen-bearing position is methylated, while the sulfonyl oxygens, the phosphorus-bound sulfur, and the ether-type oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its overall shape is asymmetric, since the two ends of the molecule carry different functional groups.

The molecule is a xanthine-type bicyclic scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidinedione ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, with the fusion sharing one carbon-carbon bond. The two carbonyl groups sit on the six-membered ring, flanked by nitrogen atoms that carry an N-methyl and an N-alkyl substituent. The imidazole nitrogen bears an n-propyl chain, while the remaining ring nitrogen carries a four-carbon linker ending in a ketone. The fused core is largely planar and rigid, with the side chains providing the main conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since all ring nitrogens are substituted.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic core in which a five-membered pyrrole ring is fused to a six-membered ring, giving a partially saturated pyrrolizine-type scaffold, with the nitrogen at the ring fusion. The pyrrole portion is aromatic and carries a benzoyl group (a phenyl ring bonded through a ketone carbonyl) at one carbon adjacent to the nitrogen. The saturated ring contains two methylene units and a carbon bearing a carboxylic acid group, which provides one hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor oxygens. The benzoyl ketone adds a further hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall, the fused core is fairly rigid while the phenyl ketone and carboxylic acid substituents retain some rotational freedom, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry.

The molecule is built around a 4-aminoquinoline core, in which an anilino-type nitrogen links a benzene ring to the quinoline's pyridine-derived ring, which is itself fused to a second benzene ring. The quinoline bears a single chlorine substituent on the carbocyclic ring, placed para-like relative to the ring fusion. A second benzene ring is attached through the NH bridge and carries an ester group at the position ortho to the amine, so the two aromatic systems sit close together. The ester links to a flexible three-carbon chain bearing two free hydroxyl groups, which adds conformational freedom to an otherwise planar, rigid aromatic framework. Overall the molecule offers several hydrogen-bond donors (the NH and two OH groups) and multiple acceptors (the quinoline nitrogen, the ester oxygens, and the hydroxyls).

The molecule is a short, acyclic amino acid built on a linear carbon chain. It contains a carboxylic acid group at one end and a primary amine on the carbon immediately adjacent to the acid, making it an alpha-amino acid. A straight three-carbon alkyl tail extends from the alpha carbon, so the structure has no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroaromatic systems. The single stereogenic alpha carbon means the molecule is chiral, and it lacks any internal symmetry. Because it is flexible and rotatable about its single bonds, it can adopt many conformations. Both the amine and the carboxylic acid act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the alkyl chain contributes only nonpolar, non-hydrogen-bonding character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing six substituents in a 1,2,3,5-type pattern around the ring. An N-propyl-N-(2-chloroethyl) amino group sits on one carbon and is flanked on each side by a nitro group, with a second nitro group positioned meta to the amine, and a trifluoromethyl group sits on the remaining ring carbon opposite the amine. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the propyl and chloroethyl chains attached to the nitrogen provide conformational flexibility. The two nitro groups are strong electron-withdrawing acceptors that can accept hydrogen bonds through their oxygen atoms, and the tertiary amine nitrogen and fluorine atoms also act as weak acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no molecular symmetry, since the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic primary amine: a fourteen-carbon... let me count the carbons precisely. The SMILES CCCCCCCCCCCCCN contains thirteen carbon atoms followed by a nitrogen, so the skeleton is an unbranched tridecyl chain terminated by a single amino group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroaromatic systems. The only functional group is the primary amine, which sits at one terminus of the chain, so the substitution pattern is entirely linear with no branching or side groups. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror relationship of an unbranched chain, and its long saturated backbone is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds. The nitrogen bears two hydrogens, so it can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 (meta) pattern: two isopropyl ester groups and one nitro group. Each ester carries a carbonyl directly attached to the aromatic ring, with the oxygen linked to a branched isopropyl (propan-2-yl) group, giving the molecule a bilateral arrangement of two identical side chains on opposite sides of the core. The aromatic ring is flat and fully conjugated, while the isopropyl ester arms add some rotational flexibility around their single bonds. Because the two ester groups are equivalent, the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring and the nitro group. The carbonyl oxygens and nitro oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single saturated six-membered sulfur-containing heterocycle, a thiane ring, with no fused rings and no additional functional groups. One carbon adjacent to the sulfur atom carries a methyl substituent, so the substitution pattern is a monosubstituted ring at the alpha position relative to sulfur. The ring is fully sp3-hybridized and adopts a chair-like conformation, giving moderate conformational flexibility, while the methyl group creates a stereocenter at that carbon. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the methyl group breaks the mirror relationship of the ring. Its only heteroatom is the thioether sulfur, which can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a linear, fully saturated aliphatic ester with no rings, aromatic systems, or branching. Its carbon skeleton consists of an eight-carbon straight alkyl chain attached through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon, which is in turn bonded to a two-carbon ethyl group on the acyl side. The ester functional group (–C(=O)–O–) is the only polar feature, and the carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The absence of ring systems and the freely rotatable single bonds make the structure highly flexible, with no meaningful symmetry beyond a general elongated, rod-like overall shape.

This molecule is a small, fully saturated two-carbon skeleton (an ethane backbone) with no rings, no double or triple bonds, and no aromatic character. Each carbon carries a set of halogen substituents: one carbon bears a fluorine and two chlorines, while the other bears two chlorines, giving a highly halogenated, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. Rotation about the central carbon–carbon single bond is free, so the molecule is fairly flexible and has no fixed rigid framework. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, and its only C–H bonds are weakly polar; it has no lone-pair-bearing heteroatoms that could act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, though the halogens provide weak polar character.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, with no ring fusion and no heteroatoms within the ring itself. Three of the ring positions carry nitro groups, which are strongly electron-withdrawing and act as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms but cannot donate hydrogen bonds. Two positions carry methyl groups, and one carries a bulky tert-butyl group, so the substitution pattern alternates across the ring with the three nitro groups and the three alkyl groups interleaved. The molecule has an approximate threefold symmetry axis through the ring centre, with the bulky tert-butyl group breaking any higher symmetry. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the nitro and alkyl groups can rotate about their single bonds to the ring.

This molecule is a dicarboxylic-acid-type scaffold built on a three-carbon chain: a central carbon bears a carboxylic acid group and is flanked by two benzyl arms, one on each side. Each benzyl arm ends in a monosubstituted benzene ring, so the molecule contains two separate, unfused six-membered aromatic rings with no ring fusion between them. The only polar functional group is the terminal carboxylic acid, which can both donate one hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen. The two phenyl groups are attached through flexible methylene linkers, giving the molecule considerable conformational freedom, and the central carbon is a stereogenic center. The arrangement is approximately symmetric about that central carbon, though the carboxylic acid breaks the symmetry of the overall framework.

The molecule is built on a benzamide-type scaffold with two benzene rings linked through an acyl sulfonamide bridge. One ring carries an isopropoxy group (an oxygen bearing a branched two-carbon alkyl group) at the position para to the carbonyl, while the other ring carries a primary amino group para to the sulfonyl attachment. The central C(=O)–NH–SO2 unit contains an amide-like carbonyl and an acidic N–H flanked by a sulfonyl group. The two aromatic rings are planar and rigid, but the sulfonyl linker introduces some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks a symmetry plane because the two rings bear different substituents. Hydrogen-bond donors include the sulfonamide N–H and the aniline NH2, while acceptors include the carbonyl oxygen, the sulfonyl oxygens, the ether oxygen, and the amino nitrogen.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Four of the ring positions carry methyl groups, and the remaining two carry nitro groups, with a tert-butyl group placed between them, so the substitution pattern is highly crowded and asymmetric in its arrangement. Each nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing functional group whose oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites since every substituent is a carbon-based alkyl group or a nitro group. The bulky tert-butyl group and the adjacent methyl and nitro substituents restrict rotation and make the scaffold fairly rigid, with few conformational degrees of freedom beyond the orientation of the nitro groups and the methyl rotors.

The molecule is a six-membered saturated heterocycle, a 1,3,5-thiadiazinane ring, bearing a thiocarbonyl group at the carbon between the two nitrogens and sulfur atoms. Its two ring nitrogens each carry a benzyl substituent (a phenylmethyl group attached to a benzene ring), placed symmetrically on either side of the ring. The thiocarbonyl carbon is a C=S group, and the ring contains a thioether sulfur and an aminal-type CH2 unit linking the nitrogens. The two aromatic rings are flexible, freely rotating appendages, giving the overall framework moderate conformational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are tertiary, but the sulfur atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single sp3 carbon that bridges two para-aminophenyl rings and is also part of a five-membered lactone ring, making it a phthalide (isobenzofuranone) scaffold with a spiro-like quaternary center at the 3-position. The lactone is fused to a benzene ring, giving a rigid bicyclic core, while the two pendant aniline rings are attached at the same carbon and are each substituted with a primary amino group at the para position, giving the molecule a two-fold symmetric arrangement about that central carbon. The ester carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the two aromatic amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and additional acceptors. Overall the framework is largely rigid apart from rotation of the two pendant phenyl rings about their bonds to the central carbon.

The molecule is a small acyclic primary amine built on a single saturated carbon chain with no rings. Its backbone is a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, an ethyl group, and an amino group, so the amine sits on a fully substituted carbon, giving a branched, sterically crowded arrangement. Because there are no double bonds or rings, the scaffold is entirely sp3 and highly flexible, with free rotation about each C–C bond. The only functional group is the primary amine, which can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through the nitrogen lone pair. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the two equivalent methyl groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which is linear and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor without any donor capability. The other is a chloromethyl group, a single methylene carbon bearing a chlorine atom, which adds a flexible sp3 center and a polarized carbon-chlorine bond. The aromatic core is planar and fully rigid, while the chloromethyl arm can rotate freely about its single bonds. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a bicyclic hydrocarbon built from a six-membered ring fused to a benzene ring, giving a dihydronaphthalene-type scaffold. The fused aromatic ring is fully unsaturated, while the second ring contains one carbon-carbon double bond and two sp3 methylene carbons, so the partially saturated ring adopts a non-planar, somewhat flexible conformation. The molecule carries no substituents or heteroatoms, meaning it has no functional groups, no hydrogen-bond donors, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its overall shape is largely planar across the aromatic portion and possesses no stereocenters, so it is achiral.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, namely a thiophene ring, with no fused ring system. A nitro group (–NO2, drawn as a charge-separated nitronium-type group) is attached to a ring carbon at the 3-position, meaning it sits one carbon removed from the sulfur. The scaffold is small, planar, and essentially rigid, with only the nitro group's rotation as a minor degree of freedom and no molecular symmetry beyond the ring's local planarity. The nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the ring has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, and the ring sulfur is only a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, two fused six-membered aromatic rings sharing one carbon-carbon bond. A methyl group sits on one ring at a position adjacent to the fusion carbon, and a nitro group, with a nitrogen bearing a formal positive charge and two oxygens (one negative), is attached on the same ring at the position across from the methyl. The fused aromatic system is fully planar and rigid, with the methyl group and nitro group projecting outward from it in the plane. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms but cannot donate hydrogen bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, and its overall structure has no rotational symmetry.

This molecule is built around a central sulfur atom bearing two doubly bonded oxygen atoms, forming a sulfonyl group with no rings in the structure. One side of the sulfur is bonded to a chlorine atom, and the other side is bonded to a nitrogen that is double-bonded to a carbon, which is in turn double-bonded to an oxygen, giving an isocyanate-type linkage. The arrangement is linear and acyclic, so there is no ring fusion, and the molecule is essentially rigid around the tetrahedral-like sulfur center with little conformational freedom. There is no internal symmetry because the two ends of the chain carry different atoms. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H bonds, but its oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on an indene-type bicyclic scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring that contains a carbon–carbon double bond. The aromatic ring carries a single ether oxygen at one position, which links to a three-carbon chain bearing a secondary alcohol. That chain terminates in an isopropylamino group, a secondary amine attached to the terminal carbon. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the side chain attaches only at one position on the fused ring system, so the molecule has no internal symmetry. The fused ring system is largely rigid, while the flexible propanolamine side chain can rotate freely. The secondary amine nitrogen and the hydroxyl oxygen can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the ether oxygen, alcohol oxygen, and amine nitrogen can all act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an aryl azide built on a benzene ring. A linear azido group (-N=N+=N-, drawn here as an azide anion-cation pair) is attached directly to one carbon of the aromatic ring. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly opposite it, at the para position, giving a 1,4-disubstituted benzene scaffold. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the azido group is nearly collinear with the ring plane, so the overall structure is rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds beyond the C-N attachment. The molecule has a two-fold axis of symmetry running through the two substituents. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen atoms of the azide and the chlorine can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a silicon-centered compound: a single tetrahedral silicon atom bearing two methyl groups and two phenoxy groups. Each phenoxy unit consists of a benzene ring attached through an oxygen atom to the silicon, so the scaffold is a dialkyl diaryloxy silane. The two aromatic rings are unfused, monosubstituted benzene rings, and the flexible Si–O linkages let them orient somewhat independently. The molecule has no stereocenters, and the two phenyl groups are related by a mirror-type symmetry through the Si center. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the two ether-type oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic tertiary amine built on a simple linear scaffold: a central nitrogen bearing one methyl group and two unbranched eight-carbon chains. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the single amine nitrogen. The two octyl arms are identical, so the molecule has approximate mirror symmetry through the nitrogen and the methyl group. Its long saturated chains give it considerable conformational flexibility with no rigid elements. The nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a fully saturated-at-the-bridges polycyclic hydrocarbon built from two benzene-type rings fused together and each further fused to a saturated six-membered carbocycle. Its skeleton is a tetracyclic, fused arrangement with a central aromatic ring bearing two peri-fused cyclohexane-like rings on opposite sides. The only aromatic unit is the one ring that carries the two C–H positions, while the remaining rings are fully aliphatic, so the molecule has no functional groups, no heteroatoms, and no substituents beyond hydrogen. The fused framework is rigid and largely planar in its aromatic core, with the saturated rings adding some conformational flexibility, and the structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the aromatic ring. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Two hydroxyl groups are attached directly to the ring, so it is a benzenediol, and a bromine atom sits on the ring between them in a 1,2,4 arrangement, giving the ring an asymmetric substitution pattern. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and an acceptor through its lone pairs, and the bromine contributes a weakly polarizable halogen site. The ring is rigid and planar, and the only conformational freedom comes from rotation of the two O–H bonds.

This molecule is built from a cyclopropane ring carrying two geminal methyl groups, with a 2-methylpropenyl (isobutenyl) side chain on one ring carbon and a carboxylate ester on the adjacent carbon. The ester oxygen is attached to a CH2 linker that bridges to the nitrogen of a cyclic imide, a phthalimide-type unit in which a fused cyclohexene ring is joined to the five-membered succinimide-like ring. The cyclopropane and the fused bicyclic imide make the structure rigid in its ring portions, while the ester–CH2–N linkage provides a flexible hinge between the two halves. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ends differ in substitution. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogen and oxygen atoms are fully substituted, but it offers several acceptors through the two imide carbonyls and the ester oxygens.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a methyl group and an N,N-dimethylcarboxamide group. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and it is planar and rigid. The amide carbonyl (C=O) attached to the ring is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the amide nitrogen carries two methyl groups and therefore has no N–H, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The two N-methyl groups are not hydrogen-bond donors, and the amide bond gives the side chain limited rotational flexibility. The overall structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the ring, though the amide group breaks full symmetry.

The molecule is built on a three-carbon chain in which a central carbon bears two methyl groups and a hydroxyl group, and a second quaternary carbon, also carrying two substituents, is bonded to a para-chlorophenyl ring. Its scaffold is therefore a simple acyclic diol attached to a single benzene ring, with the only ring system being that six-membered aromatic ring. The phenyl ring carries one chlorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, giving a para substitution pattern. Both hydroxyl groups are tertiary alcohols, so they can each donate one hydrogen bond and accept another, while the chlorine contributes only weak acceptor character. The aliphatic portion is flexible, with rotatable single bonds, whereas the aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local equivalence of the two methyl pairs.

The molecule is built on a cyclopropane ring that carries a carboxylic acid group on one carbon and a carboxamide group on the adjacent carbon, giving a compact, strained three-membered scaffold. The amide nitrogen is bonded to a benzene ring bearing two chlorine atoms at the 2 and 4 positions, which creates an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The cyclopropane and the aromatic ring are joined through the rigid amide linkage, which limits conformational freedom around that bond. The carboxylic acid offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the amide N-H serves as a donor and its carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a cyclopropane ring, a small three-membered carbocycle that makes the core rigid and strained. One carbon of that ring carries two substituents: a tert-butyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is attached to a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups) and a sulfonyl group linked to a para-chlorophenyl ring. The sulfone is a strongly polar, hydrogen-bond-accepting unit, with its two oxygens as acceptors, while the ester carbonyl contributes a further acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The bulky tert-butyl group and the flat, symmetric aryl ring add some steric and conformational character, but the cyclopropane framework keeps the overall structure fairly compact and rigid.

The molecule is built on a single four-carbon chain with a quaternary carbon at its center, meaning that central carbon carries no hydrogens and is bonded to four different substituents. Three of those substituents are hydroxymethyl groups (CH2OH), each providing a primary alcohol, while the fourth is a bromomethyl group (CH2Br) attached to a carbon-bromine bond. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no double bonds, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and saturated. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the bromomethyl arm differs from the three hydroxymethyl arms, though the three alcohol arms are chemically equivalent to one another. Its flexibility comes from freely rotating single bonds, and it presents three hydrogen-bond donors from the hydroxyl groups and three acceptors from the oxygen atoms.

The molecule is built around a six-membered 1,2,4-triazin-5(4H)-one ring, a nitrogen-rich heterocycle with three ring nitrogens and a carbonyl carbon. An ethylthio group (a sulfur bonded to an ethyl chain) is attached to one ring carbon, and a tert-butyl group occupies the adjacent carbon. The ring nitrogen next to the carbonyl carries a free amino group, so the scaffold is decorated on several sides rather than symmetrically. The aromatic-like core is planar and rigid, while the ethyl and tert-butyl groups add limited conformational freedom. The amino group and ring NH-type nitrogen can donate hydrogen bonds, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a large, highly substituted acyclic-to-cyclic polyether scaffold containing several saturated rings, including multiple tetrahydrofuran and tetrahydropyran units, one of which is a spiro-fused ketal-type center joined to a further ring system. The chain carries a propanoate ester on one end and a free carboxylic acid on the other, with many methyl branches distributed along the backbone. Several hydroxyl groups are present, including a hemiketal hydroxyl and a primary alcohol, giving the molecule numerous hydrogen-bond donor sites and an abundance of ether and carbonyl acceptor oxygens. The stereochemically dense arrangement of rings and branches makes the overall structure rigid in its core regions but flexible at the peripheral side chains. The molecule lacks any obvious symmetry, as its substituents and ring fusions are arranged asymmetrically.

This molecule is built on a dibenzazepine-type tricyclic core: two benzene rings joined through a seven-membered ring containing a saturated two-carbon bridge and a tertiary nitrogen. The nitrogen is also bonded to a bicyclic quinuclidine-type unit, a fused cage of saturated rings containing a second tertiary amine. The two aromatic rings are unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule lacks any symmetry that would make the two aryl halves fully equivalent. The bridged aliphatic cage and fused tricyclic framework make the structure fairly rigid, with limited rotation about the bulky ring junctions. Both nitrogens are tertiary amines with no N-H groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two nitrogen lone pairs can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with the fusion creating a rigid, planar bicyclic aromatic core. One ring carries a hydroxyl group attached to a carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, giving a phenolic functional group, while the other ring bears a single chlorine substituent on a carbon positioned on the opposite side of the system. The two substituents are placed at distinct, non-equivalent positions, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. Because the aromatic core is fully rigid and the substituents are small, conformational flexibility is minimal. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atom serves only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing one substituent, a two-carbon chain. The chain features an acetate ester, where an acetyl group is joined through an oxygen to a stereogenic carbon that also carries the phenyl ring. That same carbon is bonded to an acyl chloride group, giving the molecule a reactive C(=O)Cl functionality. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion is monosubstituted and highly symmetric, while the side chain is flexible about its single bonds. The molecule has no fused ring systems and no hydrogen-bond donors, with its hydrogen-bond acceptors limited to the carbonyl oxygens and the ester oxygen.

This molecule is a steroid-type tetracyclic scaffold built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, with angular methyl groups at two ring junctions. The fully saturated ring system contains no double bonds, so the core is conformationally rigid, with the fused rings locked in defined three-dimensional arrangements. A side chain projecting from the five-membered ring terminates in a carboxylic acid, which is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Apart from that acid group, the scaffold is entirely aliphatic carbon and hydrogen, offering no other heteroatoms or aromatic rings. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the side chain and the methyl substitution pattern break the scaffold's otherwise near-symmetric layout.

The molecule is a saturated, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, so its scaffold is a long flexible hydrocarbon backbone. At one end sits a carboxylic acid group, which is the only functional group present. A single methyl branch sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the carboxyl carbon, creating an asymmetric, alpha-substituted pattern with a stereocenter at that position. Because the chain has many freely rotatable single bonds, the molecule is highly flexible and lacks any rigid ring framework. The carboxylic acid provides one hydrogen-bond donor from its hydroxyl hydrogen and two acceptor sites from its oxygen atoms, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar.

The molecule is built on a cyclopentene core, a five-membered carbocyclic ring containing one carbon-carbon double bond. Two sec-butyl groups are attached to the ring, one on the saturated carbon adjacent to the alkene and one on the carbon beside the vinylic carbon that bears the side chain. The side chain on the alkene carbon is a linear fragment containing a secondary alcohol, a ketone, and a terminal carboxylic acid, arranged as a beta-keto acid chain. The ring is a single unfused system with no bridging, so the overall scaffold is only moderately flexible, with rotation possible around the single bonds of the alkyl and side-chain substituents. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two alkyl groups and the side chain sit at different positions on the ring. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated in the hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups, which can act as both donors and acceptors, while the ketone and carbonyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a piperidine ring, a six-membered saturated nitrogen heterocycle, that carries a methyl group on one carbon next to the ring nitrogen's neighboring position. The nitrogen bears a phenethyl chain, a two-carbon linker ending in an unsubstituted benzene ring. At the carbon bearing the methyl ester, a quaternary center also holds an N-phenyl propanamide group, so the amide nitrogen connects two phenyl and carbonyl-containing substituents. The molecule has two separate benzene rings, one on the amide nitrogen and one at the chain end, and both are unsubstituted, so the aromatic portions are unrelated and no fused ring system is present. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since no N-H or O-H groups exist, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the tertiary amine nitrogen act as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is an ethoxy group, an oxygen atom bonded to an ethyl chain, and the other is a single fluorine atom. The benzene core is a flat, fully conjugated six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The ethoxy chain provides some rotational flexibility, while the aromatic ring remains rigid. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the fluorine can also weakly accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. It lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a single tert-butyl group attached to a carbon adjacent to the nitrogen (the 2-position). The tert-butyl substituent is a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups, giving it a bulky, sterically demanding, nonpolar aliphatic character with no heteroatoms. The ring itself is planar and fully unsaturated, so the scaffold is rigid, while the tert-butyl group is attached by a single bond and rotates freely. The molecule has an approximate local threefold symmetry around the tert-butyl C–ring bond axis, but no overall plane of symmetry is imposed by the ring nitrogen. The pyridine nitrogen's lone pair, lying in the plane of the ring, can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups present.

This molecule is built around a five-membered 2-oxazoline (4,5-dihydrooxazole) ring, in which the C=N double bond is conjugated with a 2,6-difluorophenyl group attached at the carbon between the ring oxygen and nitrogen. A second aromatic ring, a benzene bearing an ethoxy group and a tert-butyl group, is attached to the saturated carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, giving a para-tert-butyl and ortho-ethoxy substitution pattern. The two fluorines on the difluorophenyl ring sit symmetrically at the positions flanking the attachment point, which gives that ring a mirror-symmetric arrangement. The molecule is moderately rigid around its aromatic and oxazoline portions, while the ethoxy and tert-butyl groups add some conformational freedom. The oxazoline nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the ether oxygens and fluorine atoms can act as weak acceptors, and the molecule has no strong hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a steroid, built on a fused tetracyclic scaffold of three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, typical of the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene framework. The first ring carries an alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone, with a C=C double bond conjugated to a carbonyl within the ring system. A secondary hydroxyl group sits on one of the saturated rings, and a two-carbon acetyl side chain (a ketone) extends from the five-membered ring. Two angular methyl groups are positioned at the ring junctions. The fused ring system is rigid and largely non-planar, with a single flexible acetyl side chain. The molecule has no overall symmetry, and the hydroxyl and ketone oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl hydrogen can act as a donor.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carbamate built on a linear four-carbon chain. A straight n-butyl group is bonded through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon, which in turn carries an amide-type nitrogen bearing a single methyl substituent. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely flexible, with free rotation around its single bonds and no fused or aromatic systems. The carbamate unit contributes a carbonyl oxygen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and a secondary N–H that acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ester-type oxygen is a weaker acceptor. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the carbamate linkage.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two methyl groups and a hydroxyl group, giving a trisubstituted aromatic core with the methyls meta to each other and the hydroxyl flanked by one methyl and an acyl side chain. The adjacent hydroxyl and ketone carbonyl are positioned so they can engage in intramolecular hydrogen bonding. A two-carbon linker connects the ketone to a six-membered glutarimide-type ring, a saturated heterocycle containing an imide unit with two carbonyl groups flanking an NH. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the linker and saturated ring add conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donors include the phenolic OH and the imide NH, and the acceptors include the phenolic oxygen, the ketone oxygen, and the two imide carbonyl oxygens. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because the two halves differ in composition.

The molecule is a single six-membered heteroaromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a carbonyl group adjacent to that nitrogen, which makes it a pyridone-type scaffold. The nitrogen carries a hydrogen atom and the ring carbon next to the carbonyl is not substituted, while a methyl group sits on the carbon at the position two atoms away from the carbonyl carbon, giving a non-symmetric substitution pattern. The ring is planar and fully rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group. The N–H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the exocyclic carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a short acyclic chain attached to a pyridine ring. A three-carbon unit carries a ketone at one position and a second ketone at the terminal carbon, making it a 1,3-diketone with the carbonyl groups separated by a methylene. The second carbonyl is bonded directly to the 3-position of a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, which contains one nitrogen atom. Substitution is at a single ring position, so the aromatic portion has no fused rings and no symmetry axis beyond the flat ring itself. The chain is flexible, with rotatable single bonds linking it to the ring. Both carbonyl oxygens and the pyridine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a cardenolide-type steroid glycoside built on a fused four-ring steroidal scaffold of three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring, with angular methyl and aldehyde groups at ring junctions. The cyclopentane ring carries a pendant unsaturated six-membered lactone (a 2-pyranone ring) at the 17-position, which provides both carbonyl and ring-ester oxygen acceptors. Two tertiary hydroxyl groups sit at ring-fusion carbons, adding hydrogen-bond donor capacity. A trisaccharide chain, made of linked deoxy-sugar and hexose rings bearing several hydroxyl groups, is attached through an acetal linkage at one position of the steroid core. The molecule is asymmetric overall, with a rigid fused core and a flexible, highly polar sugar tail that offers many hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing an ether-linked propargyl group (a terminal alkyne attached via an O-CH2 linkage) and two chlorine atoms at positions that leave the ring asymmetrically substituted. The benzene ring is directly bonded to a nitrogen of a fused bicyclic heterocycle: a five-membered triazolone ring, with a carbonyl adjacent to one nitrogen, is fused to a saturated six-membered ring containing three methylene units, giving a partially saturated bicyclic core. The aryl-heterocycle bond allows free rotation, so the molecule is moderately flexible, though the fused ring system itself is rigid. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents on the benzene ring differ in position. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the carbonyl oxygen, the ether oxygen and the ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic terpene-like scaffold with a bridged bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) core bearing three methyl groups on the bridgehead and adjacent carbons. Its one functional group is an acrylate ester, a vinyl group conjugated to a carbonyl that is bonded through oxygen to the ring carbon at position 2 of the bicyclic framework. The ring system is fully saturated apart from that terminal alkene, so the skeleton is rigid and cage-like with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no O–H or N–H groups, but the ester oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its overall shape is asymmetric because the ester substituent sits on one side of the bridged cage.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused polycyclic scaffold built from four rings: three fused six-membered rings and one five-membered ring at the end, giving the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene framework. The rings are fused cis and trans at several junctions, which makes the overall shape rigid and compact. A single hydroxyl group sits on one of the six-membered rings, and two angular methyl groups project from ring-junction carbons. One ring carries a carbon-carbon double bond, so the structure is largely saturated with one point of unsaturation. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the skeleton is essentially hydrocarbon and offers no further hydrogen-bonding sites. The molecule lacks any obvious symmetry because the hydroxyl and the double bond break the mirror-like pattern of the ring system.

This molecule is a rigid, fused polycyclic alkaloid built around a morphinan-like scaffold of four to five interlocking rings, including a partially saturated piperidine-type ring carrying an N-methyl group. A benzene ring bears a free phenolic hydroxyl group, and an aromatic ring is fused into the framework through a nitrogen-containing lactam. The lactam carbonyl and the ketone sit within the polycycle, and an ether oxygen links a bridging ring. The molecule is non-symmetric, with the substituents distributed unevenly across its three-dimensional cage. Its tertiary amine and phenolic hydroxyl can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the phenol provides one hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygens serve as additional acceptors.

This molecule is a small five-membered heterocycle, a saturated ring containing one carbonyl carbon, one methylene carbon, and two nitrogen atoms with a thiocarbonyl group bridging the nitrogens. The ring is a cyclic thiourea fused to a lactam-type amide, so the scaffold is a 2-thioxoimidazolidin-4-one core with no additional fused or pendant rings. Its functional groups are a ring amide carbonyl, a thiocarbonyl (C=S), and two secondary N–H groups, which together give it two hydrogen-bond donors. The carbonyl oxygen and thiocarbonyl sulfur serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is unsubstituted on the ring carbons, is small and nearly planar, and has limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on an acyclic glycolate-type backbone: a tert-butyl group is attached to an amide nitrogen, which is bonded to a carbonyl that links through a methylene to an ester oxygen. The ester carbonyl is attached to a benzene ring, making the single aromatic ring a monosubstituted phenyl group with no fusion and no additional substituents on the ring. The molecule contains one secondary amide (N–H donor and C=O acceptor) and one ester (two oxygen acceptors, with no donor). The bulky tert-butyl group provides steric shielding near the amide, while the methylene and ester linkages allow moderate conformational flexibility. Overall the molecule has no rotational symmetry beyond the local three-fold symmetry of the tert-butyl group.

This molecule is a morphinan-type polycyclic alkaloid scaffold, with a rigid, cage-like framework built from fused and bridged rings. A benzene ring bears a methoxy group and an adjacent free hydroxyl group, giving it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic pattern that is fused to a piperidine-containing ring system. The nitrogen is a tertiary amine carrying an N-methyl group, and an α,β-unsaturated cyclohexenone ring is present, with its ketone acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The hydroxyl group is the only hydrogen-bond donor, while the ether oxygen, ketone oxygen, and amine nitrogen serve as acceptors. Overall the structure is conformationally constrained, with little rotational freedom.

This molecule is a flavone, built on a benzopyran-4-one core in which a fused benzene ring is joined to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring. A second benzene ring hangs off the 2-position of that pyranone through a single bond, giving the molecule a largely planar, conjugated scaffold with limited rotational freedom. The fused ring carries two hydroxyl groups, one on each of the two positions flanking the ring-fusion oxygen side, while the pendant ring bears a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group in adjacent positions. The ketone carbonyl and the ring oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the phenolic hydroxyl groups supply several hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically on the two aromatic rings.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a nitro group, with the nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one as a formal double bond and one as a charged oxygen. The other substituent is an oxime group, attached through a carbon-nitrogen double bond with the nitrogen carrying a hydroxyl. The aromatic ring is flat and rigid, while the oxime linkage is largely planar and adds limited rotational freedom. The overall shape has a roughly two-fold, elongated symmetry along the ring axis. The hydroxyl group of the oxime can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the oxygen atoms of the nitro group and the oxime nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a stilbene-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a central carbon–carbon double bond, with the connecting alkene drawn in the trans (E) geometry. Each aromatic ring carries a single methyl group on the carbon directly adjacent to the vinyl linkage, placing the two methyl substituents at the ortho positions of their respective rings. This arrangement gives the molecule a two-fold symmetric shape, with the rings and the alkene roughly coplanar and the bridge fairly rigid. Neither ring contains heteroatoms, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is an acyclic, open-chain polyene built on a long linear carbon skeleton with no rings at all. It contains a long run of conjugated carbon-carbon double bonds, interrupted near one end by a fully saturated segment, and its methyl groups are placed at regular intervals along the chain. Most of the double bonds have defined geometry, giving the chain an extended, rod-like shape that is flexible along its single bonds but largely stiff across its conjugated core. A tertiary alcohol sits at one terminus, which is the only hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor present, while the remaining hydrocarbon portion is non-polar and offers no hydrogen-bonding capability. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the methyl substitution is not identical at the two ends.

This molecule is an acyclic oxime carbamate built around a short aliphatic chain. A methylcarbamoyl group (N-methyl amide linked through its carbonyl to an oxygen) is bonded to the oxygen of an oxime, whose C=N double bond carries an E-configured geometry. The imine carbon is attached to a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups and a methylsulfonyl substituent, giving a sterically congested, branched arrangement. There are no ring systems, so the scaffold is fully flexible apart from the planar carbamate and oxime segments. The molecule has an NH donor and several acceptor oxygens from the carbonyl, the N-O linkage, and the sulfonyl group.

The molecule is built around a five-membered pyrazole ring, which carries a methyl group on one carbon, an N-methyl group on a ring nitrogen, and a phenoxy group (an oxygen linking to a benzene ring) on the adjacent carbon. A carbon on the next ring position bears an oxime-ether chain, a C=N-O unit whose oxygen connects to a benzyl group. That benzyl ring is para-substituted with a tert-butyl ester. The two terminal benzene rings are unsubstituted aside from their attachments and are free to rotate, giving the molecule considerable conformational flexibility. The ester and ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a para-nitrophenyl ring attached to a hydrazone linkage (a C=N bond connecting to an N-nitrogen). That nitrogen also carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring and a phosphoramide center, which bears two aziridine rings, each a three-membered saturated heterocycle fused to nothing else but bonded through its nitrogen. The nitro group sits para to the hydrazone carbon, giving the aromatic ring a strongly electron-poor, linear substitution pattern. The C=N double bond introduces a rigid, planar segment, while the N-N and N-P bonds allow more rotational freedom. There is no internal symmetry because the two aromatic rings and the two aziridines differ in their attachments. The nitro oxygens and the phosphoryl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all nitrogens are fully substituted.

This molecule is built on a hydantoin core, a five-membered ring containing two carbonyl groups and two nitrogens, with the 5-position bearing two phenyl rings, so it has a quaternary carbon at the ring junction. The ring is non-aromatic and fairly rigid, while the two phenyl groups are attached to the same carbon and project in opposite directions, giving a propeller-like arrangement. Attached to one ring nitrogen is an N-CH2-O linkage that connects to a butanoate ester, a flexible four-carbon acyl chain. The structure contains two amide-type carbonyls and an ester carbonyl, and the remaining ring N-H provides one hydrogen-bond donor, with the carbonyl oxygens serving as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a 2-methylpropanoic acid unit, where a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups is attached to a carboxylic acid group and to a nitrogen of a benzotriazole-type heterocycle.
