The heterocycle is a 1,2,3-triazole ring fused to a benzene ring, giving a planar bicyclic aromatic system with a benzo-fused five-membered triazole. The substitution is at one nitrogen of the triazole, so the bulky gem-dimethyl carboxylic acid branch projects out from the flat aromatic core. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the triazole nitrogens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid, whereas the single bond to the quaternary carbon allows some rotational freedom in the side chain.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Four of the six ring positions carry chlorine atoms, and one carries a methyl group, so the ring is heavily substituted with a pattern of one methyl and four halogens around the periphery and two remaining positions bearing hydrogen. The structure has no stereocenters and only a low degree of conformational freedom, since the methyl group is the sole rotatable element attached to the rigid aromatic core. Because the substitution pattern is asymmetric, the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry axis. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors in the conventional sense, as the chlorines are weak halogen-type acceptors and the rest of the framework is hydrocarbon.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing a single ester group, which links through a carbonyl carbon to an oxygen-bridged two-carbon chain ending in an amide. The aromatic ring is monosubstituted and unfused, so it is planar and rigid, while the glycolate-type linker between the ester and the amide is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds. The amide nitrogen is fully substituted, carrying an ethyl group and a methyl group, so it has no N–H donor. Overall the molecule contains two carbonyl oxygens and one additional ether-type oxygen that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but it has no hydrogen-bond donors. It lacks any internal symmetry because the two ends of the chain differ.

The molecule is built around a five-membered isoxazolone-type ring, containing an oxygen and a nitrogen atom adjacent to each other, with a carbonyl group on the ring carbon next to the oxygen. A methyl group is attached to the ring carbon that is double-bonded to nitrogen. The ring's other carbon bears an exocyclic hydrazone-like linkage, C=N-NH, which connects to a phenyl ring. That phenyl ring carries a chlorine atom on the position adjacent to the point of attachment, giving an ortho-substitution pattern. The conjugated system is largely planar, which gives the molecule considerable rigidity, with only the single bonds to the methyl group and the chlorophenyl unit permitting rotation. The N-H donor and the carbonyl and ring oxygen and nitrogen acceptors give it hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One side bears a three-carbon chain ending in an acetate ester, so the ester oxygen links the propyl chain to an acetyl group. The other side carries a primary sulfonamide, a sulfur atom bonded to two oxygens and an NH2 group. The aromatic core is flat and rigid, while the propyl linker and ester add conformational flexibility. The ester carbonyl and its ether oxygen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the sulfonamide offers both donor NH2 hydrogens and acceptor sulfonyl oxygens. The overall arrangement has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the para-disubstituted ring.

The molecule is built on a central nitrogen-nitrogen linkage bearing two benzoyl-type acyl groups and a tert-butyl group on one nitrogen, making it an acyl hydrazide scaffold. One carbonyl is attached to a para-methoxyphenyl ring, while the other is attached to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the two aromatic rings are not symmetrically equivalent. The bulky tert-butyl group on the nitrogen adds steric hindrance and restricts rotation around the adjacent bonds, giving the molecule a moderately rigid, non-planar shape. The two amide-type carbonyl oxygens and the methoxy oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydrazide NH provides one hydrogen-bond donor site.

The molecule is an anthraquinone-type tricyclic scaffold: two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring that carries two carbonyl groups at the 9 and 10 positions, making it a planar, rigid aromatic-diketone framework. A primary aminomethyl group (–CH2–NH2) is attached to one of the outer benzene rings, adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution is asymmetric and the two outer rings are not equivalent. The core is largely flat and conjugated, with limited conformational flexibility apart from rotation of the aminomethyl side chain. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the primary amine provides two N–H groups that can serve as hydrogen-bond donors and a lone pair that can also accept hydrogen bonds.

This molecule is a symmetric polyene-linked bis-epoxide, with the two halves related by a mirror-like arrangement across a long conjugated central chain. Each terminus carries a spiro-fused epoxide on a substituted cyclohexane ring, where the epoxide and the six-membered carbocycle share a single quaternary carbon. Each cyclohexane ring bears gem-dimethyl groups, an additional methyl on the epoxide carbon, and a secondary hydroxyl group that serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The central backbone is an extended chain of alternating carbon-carbon double bonds with methyl branches along its length, giving it a rigid, rod-like, and largely planar conjugated character. Overall, the molecule is highly elongated and conformationally constrained at its ends, with the epoxide-cyclohexane units providing defined three-dimensional bulk.

The molecule is built on a six-membered piperidine-type ring that contains an imide arrangement, with a ring carbonyl and an adjacent exocyclic carbonyl flanking a nitrogen that bears a 2-phenylethyl substituent. A 2-methylbutanoyl amide group is attached at the ring carbon adjacent to the imide, giving an NH amide that can donate one hydrogen bond and accept another through its carbonyl oxygen. The phenyl ring is a simple unsubstituted benzene connected through a flexible two-carbon linker, so that portion adds conformational freedom. The core ring is largely saturated and not symmetric, and the stereocentres on the ring and side chain make the overall shape non-planar. Several carbonyl oxygens provide multiple hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while only the amide N–H serves as a donor.

This molecule is a secosteroid built on a fused polycyclic scaffold with a conjugated triene linking two ring systems. One ring system is a hydrindane-type bicyclic core bearing an angular methyl group and a branched eight-carbon side chain ending in an isopropyl terminus, which is flexible. The other ring is a cyclohexane-type ring carrying an exocyclic methylene group and two secondary hydroxyl substituents at positions 1 and 3, giving it hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability. The molecule has no symmetry, and its diene and triene segments impart partial rigidity while the saturated side chain and ring CH2 units remain flexible.

This molecule is a diethyl ester built on a straight, unbranched chain of ten carbons, with a carboxylate ester group at each end. Each ester consists of a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to an ethoxy group, so the structure is symmetric about the midpoint of the central methylene chain. There are no rings, ring fusions, or aromatic rings, and no substituents branch off the chain. The backbone is highly flexible, with freely rotating single bonds throughout. Each ester contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on an indolin-2-one (oxindole) core, with the five-membered lactam ring fused to a benzene ring. The nitrogen of the lactam carries an acetyl group, making it an N-acyl amide. The C3 position of the oxindole is a quaternary stereocenter bearing both a hydroxyl group and a benzofuran-3-yl ring, which is itself a fused bicyclic system of a furan and a benzene ring. Because of this tetrahedral C3 center, the two ring systems are held out of plane with one another, which gives the molecule a rigid, non-planar three-dimensional shape. The hydroxyl group and the lactam carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, while the acetyl carbonyl and the furan oxygen provide additional acceptor capability.

The molecule is a bicyclic fused system: a five-membered ring containing a succinimide-like imide (two carbonyls flanking a nitrogen) is fused through a shared carbon-carbon bond to a cyclopentene ring. The imide nitrogen bears an unsubstituted phenyl ring, and a second phenyl ring is attached to the alkene carbon of the cyclopentene. Two quaternary sp3 bridgehead-type carbons each carry a chlorine atom, giving a rigid, cage-like framework with defined stereochemistry at both ring-fusion centers. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis, since the two phenyl groups sit in different chemical environments. It offers no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two imide carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered carbocycle, a cyclopentanone ring, with a ketone carbonyl at one ring carbon. Two carbons of the ring each carry a three-carbon chain that terminates in a carboxylic acid, so the two chains are attached at the positions flanking the ketone on one side and at the adjacent position across it, forming a 2,5-disubstituted cyclopentanone pattern. The ring is saturated apart from the ketone, so it is conformationally flexible at its methylene carbons, while the two stereogenic ring carbons fix the relative arrangement of the side chains. Both terminal carboxylic acids are strong hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the ketone oxygen adds an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor site.

The molecule is a bridged polycyclic scaffold built around a bicyclo[2.2.2]octadiene core fused to a benzene ring, giving a rigid three-dimensional framework. A methyl ester group and a benzoyl (phenyl ketone) group sit on adjacent carbons of a cyclic alkene, which is conjugated with the ester and ketone. Two phenyl rings are present: one fused into the polycycle and one pendant on the ketone, so the overall shape is asymmetric. The two stereocenters lock the ring system into a fixed conformation with limited flexibility. The ester and ketone carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered tetrahydropyran ring containing one oxygen atom, which serves as the core scaffold. The ring carries a ketone at one carbon adjacent to the oxygen-bearing carbons, and it is substituted with two methyl groups and two para-chlorophenyl rings attached at the carbons flanking the ring oxygen, giving a 2,6-diaryl arrangement. The stereocenters are defined, so the substituents adopt a specific spatial orientation that is largely fixed by the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring oxygen and ketone oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central two-carbon chain linking two aromatic systems through an ether oxygen, giving it a flexible, non-fused skeleton with several stereocenters. One terminus is a 3,5-dimethoxy-4-hydroxyphenyl ring, which carries a secondary benzylic alcohol, while the other is a 2,6-dimethoxyphenyl ring attached through an aryl ether linkage. Both benzene rings are unfused and bear methoxy groups, with the phenolic hydroxyl adding an additional substituent on the first ring. The side chain also contains a primary hydroxymethyl group, so the molecule has multiple hydroxyl donors alongside many ether and phenolic oxygen acceptors.

This molecule is a tricyclic cage hydrocarbon framework, the adamantane skeleton, built from three fused cyclohexane-type rings that share a rigid, diamond-like arrangement of carbon atoms. It bears a single hydroxyl group attached to one of the bridgehead carbons, which gives it a hydrogen-bond donor and a weak acceptor at oxygen. The cage is highly symmetric, with the hydroxyl group sitting on a bridgehead position, and its rings are locked in place with almost no conformational flexibility. Aside from the one hydroxyl, the rest of the scaffold consists of saturated carbons and methylene bridges, so its polar character is limited to that single site.

This molecule is built from two para-hydroxylated benzene rings joined by a three-carbon chain containing a ketone and a carbon-carbon double bond, giving an extended, conjugated enone scaffold. The ring on the left side of the ketone is attached directly to the carbonyl carbon, while the ring on the right is attached through the alkene, so the two aromatic systems are connected through a planar, rigid linker. Each benzene ring carries a single hydroxyl group at the position opposite its point of attachment, producing a symmetric-looking para-substitution pattern on both rings, though the overall molecule is not perfectly symmetric because the carbonyl and alkene sit between them. The two phenolic hydroxyls act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The conjugated framework is largely flat and conformationally restricted.

The molecule is built on a pyrrole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen. That nitrogen bears a para-fluorophenyl group, so an aryl ring is attached directly to the heterocycle through a single bond. The pyrrole ring carries two methyl substituents and a formyl (aldehyde) group, giving a trisubstituted pattern with the aldehyde positioned adjacent to one methyl group. The structure is fairly rigid, with the two aromatic rings able to twist relative to one another about the connecting bond. The aldehyde oxygen and the fluorine act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a central five-membered pyrrole ring, with nitrogen at position 1 bearing a para-tolyl group (a benzene ring carrying a methyl substituent opposite the point of attachment). The pyrrole carries methyl groups at the two carbons flanking the nitrogen, leaving one ring carbon unsubstituted apart from a formyl group (an aldehyde, CH=O) on the carbon two positions from nitrogen. The aromatic pyrrole and phenyl rings are connected by a single N–C bond, so they are not fused but can rotate relative to one another, giving the molecule moderate flexibility at that linkage. The overall substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry axis that maps the molecule onto itself. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all N–H or O–H groups are absent, while the aldehyde oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the pyrrole nitrogen contributes only weakly as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent ether substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic core. One oxygen links to an allyl group (a terminal vinyl-bearing CH2 unit), while the other links to a three-carbon chain containing a secondary alcohol and a secondary amine bearing an isopropyl group. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, while the side chains are flexible, with several rotatable single bonds. The secondary hydroxyl and the secondary amine N–H each act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the two ether oxygens, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the amine nitrogen serve as acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry element because the two ortho side chains differ.

This molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a six-membered pyrimidine-dione ring is joined to a five-membered imidazole ring, forming a purine-type core. The six-membered ring carries two carbonyl groups (C=O) and two N-methyl substituents on its nitrogens, one on each side of the ring junction. The five-membered ring contains one N-H, which gives it a hydrogen-bond donor site, while the unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen and the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fused system is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the methyl groups are the only flexible elements. The molecule lacks any symmetry that would make its two methylated nitrogens equivalent, because the N-H sits on the imidazole ring rather than being mirrored elsewhere.

The molecule is built around a para-tolyl ring attached to a central sp3 carbon that carries a tertiary amide (N-tert-butyl) and a tertiary N-methyl amide nitrogen bearing a butanoyl chain. That chain runs three methylenes before reaching a large polycyclic aromatic system: a pyrene-type four-ring fused framework with extensive ring fusion and flat, delocalized rings. The two amide carbonyls act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the single secondary amide N-H serves as the only hydrogen-bond donor. The aliphatic linker and branched tert-butyl group give moderate conformational flexibility, whereas the polyaromatic core is rigid and planar, and the overall molecule lacks any internal symmetry.
